A public health agency possesses a district-level shapefile listing COVID-19 incidence counts, population totals, and several dated, inconsistently-named columns. The city planning office has already merged a flood-risk indicator into its building footprint shapefile, so every feature now carries the name of the flood zone it intersects (or NULL if none). A regional planning office is readying parcel shapefiles for statewide hydrological modelling. A regional planning office is compiling a municipal boundary dataset, supplied as a .shp file from the provincial geoportal, for a public web map. While preparing a lightweight lookup layer for our mobile data-collection app, we have a municipal parcels shapefile that contains more than fifty attribute columns—ownership history, assessed values, zoning codes, and many others. A city logistics company maintains a point layer of parcel lockers, each storing the average daily number of incoming packages as an integer attribute. Tool: Distance matrix\nAlgorithm ID: qgi: In support of emergency response planning, the city maintains a .shp file with the coordinates of every fire station and another .shp file showing the locations of all high-rise buildings. A research team has a .shp file with time-stamped GPS positions recorded every minute from a scientific survey vessel operating along a coastal shelf. They need to turn these scattered positions into a single continuous track so they can visualise the exact route the ship followed and receive a simple text summary listing each leg’s compass direction and distance.

A marine research institute has collected a sequence of GPS recordings taken every 15 minutes from a tagged humpback whale during its spring migration. The recordings are stored in a shapefile that lists each position with a timestamp. The institute needs to transform these scattered positions into a single continuous track so it can visualize the whale’s exact route and generate a report that lists every leg of the journey with its compass direction and length.

A national park service has collected GPS coordinates of rare plant sightings along a proposed hiking route and would like to turn the recorded waypoints into a single, ordered trail line so rangers can follow the exact path during future monitoring visits. The sightings are stored in a .shp file that includes a timestamp field indicating the sequence in which the plants were observed.

A wildlife research team has collected a series of GPS waypoints (.shp file) taken every 30 minutes while following a mountain gorilla group during a one-day behavioural observation. They need to turn these waypoints into a single continuous track so they can later measure the total distance the group travelled and visualise the exact route taken through the forest.

A survey crew has collected a sequence of GPS coordinates saved as a shapefile that marks every bend and valve location along a newly installed water main. The engineering office needs the ordered set of these field points turned into a single continuous line that traces the exact pipe run as it was laid in the ground, so the as-built alignment can be plotted on the municipal map and checked against the design drawings.

A utility company has delivered a .shp file of GPS-surveyed manhole and valve locations recorded while installing a new water main. They need the field notes turned into a single continuous centre-line of the laid pipe so the as-built drawing can be compared with the approved route. The points carry a sequence number captured on site and should be joined in that order to show the exact path the pipeline follows.

An archive of digitised daily campsite coordinates from the 1893 expedition journal is stored as a .shp file. The research team needs to transform these campsite locations into a single continuous trail so the exact sequence of travel taken by the explorers can be drawn on a map for the upcoming centenary publication.

A historian has collected GPS waypoints recorded during a 19th-century surveying expedition, stored as a .shp file with a date-time field. The goal is to reconstruct the exact route taken by the explorers so that it can be drawn on period maps for publication.

A hiking club has recorded a series of GPS waypoints marking key viewpoints and rest stops along an intended trail and now needs these individual points turned into a single continuous route file so the leader can load it onto a handheld navigator and guide the group in the correct sequence.

A local hiking club has recorded a series of geocache locations as a sequence of waypoints in a .gpx file gathered during weekend walks. They would like to turn these scattered waypoint stops into a single, ordered trail so newcomers can follow the same treasure-hunt path on their GPS devices.

Our drone flight records are stored as a GPX file containing the continuous track points captured during each survey. To simplify post-processing and sharing with field teams, we need to transform these dense track points into a single, ordered route that summarizes the flown path.

To facilitate regulatory review, a drone operator has a flight log saved as a .gpx file that holds only discrete recorded positions. The requirement is to transform those scattered points into a single, ordered flight trace so reviewers can see the exact route taken during the mission.
Tool: Random points in polygons\nAlgorit: To design a practical soil-sampling scheme for a precision-agriculture study, we have a farm boundary map saved as a shapefile that outlines every field parcel. We would like to place, inside each parcel, a set number of individual sampling locations that are at least 30 m apart so that the collected cores do not overlap. The generated list of sampling positions should carry the parcel name from the map so scouts can navigate to the correct field.

To support variable-rate fertilizer application, the agronomy team needs a set of candidate sampling locations inside every field mapped as a shapefile of farm parcels. Each parcel should receive 12 candidate points, and the points must be at least 30 m apart so that a single soil core does not influence its neighbor. The resulting list of coordinates will be loaded into the GPS handhelds for the autumn soil-campaign.

A wildlife research team has a shapefile of forest habitat patches across the study region and needs to position 30 vegetation-survey transect starting points inside each patch.  The patch boundaries must be respected, and the starting locations should carry the patch ID and dominant tree-species code from the original habitat file.

To support a Monte-Carlo site-suitability study for a residential development, we have a municipal shapefile containing every land-parcel polygon inside the city limits. We need to create a set of candidate sampling locations—specifically, one hypothetical house footprint placed at random inside each parcel—so that later rounds of the analysis can test how often these random sites meet suitability criteria. The resulting point file should carry the parcel ID and zoning code from the original polygons so each random site remains linked to its parent property.

Following the recent earthquake, the emergency assessment team has received a shapefile of city-block polygons from the municipal planning department. To speed up field inspections, they need to create a set of exact building-inspection locations inside each block so that every neighbourhood is represented. The team would like 15 inspection sites per block, with no two sites closer than 20 m so that inspectors do not revisit the same cluster of buildings. Preference is to keep the block name and ID attached to each site for easy reference during the survey.

To support rapid damage assessment after the recent earthquake, the disaster-response team has a shapefile showing the outlines of every city block in the affected district. They need a set of randomly chosen building-locations inside each block—ten per block—to send field crews for detailed inspections, while ensuring the selected sites within any single block are at least 15 m apart so inspectors do not interfere with one another. The resulting list of inspection points should carry the block ID and name so crews know which block each site belongs to.

A forestry department needs to check regeneration success inside a recently replanted watershed.  They have a shapefile showing the outer boundary of the replanted area and want to mark 50 inspection sites that are spread out so no two are closer than 100 m; the chosen spots will be visited by field crews to record seedling counts.

For a Monte-Carlo exposure analysis in a flood-prone urban district, we have a city neighbourhood boundary file (.shp) that outlines the built-up area selected for the study. We would like to place 5 000 hypothetical building locations evenly scattered across that neighbourhood, ensuring no two locations are closer than 15 m so they represent distinct properties. The resulting set of points will be used as candidate exposure units for subsequent risk simulations.

A wildlife research team is preparing species-distribution models for a rare orchid recorded only within the boundaries of a protected forest reserve.  They have a shapefile outlining the reserve’s perimeter and need to generate 200 plausible survey locations across the entire reserve for field teams to check for the plant, ensuring that no two suggested spots are closer than 250 m so observers do not duplicate effort.

A regional wildlife research team is comparing observed nest-site locations to what would be expected by chance across the province’s study landscape. They possess a single rectangular administrative boundary shapefile (.shp) that exactly delimits the forested parks of interest and need 5 000 point locations scattered randomly inside that rectangle, with no two points closer than 250 m, to serve as a null-distribution for their statistical tests.

We have a region-wide vegetation survey that will use drone imagery to monitor plant health inside 2,300 forest stands mapped as irregular polygons (GeoPackage). To plan the flight paths efficiently, we need to identify one exact location that lies inside each stand so the drone can centre its photo capture on that spot. Provide a single set of coordinates for every stand that is guaranteed to fall within its boundary.

A forestry survey team has a set of irregularly shaped stand polygons (delivered as a shapefile) delineating different forest compartments. They need a single, representative location inside each compartment where they can place a sampling plot for ground-truth measurements, ensuring the point lies safely within the actual forest area rather than on an edge or outside.

The city’s planning department has a shapefile of every building footprint in the historic quarter and needs a single dot placed inside each outline so that the resultant dots can serve as the official address-anchor locations for geocoding new business licences.

A coastal-planning team has a shoreline polygon layer (.shp) that outlines the landward edge of the intertidal zone and needs a single representative location placed inside every land parcel so these spots can later seed Thiessen polygons that stay strictly on land. Provide a new point layer with one guaranteed on-shore position for each shoreline polygon.

To support a habitat classification study, we have a shapefile of forest stand polygons delineated from aerial photography. Each polygon carries attributes such as dominant species and canopy density. We need a set of point locations that are guaranteed to fall inside every stand so that we can later extract spectral values from a Landsat raster at exactly these spots, ensuring no measurement is taken from an adjacent stand or from the border itself.

The city parks department has digitised every public green-space as a separate parcel in a shapefile and now needs to generate 50 potential interview-spot locations inside each park so that field teams can choose among them while ensuring no two spots are closer than 10 m; a new file with these candidate points is required.

Following the earthquake, the city’s building-permit department has a GeoPackage of every city block polygon and needs to generate 20 random inspection sites inside each block so that field teams can be dispatched quickly; the list of locations must keep any two sites at least 10 m apart to avoid duplicate visits.

After the recent earthquake, the city’s building department has a shapefile that delineates inspection sectors (each outlined as a polygon). Tool: Select by location\nAlgorithm ID:: The city planning office needs to identify all privately owned land parcels that fall inside the newly proposed flood-risk zone so that owners can be notified of possible future building restrictions.  A current parcel map in .shp format and the official flood-zone boundary drawn by the environmental agency (also a .shp file) are on hand.  The task is to single out every parcel that lies within, touches, or crosses the flood-zone outline.

A regional planning office has received a draft flood-risk map (polygon shapefile) from the environmental agency and needs to identify every land-parcel (parcel shapefile) that lies inside or touches the proposed flood zone so that affected owners can be notified. The task is to single out these parcels from the full cadastral dataset.

A state environmental agency has compiled two shapefiles from recent field surveys: one holding the locations of active drinking-water wells and another mapping polygons of soil zones where contaminants exceed safety thresholds. The agency needs to identify which wells are situated inside these risky zones so it can issue immediate advisory notices and schedule further testing.

A regional health office has a .shp file of private water wells and a second .shp file showing areas where soil contamination has been confirmed. They need to identify every well that falls inside one of these contaminated zones so they can schedule immediate water-quality testing and notify the owners.

The regional planning office needs to identify every road segment that lies entirely inside the county boundary to update its maintenance schedule. We have a shapefile of all road centerlines and another shapefile showing the single county polygon. Please pick out only those road segments that are completely inside the county border.

A national park is conducting a wildlife monitoring study using GPS-tagged animal sighting records stored in a .shp file. The park also has a .shp file that outlines all designated protected zones within its boundaries. To focus patrol and conservation efforts on areas that receive less formal protection, the study needs to single out every sighting that lies completely outside these protected zones.

A wildlife research team has a point shapefile recording GPS locations of rare bird sightings across the state and a polygon shapefile of all designated nature reserves. They need to single out every sighting that lies completely outside any reserve so they can prioritise these locations for new conservation proposals.

A regional planning office has a .shp file of candidate sites for new recreation facilities and wishes to narrow the list to only those parcels that touch the river network shown in another .shp file.

I have previously identified a set of potential wetland restoration sites stored in a .shp file. Now I need to refine this list by keeping only those sites that share a boundary with the river network contained in a separate .shp file.

A regional planning office needs to compile a list of road segments that a county can reasonably claim responsibility for maintaining. The office holds a shapefile of the county boundary and another shapefile showing every road segment in the wider region. The intention is to highlight the road segments whose position is inside the county boundary, acknowledging that segments merely touching the border will also be captured, and any further exclusion of these border-touching segments will be handled separately after this initial identification.

A regional forestry office is updating its wildfire risk map for the eastern slopes of the Sierra Nevada. They need to isolate only the campgrounds that fall inside that rectangle so subsequent fuel-load surveys can focus on those specific facilities.

The regional planning office has received a shapefile containing the planned path of a new bypass road and a second shapefile holding every land-parcel polygon in the county. We would like to isolate and list only those parcels that the planned road will pass through, so that owners can be contacted for right-of-way negotiations.

A national nature-conservation programme needs to identify which wetland polygons from a country-wide .shp file fall inside the boundaries of officially designated protected areas supplied as a second .shp file, so that field surveys can be prioritised for those wetlands that already enjoy legal protection.

It wishes to receive a new list that retains only those stations that touch a county border.

A regional planning office maintains a PostgreSQL database of land-parcel polygons. To speed up future map-drawing and spatial searches, they need to refresh the spatial index that supports the parcel layer so that every geometry is correctly registered for quick retrieval.

The open-data portal team has received a parcel-boundary .shp file from the county assessor’s office that fails to load in the public viewer; the file is missing its supporting index. We need to restore the dataset so it can be published on the portal for residents to view and download property outlines.
Tool: SpatiaLite execute SQL (registered: As part of a nationwide property-tax update, the cadastral office needs to repeatedly look up which land parcels fall inside each city’s planning zones. They have the parcel map as a GeoPackage layer and the planning-zone map as another GeoPackage layer. To keep the nightly batch join process from slowing down, they first want to prepare the parcel layer so that spatial searches run faster.

The Geological Survey has compiled a province-wide lithology map in a SpatiaLite database.  After field verification, geologists need to standardise the rock-type names currently stored in the ‘lith_unit’ column so that every occurrence of ‘Grano-diorite’ is changed to ‘Granodiorite’ and every ‘Basaltic Andesite’ is shortened to ‘Andesite’.  Only the database file itself is to be updated; no new map layer is required.

We have a SpatiaLite database (.sqlite) that stores geochemical sample locations together with their laboratory results. To support the QA/QC review, we need to flag every record whose copper value exceeds 500 ppm and mark it as “high Cu” in a dedicated text column so that reviewers can immediately spot anomalous samples.

Within a SpatiaLite database holding geochemical sample points, identify and flag any records whose coordinates place them outside the permitted national territory so that the QA/QC team can later review or exclude suspect entries.

A mineral exploration company maintains a SpatiaLite database holding existing tenement polygons and needs to mark every parcel that is currently under application so that field teams do not accidentally peg overlapping ground. Using the database file supplied by the tenements office, update the status column of each polygon record to ‘Application Pending’ wherever the existing value is null.

A geologist has a SpatiaLite database (.sqlite) holding collar coordinates for historic drill-holes and a separate table with the most recent digital elevation model (DEM) values stored as point heights. To check whether the collar elevations recorded in the field still match the current ground surface, they need to run an update that replaces the old collar height in the drill-hole table with the latest elevation taken from the DEM points that fall at the same x,y location.

Within a SpatiaLite database that stores both the collar coordinates of exploration drill-holes and a recent high-resolution DEM, update the collar elevation field so that each hole is assigned the ground-surface height recorded in the DEM at the same horizontal position.

We have a county-wide geological map stored as a SpatiaLite database (.sqlite) that was compiled during a recent survey. Each polygon currently carries provisional age descriptions such as “Cretaceous undifferentiated.” The state board now requires every polygon to instead show the formal stratigraphic formation name (e.g., “Pierre Shale,” “Niobrara Formation”). Provide a SpatiaLite-ready SQL statement that will update the formation-name field in-place for every polygon record so the map can be submitted without creating an additional layer. The statement must include the complete mapping logic (CASE block or reference table join) that translates each provisional age description into the correct formation name.

A mineral exploration team keeps a SpatiaLite database (.sqlite) that records every granted lease and cadastral boundary.  Before heading into the field they need a list of the 1-minute by 1-minute grid squares that remain unclaimed inside the boundary of a new licence application already stored in the same database.  Using only the information already held in the database, produce a table that flags each relevant grid square identifier as either occupied or still open, so crews can focus staking efforts on the open squares without leaving the SQL environment.

A web service that streams live bus positions needs to update each vehicle’s geometry in the database so that the point snaps to the nearest road segment whenever a new GPS reading arrives; the database already stores the bus table and the road centerline table and is refreshed every 30 seconds.

To accelerate downstream tracing queries on the city’s water-supply pipe layer (a GeoPackage of mains and laterals), the utility team needs the ID column that stores each pipe’s unique identifier to be internally organised so searches by that number respond instantly during network isolation exercises.

A live-updating GeoPackage of traffic incidents for the metro area is refreshed every 30 seconds. Dashboards and public feeds must filter instantly by incident type, severity, and road name, yet queries on any one of these fields are lagging. To ensure rapid retrieval, we need to prepare the layer so that searches on incident type, on severity, and on road name each respond without delay.

After this spring’s street-tree survey, the city’s urban-forest officer needs to update every tree record in the SpatiaLite database that is attached to the QGIS project: change the ‘condition’ field from ‘unknown’ to ‘good’ for every oak that was revisited and rated healthy, and set the ‘survey_year’ to 2024 for those same rows. The database already contains the point layer with all city trees and the two fields to be updated.

After completing a street-tree inventory field survey, the city’s urban forestry team has loaded the updated measurements into the same SpatiaLite database that already holds the existing tree layer. They now need to refresh the ‘last_surveyed’, ‘height_m’, and ‘condition’ values for every tree record so that the digital map reflects the latest site information without creating an additional file.

A municipal roads department maintains a SpatiaLite database holding a layer of all city streets. To update their road inventory, they need to calculate the exact length of every street segment and store those values in a dedicated column so that each record permanently records its own length in metres.

A city planning department maintains a SpatiaLite database of all road segments in the municipality. They need to update each record in the roads table so that it permanently stores the measured length of that segment, expressed in metres, to support annual maintenance budgeting and pavement-wear modelling.

Within the SpatiaLite database that already holds our watershed sub-basin polygons, update every record so that the geometry column stores a single merged shape for each major basin identifier, preparing the layer for catchment-wide management without adding any new files.

To support a watershed-consolidation project, we have a SpatiaLite database holding sub-catchment polygons with a ‘basin_id’ field. The task is to merge (dissolve) all polygons that share the same basin identifier so that the database itself stores a single, consolidated boundary for each management unit, ready for downstream planning without creating any extra file.

A city planning office maintains a SpatiaLite database of cadastral parcels and needs to ensure that no two parcel polygons overlap anywhere in the jurisdiction. Using the existing database that holds the parcel layer, run a query to identify any pairs of parcels whose geometries intersect and list their unique parcel IDs so staff can investigate and correct the boundary errors.

I have a SpatiaLite database that stores parcel polygons for the county. To ensure the cadastral map remains reliable, I need to locate any lots that overlap one another so the assessor’s office can correct the geometry.

A city planning office maintains a SpatiaLite database of street trees whose coordinates are still in a local projected system. To display the layer correctly in the municipal web-map portal, the office needs to update every geometry so that each tree’s location is expressed in WGS84 longitude and latitude, performing the conversion directly inside the existing database table.

A university research team maintains a SpatiaLite database of tree-survey points collected with handheld GPS units. Before publishing the dataset for an interactive web map, the coordinates must be re-projected in-place from the local UTM zone to WGS 84 so the locations align correctly with online basemaps.
Tool: Keep N biggest parts\nAlgorithm ID: A regional land-registry office has digitised cadastral parcels for a rural county; each parcel record is stored as a single polygon feature that may contain several non-contiguous field fragments. For crop-subsidy audits, the office needs to retain only the two largest contiguous pieces of land within every parcel, discarding any smaller scattered fragments. The dataset is provided as a polygon shapefile named county_parcels.shp.

A regional conservation group is mapping priority wetland habitats across the province; they have received a single GeoPackage file that stores every wetland complex as one large multi-part polygon per watershed. Each complex often contains dozens of scattered ponds and marshes, yet only the largest few patches within each watershed are ecologically significant for waterfowl breeding. The group needs a new file that retains just the three biggest wetland fragments from every watershed polygon so the final habitat layer is clear enough for field-team navigation and reporting.

Within a province-wide wetland inventory provided as a shapefile of complex wetland polygons, each wetland complex often contains many scattered pond-like areas. For a simplified habitat overview map that will be printed at 1:250 000, we need to retain only the three most extensive open-water or marsh sections of every complex, discarding the smaller fragments so the final layer remains legible and uncluttered.

A coastal engineering team has mapped rockfall polygons along a cliffed shoreline from recent drone imagery saved as a shapefile; each mapped area can consist of several detached fragments. To focus the stability assessment on the most significant detachments, the team needs a new map that keeps only the largest fragment of every recorded rockfall zone, discarding smaller splinters.

A national geological survey is consolidating the digital cadastre of historical mining tenements. Each tenement licence was originally digitised as a single multi-part polygon that may now contain dozens of disconnected parcels scattered across the landscape. We have received a shapefile holding these multi-part tenement outlines and need to retain only the three largest contiguous land blocks for every licence so that the cleaned dataset reflects the principal areas of interest for current resource planning.

We have a single .shp file that stores every agricultural plot of one large cooperative as one enormous multi-piece polygon. For the cooperative’s annual area report we must isolate the three largest contiguous plots within that single feature, ignoring all smaller fragments. Please create a new layer that retains only those three biggest pieces.

A coastal engineering team has grouped drone-mapped rockfall fragments into cliff-segment multipolygons stored in a single shapefile; each segment now appears as one feature containing many detached-block polygons. To focus stabilization work on the most significant hazards, they need a new version of this file that retains only the three largest intact rockfall areas within every cliff segment, omitting all smaller pieces.

A regional emergency-response team has received a single GeoPackage layer in which every flooded building outline is stored as one multipart polygon grouping all detected roof fragments belonging to that structure. Because the extraction process also captured small rooftop debris and adjacent sheds, each building’s footprint now contains several disconnected pieces. To focus recovery resources on the main structure, the team needs a refined layer that retains only the single largest fragment for every building, discarding the smaller ancillary parts.

After the recent flood, a municipal GIS team received a shapefile in which each building footprint is stored as a single multipolygon feature that may contain several disconnected fragments. They need to discard all but the largest intact section of every building so the resulting map clearly shows only the main structure for rapid damage assessment.

A mining company’s tenement registry holds one consolidated polygon layer (.shp) where each tenement block is already stored as a single record enclosing every licence patch belonging to that block. For corporate reporting they need to discard the smaller fragments and retain only the two most extensive contiguous licence areas within each of these blocks.
Tool: Fuzzify raster (power membership)\: As part of a regional planning study, we have a GeoTIFF showing slope gradients across the metropolitan fringe.  We need to translate these slope values into a gradual suitability scale ranging from 0 (unsuitable) to 1 (fully suitable) for future urban expansion, treating steeper areas as progressively less preferable.  The resulting layer will feed directly into a broader land-use suitability model.

A regional water board is preparing a groundwater-vulnerability screening map to guide well-protection policies. They have a GeoTIFF showing nitrate concentration (mg/L) across the aquifer and need to translate these concentration values into a scale that indicates how strongly each location belongs to the category "high risk." Locations with concentrations below 5 mg/L should be considered not at risk (score 0), those above 40 mg/L fully at risk (score 1), and intermediate values should transition smoothly so that the certainty of being "at risk" rises more rapidly once concentrations exceed the lower threshold. The resulting layer will serve as the risk input for subsequent composite vulnerability modelling.

A regional agricultural agency has produced a raster map of soil nutrient index values across its farmland. To support the next phase of a crop-yield forecasting study, planners need to convert the nutrient index scores into a graduated suitability scale that expresses how strongly each location belongs to the category of “high-fertility” land. The agency can supply the nutrient index raster (GeoTIFF, band 1). They wish to set 40 as the lower reference score (below which suitability is nil) and 80 as the upper reference score (above which suitability is full), with a moderate transition curve controlled by a power of 2, producing a new map in which every pixel carries a value between 0 and 1 indicating its degree of membership in the high-fertility class.

A regional agronomy unit has compiled a 30-metre resolution GeoTIFF of soil-nutrient indices across the province. They need to translate these continuous index values into gradual suitability scores that rise smoothly from clearly unsuitable to fully suitable, so the resulting map can be used to rank parcels for fertility-based subsidy allocation. The team will supply the nutrient-index raster and specify the index thresholds that mark the bottom and top of the transition range, along with a curve factor that controls how quickly the scores increase between those limits.

As part of a regional wildlife habitat quality indexing project, we have a GeoTIFF of continuous canopy-density values derived from satellite imagery covering the entire forest reserve.  We need to translate these raw density numbers into a smooth gradation of habitat favourability, where the lowest densities indicate no favourability, the highest densities indicate full favourability, and intermediate densities are expressed on a gentle increasing curve rather than a sharp step, so the resulting surface can be combined with other ecological indicators in later stages of the assessment.

A national park authority has received a 30 m Landsat-derived burn-severity index raster covering the area affected by last summer’s wildfire. To prioritise post-fire recovery actions, they need to translate the continuous index values into a graduated scale that expresses how strongly each pixel belongs to the category "severely burnt". The output should run from 0 (not burnt) to 1 (fully burnt) so that lightly scorched areas receive low scores and the most intensely burnt zones receive high scores, allowing managers to visualise and rank treatment areas without abrupt class breaks.

Following the recent wildfire, we have a GeoTIFF showing the differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR) for the affected forest. To prepare a suitability layer for rapid reseeding efforts, we need to translate the raw dNBR values into a scale that indicates how strongly each pixel belongs to the category "severely burnt ground"—from not at all (0) to fully (1)—so that areas with the highest burn intensity receive priority treatment.

A regional water board is screening for zones where the depth-to-water table is shallow enough to pose a high contamination risk. They have a GeoTIFF from last year’s survey giving the depth to groundwater in metres and need a new map that shows, for every pixel, how strongly the area belongs to the “deep water table” category, expressed on a scale from 0 (definitely not deep) to 1 (definitely deep). Areas shallower than 3 m should score 0, areas deeper than 15 m should score 1, and the transition in between should follow a smoothly rising curve rather than a sharp step.

A regional conservation authority is preparing a habitat-quality map for a keystone songbird species. It has a 10 m resolution GeoTIFF showing canopy-density values across the forested landscape, ranging from 0 (open ground) to 100 (closed canopy). The authority wishes to translate these densities into a gradual ‘suitability score’ from 0 (unsuitable) to 1 (fully suitable), recognising that suitability should be nil below 40 % canopy, then climb smoothly but with accelerating favourability up to 100 %. Provide a layer in which each pixel carries such a score.
Tool: Combine style databases\nAlgorithm: The Geological Survey of Canada, the U.S. Geological Survey, and Mexico’s Servicio Geológico Mexicano each maintain their own QGIS style files (.xml) containing the colours, line patterns, and text labels used for their national geological maps. To produce a seamless harmonized North American geological map, we need to merge all three style collections into a single shared file that preserves every colour scheme, symbol set, and label format while automatically renaming any identically named items so nothing is lost or overwritten.

Three geological survey teams have each produced their own QGIS style libraries (saved as .xml files) for the recently harmonized 1:50 000 bedrock map. To ensure the final printed map has a single, consistent appearance, we need to merge all the separate libraries—containing point symbols for fossils, color ramps for stratigraphic ages, text formats for formation labels, and label settings for fault names—into one unified style file that can be shared across the cooperating agencies.

The national mapping agency has accumulated several separate QGIS style libraries (.xml files) from its regional offices, each containing unique symbols, color ramps, text formats, and label settings for topographic maps. To ensure consistent cartography across the country, the agency needs to merge all these individual style libraries into one unified master library that retains every distinct style element under a single file.

To support the creation of a unified enterprise map series, several departmental teams have independently prepared .xml files that hold their preferred point, line and polygon appearances, colour gradients for elevation layers, text fonts for titles, and label placements for parcel numbers. We need to gather all these styling preferences into one single .xml file so that every future map across the organisation uses the same symbols, colour ramps, fonts and label rules without manual re-creation.

After three years of collaborative field-mapping across six university teams, each group has produced its own set of map symbols, colour gradients, text fonts, and label styles stored in separate .xml files. To prepare a unified atlas for publication, we need to gather all these scattered visual elements into a single, non-redundant style collection that can be shared with every partner.

Our collaborative field-mapping project has accumulated three separate QGIS style collections—one from each mapping team—containing symbols, color ramps, text formats, and label settings used for different habitat and land-use layers. To prepare a unified atlas, we need to merge these .xml style files into a single, non-redundant style library so every team can apply the same visual standards without duplicating or losing any custom symbols or palettes.

A provincial archive is digitising a 1930s topographic map series and has received separate .xml style libraries from three regional offices, each containing period-correct symbols, colour palettes, label fonts, and hill-shading ramps. To ensure a consistent appearance across the entire historical set, the archive needs to merge these individual libraries into one master style file that keeps every unique cartographic element while avoiding name clashes.

For the Historical map series re-styling project we have accumulated several separate .xml files that hold the custom colours, line symbols, label fonts, and legend graphics used across different atlas sheets. To ensure every forthcoming sheet follows the same visual standards, we need to merge these scattered style collections into one master reference file that the whole team can share.

The regional open-data portal has accumulated four separate .xml style collections—one for transport maps, one for land-cover charts, one for demographic atlases, and one for emergency plans—each maintained by a different working group. To simplify public access and guarantee consistent symbology across all future releases, the portal team needs to merge these four collections into a single, authoritative .xml style file that contains every symbol, colour gradient, text style, and label arrangement used in the repository.

The regional open-data portal curates separate style collections for transport, land-cover and demographic map series (each stored as an .xml file). To simplify distribution, these need to be merged into one consolidated style library that contains all symbols, colour ramps and label settings currently spread across the three files, without losing any items.
Tool: Mean coordinate(s)\nAlgorithm ID:: A municipal planning office has a .shp file with census-block polygons for the city, each holding a population count. They would like a single point marking the population-weighted "middle" of the city so they can site a new central library where it is easiest for most residents to reach.

A municipal planning department has a shapefile of residential parcels, each with a field recording the number of residents. They need a single location that best represents the population-weighted heart of the city so future public facilities can be sited where they are most accessible to people.

A wildlife research team has collected a .shp file of GPS collar locations recorded for several elephant herds across the savanna. Each point carries a herd identifier. They need to identify the central meeting point for every herd so that rangers can plan efficient patrol routes around these core areas.

A wildlife research team has compiled a point shapefile of GPS locations recorded for each elephant herd in the Amboseli ecosystem over the past year. They need to determine the single most representative location for every herd’s range so that patrol teams can be dispatched efficiently. Provide a new point layer showing the average position for each herd, using the herd identifier stored in the attribute table.

A nationwide wholesaler keeps a geopackage of all active retail outlets, each tagged with its annual sales volume. To redesign five sales territories so every representative travels roughly the same total business weight, the planning team needs the geographic balance point for the outlets assigned to each territory; these central locations will serve as the candidate hubs from which the reps operate.

In the aftermath of a coastal storm, an emergency-management team has received a .shp file that records every private building converted into a temporary shelter across the affected district. Each record carries a field noting the number of people currently housed. The planners need a single location map that pinpoints the average position of all shelters, weighted by the number of occupants, so they can decide the most accessible spot for setting up a central supply hub.

After the recent earthquake, we have a .shp file showing the locations of all damaged houses in the affected district. Each record includes a field indicating the number of displaced occupants. We need to identify the single most representative location that best balances the distribution of displaced people so that a temporary shelter can be placed as centrally as possible.

A regional archaeological survey has produced a shapefile of pottery scatter locations recorded across the valley. Each find spot carries a field indicating the ceramic phase (Early, Middle, Late). To help infer the probable core areas of occupation for each phase, please create a single representative location that best summarises the geographic centre of all pottery finds belonging to the same phase.

A regional survey has produced a .shp file of recorded pottery scatters across the valley. To infer the likely core area of an Iron-Age settlement, we need a single representative location that best summarises the spatial distribution of all finds, weighted by the recorded sherd counts in the ‘sherds’ column of the attribute table.

A regional sales director has already redrawn the five sales territories and now holds a .shp file of last year’s customer locations together with the annual revenue each customer generated and the territory code assigned to each account. To give every sales team a single geographic reference that reflects where the bulk of their revenue is concentrated, the director needs a representative point for each territory that is pulled toward the high-value customers within it.

A municipality is updating its address database to support a new emergency-response dispatch system. It has a shapefile of building footprints and needs to replace each footprint with a single dot placed at the mathematical center of the roof so that every address can be represented by one location for quick map display and routing.

A municipal planning office has a shapefile of city parks and would like to derive a single representative point for each park so that labels can be placed without ambiguity on the web map.  Provide a new layer that replaces every park outline with a point placed at its visual center.

To support regional planning, we have a shapefile of municipal boundaries covering the study area and need to obtain a single representative location for each municipality so the statistics office can attach census tables to these points.

The regional statistics office has received a shapefile of 2023 census blocks covering the entire province and needs a single representative location for each block to attach population-weighted survey responses; they require a corresponding point dataset that carries the same block identifiers so the survey weights can be joined without altering the original polygons.

To support a regional population-weighting study, a planner has received a .shp file of census district polygons covering the province. The planner needs a single representative location for each district so that population counts can be paired with coordinates for downstream modelling.

To support a parcel-to-address geocoding quality-assurance project, a city planning office has received a shapefile with parcel polygons covering the entire municipality. They need to generate a single representative location point for every parcel so these points can later be matched against the official address database for accuracy checks.

The county addressing office has received a parcel polygon layer (.shp) from the assessor. To verify that every parcel has a correctly assigned address point, they need a single representative location for each parcel so they can compare it against the official address point file. Produce a new point layer that places one point at the mathematical center of every parcel polygon, carrying over all parcel identifiers.

The state’s Department of Natural Resources is updating its wetland inventory and needs a single representative location for every multi-part wetland polygon recorded in their statewide .shp file so that field crews can navigate directly to the approximate center of each site for rapid ground-truthing.

A district planning team has received a shapefile with the boundaries of all 42 local health-clinic service areas. To help place a single summary marker for each area on the new accessibility web-map, they need a companion file that contains one representative point for every service-area polygon, carrying the same name and capacity attributes as the original areas.

The district planning office has a .shp file showing the outline of each of the 42 school-catchment zones. They need a single location point for every zone so they can feed these into a routing engine that calculates travel times to the nearest health clinic. Provide a new layer that gives one representative point for each zone, carrying across the zone name and enrolment figures.

A regional retail-chain analyst has a set of store trade-area polygons (delivered as a shapefile) that were drawn by hand around each outlet. She needs a single representative location for every trade-area so she can feed these simplified points into a distance-based customer-origin model. The goal is to obtain one point per polygon that best summarises its geographic centre, preserving the original store information attached to each shape.

A regional retail chain wants to identify the best representative location within each of its store trade-area polygons (provided as a .shp file from the marketing department) so that head-office planners can pin a single “store point” on the map for every catchment, keeping all existing store attributes attached to these new points.
Tool: Rasterize (vector to raster)\nAlgo: To support a land-cover classification project, we have a shapefile delineating forest stands across the study region. The modelling workflow requires these stand boundaries to be represented as a pixel grid so they can serve as a training mask. Please convert the stand-polygon shapefile into a raster image where each pixel records the presence or absence of a forest stand, using 10 m ground spacing for the output grid.

To support the creation of a land-cover classification mask, we have a GeoPackage file holding polygon boundaries for different vegetation types across the study region. We need to turn these mapped vegetation zones into a grid-based image so that every cell carries the vegetation-class value, enabling the mask to align pixel-by-pixel with upcoming satellite-derived classifications.

To prepare a distance-to-feature model for predicting wildfire risk across a national forest, we have a GeoPackage file holding mapped firebreak lines surveyed this season. We need to turn these linear barriers into a continuous grid so every 30 m pixel records whether a firebreak is present, providing the base layer for subsequent proximity calculations.

A regional planning team is developing a distance-to-feature model that requires every road segment in a statewide .shp file to be represented as a continuous grid so that proximity surfaces can be generated.  Provide a 10 m-resolution raster image in which each cell that intersects a road carries the road’s identifier, while all other cells remain empty.

To support a regional population-density surface project, we have received a shapefile of census-block polygons each carrying a population count field. The aim is to turn this set of polygons into a grid of small square cells so that every cell carries the population value of the block in which it falls, providing the basis for later density calculations.

A national statistics office needs to produce a 100-metre-resolution population-density grid for policy planning.  They possess a country-wide shapefile of census enumeration areas, each polygon carrying the official population count for 2023.  The goal is to turn these polygon boundaries and counts into a continuous raster surface so that every 100 m cell carries the population figure assigned to its enclosing census unit.

The national emergency-management agency has received a shapefile of landslide-hazard polygons mapped by field teams after recent storms. To feed these zones into the existing nationwide wildfire-risk raster model, the agency needs the hazard outlines turned into a matching-resolution grid so the two layers can be combined in subsequent analysis. A 30 m cell size is desired to align with the risk model.

A provincial emergency-management office has received a shapefile of landslide-hazard polygons mapped by field geologists. To feed the regional risk-assessment model, the office needs to turn these polygon outlines into a continuous grid image that indicates, for every 10 m on the ground, whether the cell lies inside a hazardous zone or not.

A digitised set of 1890s parish boundaries held as a .shp file needs to be turned into a simple black-and-white image layer so it can be stretched and warped onto a scanned historical map during georeferencing.  The image must have the same pixel size as the scan (0.5 m ground units) so the two layers align perfectly for on-screen rubbersheeting.

The image must have the same pixel size as the scan (0.5 m ground units) so the two layers align perfectly for on-screen rubbersheeting.

Our regional climate-monitoring project has produced an 8-bit NDVI-anomaly map in GeoTIFF format that displays vegetation stress through a predefined color palette. To share the imagery with stakeholders who lack specialized GIS viewers, we need to transform the paletted layer into a standard full-color (24-bit RGB) picture that can be opened in any common image software while preserving the exact visual appearance of the anomalies.

For an upcoming vegetation-survey campaign across the coastal plain, we have a QGIS project displaying land-cover polygons, roads, and survey grids styled for field navigation. We need a high-resolution image of the current map view that crews can load into any handheld GPS unit as a backdrop, covering the entire 20 km × 15 km study area at 1 m on the ground per pixel, with the ocean margin included and no background color so it overlays cleanly on device base-maps.

The planning team has a QGIS project containing vector layers for roads, rivers, and administrative boundaries that together show the full survey region. To share a lightweight overview with field crews who will only use standard picture viewers, we need to turn the current map display into a high-resolution image that covers the entire study area (approximately 150 km × 100 km) with each pixel representing 50 m on the ground, and with a transparent background so it can be overlaid on other imagery later.

To support a coastal erosion study comparing historic shoreline positions, we need to turn the current on-screen map—showing modern roads, buildings, and the shoreline at 1:5,000 scale—into a high-resolution image that can be overlaid on scanned 1950s aerial photographs. The area of interest is the 5 km stretch of coast between the two lighthouse landmarks visible in the view, and the image should capture every detail down to 1 m on the ground so that corresponding features can be matched visually.

For a coastal erosion study comparing historic shoreline positions, we have a digital map displaying the 1950s coastline, roads, and buildings at 1:5 000 scale. We need to turn this on-screen map into a high-resolution image covering the same area so it can be aligned with modern aerial photos for change detection.

For a land-cover accuracy-assessment project, we have a QGIS map canvas showing the final classified land-cover layer alongside the reference sample points. We need to turn this exact on-screen view into a high-resolution raster image that can be printed in the survey report. The image should cover the entire study area (currently displayed extent), use 1 m on the ground for each pixel, keep a transparent background so the page layout stays clean, and be saved as a GeoTIFF ready for publication.

Our regional land-cover accuracy assessment requires a high-resolution image of the current map canvas showing the classified land-cover polygons and the overlaid sampling grid so that field teams can print it for on-screen validation.  Please produce a GeoTIFF image covering the entire study area (supplied as the current map extent) with a pixel size of 50 m on the ground and a transparent background, ready for inclusion in the validation atlas.

To support the creation of a hillshade backdrop for a 3-D subsurface model, we need a high-resolution image that captures the current topographic view of the project area. A ready-to-use .qgz project containing styled elevation contours, drainage lines, and shaded relief layers is available. The task is to produce a single raster picture covering the full survey extent (provided as a bounding box) at 1 m ground-pixel resolution, with a transparent background, so it can be draped beneath the model without obscuring underlying geological sections.

As part of a 3-D seismic model, we have a GeoPackage of vertical cross-section sticks (polyline geometries) whose surface intercepts were surveyed in a local mine grid shifted 500 m east and 300 m north of the national coordinate system. The seismic cross-section lines provided by the contractor arrive in a local mine grid that is 500 m east and 300 m north off the official national grid used for the 3-D model. Shift each stick so it aligns with the national coordinates before loading it into the visualization environment.

A coastal management team has received a shoreline polygon from the regional mapping agency as a shapefile and needs to explore the effect of shifting the entire feature 30 metres west and 20 metres north, approximating a landward retreat movement for the 2050 scenario.

A regional energy consultancy has received a shapefile of household locations reported as sensitive to shadow-flicker from a proposed wind farm. Tool: Hypsometric curves\nAlgorithm ID:: A regional geomorphology team is comparing ten neighbouring drainage basins to see how their relief differs. They would like a set of simple tables that list, for every basin, how much land area sits at each 100-metre band of elevation, so they can plot and contrast the overall height–area profiles of the basins.

The team needs a set of simple tables that record, for every 100 m of elevation, how much land area (in percent) lies at or below that height within each tract, so the contrasting elevation signatures of the glacial and fluvial landscapes can be plotted and compared.

A geomorphology study is comparing the elevation structure of two adjacent mountain valleys suspected to have been carved by different processes—one by glaciers, the other by a river. We have a 10 m resolution elevation grid covering the entire region and a shapefile that outlines each valley floor and its enclosing watershed divide. The team needs a set of simple tables that record, for every 100 m height band within each valley polygon, how much land surface lies at or below that elevation. These tables will be saved in a project folder so the researchers can plot and contrast the two cumulative elevation profiles to decide which valley bears the typical signature of glacial erosion and which reflects fluvial incision.

As part of a regional study on erosion patterns across the southern Appalachian Highlands, we have a 30-m resolution elevation grid supplied by the USGS and a county boundary map in shapefile format from the state GIS portal. We need to obtain, for every county, a table that shows how much land lies below, within, and above successive 100-m elevation bands so that differences in upland versus lowland distribution can be compared and used as a proxy for long-term erosion intensity.

A regional geomorphology study needs to compare how land height is distributed inside each of 42 mountain catchments across the western plateau. The team has a 30 m resolution elevation grid covering the entire region and a shapefile outlining every catchment boundary. They would like to obtain a separate summary table for every catchment that lists, at 100 m height intervals, how much land surface lies at or below each level so that differences in landscape form can be related to measured erosion rates.

As part of a pre-feasibility study for dam siting, we have a 10 m resolution elevation grid covering the entire upland catchment and a shapefile outlining ten candidate reservoir basins. We need to obtain, for each basin, a table that records how much land surface lies below successive 50 m elevation bands so that we can quickly judge which basins offer the largest storage potential and most favourable depth-area relationships.

To support a comparative tectonic-geomorphology investigation of adjacent drainage basins, we possess a 10 m resolution elevation raster for the region and a shapefile that traces every basin’s outer rim. The study calls for a cumulative tally of land surface within successive 100 m height steps for each basin, saved as individual tables in a project folder, so that contrasting uplift signatures can be read directly from the curves without further calculation.

As part of a regional dam-siting study we have a 30 m resolution elevation grid covering the entire catchment and a shapefile that outlines ten candidate reservoir basins. We need a summary, for each basin, of how much land lies at every 100 m height band so that we can quickly judge which sites offer the largest storage potential; the figures should be delivered as simple spreadsheets, one file per basin.

To support stratification of forest habitats by elevation bands across a protected mountain range, we have a 30-metre elevation grid (.tif) supplied by the national mapping agency and a district boundary map (.shp) showing individual forest compartments provided by the park authority. We need a cumulative tally for each compartment that records how much land area lies below every 100-metre height step so that ecologists can derive the exact area within successive bands through simple subtraction and assign field-survey sites to the correct elevation class.

A regional forestry department is comparing the overall elevation signatures of two neighbouring mountain catchments to understand why one supports a rare endemic tree while the other does not. They possess a 30 m resolution elevation grid for the province and a shapefile outlining each catchment. The goal is to produce, for every catchment, a summary table listing the cumulative land area that lies below successive 50 m elevation steps, so planners can visually contrast the hypsometric profiles and infer which altitude zones dominate each landscape.
Tool: Filter by geometry type\nAlgorithm: A municipal GIS unit has received a single .gpkg file from a regional survey contractor that supposedly holds every streetlight, kerb line and park polygon for the upcoming asset-management audit. Before loading the dataset into the asset register, the team needs to split the contents so that each category—lights (as dots), kerbs (as lines) and parks (as outlines)—can be checked separately for completeness and accuracy.

We have been sent a single vector file that supposedly contains all road centrelines, traffic-light points and administrative boundaries for the county, but the supplier warned it is jumbled together. We need to separate the file so that each kind of shape—lines for roads, dots for lights and outlines for boundaries—lands in its own layer so we can run quality checks on each theme independently.

During the annual update of the city-wide emergency-response asset inventory, the GIS unit has received a single .gpkg file from field teams that supposedly contains every new hydrant, access road, and supply depot surveyed this quarter. Before the dataset can be forwarded to the separate point, line, and polygon tracking systems, the mixed-content file needs to be split so that each emergency asset type is handled by the appropriate database table.

During the emergency-response asset inventory, we have a single geospatial file that mixes together the locations of hospitals (points), the road segments cleared for ambulance use (lines), and the zones designated as evacuation areas (polygons). We need to separate these different kinds of features so that each category can be listed and reviewed independently.

A conservation team has compiled a single GeoPackage holding all elements of the regional habitat network—animal sighting records, river corridors, and protected forest blocks—into one layer. To prepare separate inputs for a connectivity model that treats points, lines, and areas differently, they need the contents split so that each kind of shape goes to its own file.

A conservation team studying habitat connectivity across a mixed-use landscape has received a single GeoPackage file from a regional data portal that bundles all wildlife-related elements—such as recorded animal sightings (as dots), movement corridors (as lines), and habitat patches (as shapes). To prepare separate inputs for their connectivity model, they need to split this combined file so that each kind of feature—dots, lines, and shapes—is available on its own.

A national mapping agency is preparing a 1:250,000 topographic series from its master database that contains mixed road, river, settlement and administrative elements delivered as a single GeoPackage. To support separate generalisation workflows for each graphic layer, the dataset must first be divided so that every feature is grouped according to whether it represents a point location (e.g., spot heights, lighthouses), a line course (e.g., roads, rivers) or an area shape (e.g., built-up zones, forests).

While preparing a set of 1:100 000 topographic tiles for press, the publisher has supplied a single GeoPackage holding every feature collected during field surveys—some are towns (dots), some are roads (lines), and others are woodland patches (areas). To let each cartographic team handle only the kind of shape it is responsible for redrawing, we need to split the file so that all point records go to one group, all line records to another, and all area records to a third.

For a nationwide park-mapping project we have received a single GeoPackage file holding every recreational facility recorded by the field teams. Inside that file some features are simple dots marking ranger posts, others are drawn as paths for trails, and the rest are outlined shapes for campgrounds and picnic areas. To prepare separate national-level maps for each kind of facility we first need to split the contents so that all points go to one file, all lines to another, and all polygons to a third, keeping every attribute intact.

A cartography unit preparing a regional atlas has received a single GeoPackage file from the provincial survey office that contains every planned update for the upcoming edition—some entries mark new mountain peaks as dots, others show revised river courses as lines, and several record updated administrative areas as coloured shapes. The unit needs to split this one file into three separate files so that the peak dots can be styled with summit symbols, the river lines with tapered blue strokes, and the area shapes with political-boundary hatching without manual sorting.
Tool: Orthogonalize\nAlgorithm ID: nativ: A municipal planning office has received a .shp file of building footprints digitized from aerial imagery. Because the original tracing followed roof edges rather than true wall positions, many outlines appear slightly skewed or have angles that are almost—but not exactly—90 degrees. The office needs a cleaned-up version in which every corner is either perfectly square or straight so the layer can serve as the authoritative reference for property setbacks and tax parcel alignment.

A city planning office has received a .shp file of building footprints digitised from recent aerial imagery. The outlines exhibit small angular deviations that make them unsuitable for the cadastral map, which requires every wall to meet at precise right angles. The office needs the geometries adjusted so that every corner becomes either exactly 90° or perfectly straight, while keeping the overall shape and position of each footprint unchanged.

A municipal land-registry office has received a .shp file of parcel boundaries digitised from historical scans; many lot lines that should be straight or meet at neat corners instead appear slightly crooked or misaligned. The office needs these parcels tidied so every boundary edge is either perfectly straight or forms a clean right angle, while still following the original corners as closely as possible.

The cadastral office is digitising a set of parcel boundaries from scanned historical maps saved as a polygon shapefile. Many of the originally rectangular plots now appear slightly skewed or have rounded corners due to scanning artefacts. We need to tidy these geometries so that every corner is either perfectly square or a straight line segment, while still following the same general outline, so the cleaned layer can be used for official area calculations without manual redrawing.

A university library is digitising its historical floor plans stored as .shp files containing room outlines and corridors. To prepare the plans for use in a campus navigation app, the library needs the room and corridor boundaries adjusted so every corner is either exactly square or perfectly straight, while keeping the overall layout unchanged.

A property management firm is digitising scanned floor-plans of a 1970s office block to create a clean set of CAD-ready drawings. The source file is a polygon shapefile exported from a manual tracing exercise that contains room outlines, yet the traced walls meet at odd angles instead of the expected square corners. The firm needs the room shapes adjusted so every corner is either perfectly square or perfectly straight, while keeping the overall room layout intact, and is willing to accept minor vertex shifts to achieve this.

The city planning department has received a .shp file of newly digitised road-centre lines drawn from aerial imagery. Many segments appear slightly skewed and lack the exact right-angle or straight-line junctions required for the official street grid. We need to tidy these centre-lines so every intersection and bend is either perfectly square or perfectly straight, while keeping the file format unchanged.

The city planning office has received a .shp file of road center-lines drawn during a rapid field survey. Because the sketches were made free-hand, many intersections and straight segments appear slightly crooked. We need to tidy these lines so every junction forms a proper square corner and every long stretch is perfectly straight, while keeping the survey’s original route unchanged.

A municipal mapping office has received a GeoPackage containing building footprints digitised from recent orthophotos. Because the original tracing followed pixel edges, many walls that should appear straight now show slight stair-step distortions. The office needs a cleaned version in which every façade and corner is adjusted to form proper right angles and straight lines, ready for inclusion in the official cadastral dataset.

A municipality is digitising building footprints from a recent orthophoto mosaic delivered as a GeoPackage. Many of the traced polygons appear slightly skewed, with corners that should be square showing small deviations. To prepare the layer for official cadastral use, the planning office needs to tidy these shapes so that every corner is either a right angle or a straight wall line, while keeping the original file structure intact.
Tool: Set Z value\nAlgorithm ID: native:: Within the 3-D Flood-Inundation Mapping study, we have a shapefile holding the river cross-section polylines surveyed by boat. We need to attach the constant water-level reading of 142.3 m above sea level to every vertex of those cross-sections so that they can be displayed and examined in three dimensions.

Within the 3-D Flood-Inundation Mapping project we have a shapefile of river cross-section polylines surveyed without elevation information; please prepare these lines so that every vertex carries the constant water-surface elevation of 112.5 m above sea level, enabling later extrusion into flood-depth prisms.

A survey team has collected GPS point coordinates for a set of coastal benchmarks and now needs to assign each point a uniform height of 2.5 m above the local vertical datum so the dataset can be used in a sea-level-rise visualization. A geodetic survey team has collected a set of GPS-surveyed ground-control points stored in a shapefile.
