Please update the point file so that each location is tagged with this single height value.

The regional water authority holds a 3-D polyline shapefile of pressurized mains whose vertices currently carry only horizontal coordinates; to prepare a simplified flat schematic for internal review they need every vertex to be assigned the constant elevation 185 m above sea level so the network can be exported as a true 3-D layer while remaining geometrically level.

The city’s utility department has a two-dimensional shapefile of its multi-storey pipe network, but the vertical positions are missing. They need to treat every pipe segment as if it lies at a single, uniform depth below ground—specifically 1.5 m—so the dataset can be handed to a contractor for flat-map planning. Please take the existing line layer and assign this constant depth to all features, producing a new file that records the 1.5 m elevation for every pipe.

To support the creation of pseudo-3D borehole stick plots, a geologist has a .shp file of vertical borehole traces (simple two-point lines from collar to total depth) that currently carry only x,y coordinates. She needs every vertex of every line to be given the same constant elevation value of –999 so that downstream software will treat the holes as truly vertical sticks when it extrudes them. Provide a new copy of the file with this uniform depth marker attached to all geometry.

A coastal engineering group holds a .shp file of planned breakwater alignments drawn as two-dimensional polylines. To include these structures in a harbour wave-agitation model that expects all features to carry a vertical reference, every vertex along each alignment must be given a constant height of 2 m above mean sea level so the geometry can be read as a fully three-dimensional feature.

A county geologist has received a .shp file of two-point vertical borehole sticks prepared earlier from flat traces; every stick already has its collar vertex fixed at the surveyed ground level of 250 m above sea level, while the lower vertex still carries an outdated placeholder elevation of 0 m. To harmonise the dataset with current vertical reference standards, the geologist needs to overwrite every vertex in the layer—both collar and base alike—with a single consistent elevation of 250 m above sea level, yielding a level set of lines that can later be combined with down-hole depth attributes for pseudo-3D visualisation.
Tool: Equal to frequency\nAlgorithm ID:: To support an inter-agency effort to harmonise land-cover maps produced by different institutions over the same region, we have a set of annual 10 m resolution GeoTIFF rasters (2018-2022) that record the dominant land-cover class for every pixel, plus a reference 2020 land-cover map from the national mapping agency. We need to create a new raster that shows, for every pixel, how many of the yearly maps agree exactly with the national 2020 class, so that areas of high and low consistency can be identified for further field checking.

After separate land-cover classifications were produced for the same region from three different Landsat scenes (each supplied as single-band GeoTIFFs with identical extent and cell size), the research team needs to know, for every pixel, how many of the three maps assign it to exactly the same class as the 2023 reference classification layer (also a single-band GeoTIFF).  The result should be a new map that simply counts, at each location, the number of times the other maps match the 2023 layer.

A climatology team has a set of daily snow-cover rasters (.tif) for the same region spanning ten winters and a reference raster that marks the elevation zones of that region. They need to know, for every pixel, how many of those daily rasters show exactly the same snow-cover value as the corresponding pixel in the elevation-zone reference raster, so they can identify which elevation zones most consistently match the snow-cover pattern across the decade.

A regional climate study needs to know, for every pixel in a reference snow-cover map from winter 2020 (supplied as a single-band GeoTIFF), how many of the ten yearly snow-cover maps (also single-band GeoTIFFs, 2011–2020) show exactly the same snow presence value. The result should be a new map that records this count for each location, ignoring any gaps in the reference layer.

To verify the reliability of our flood-inundation forecast, we have one reference water-depth raster from a trusted hydraulic model and a set of five scenario rasters produced by different rapid-simulation engines for the same event. We need a single map that shows, cell by cell, how many of the five scenario rasters match the reference depth exactly, so we can quickly identify areas where the forecasts consistently agree or disagree.

To verify the reliability of our flood-inundation model, we have a reference GeoTIFF showing the officially surveyed maximum flood extent from 2022 and a set of 20 yearly GeoTIFFs (2003–2022) that record, for each pixel, whether the model predicted inundation in that year. We need a new raster that tells us, for every cell, how many of the 20 yearly predictions exactly match the surveyed 2022 flood layer, so we can see how often the model agreed with the observed extent.

A regional climate-monitoring programme has produced a set of annual land-cover rasters (GeoTIFFs) spanning 2000–2020 and a reference map of predicted stable forest for 2020. The team needs to know, for every pixel, how many of the yearly maps show the same land-cover class as the 2020 stable-forest layer. This will be used to create a reliability mask indicating where the forest has remained consistently classified across the two decades.

As part of a climate-change impact study covering the Alpine foothills, we have a 30-year series of annual land-cover rasters (.tif) and a reference land-cover map for the baseline year 1990 (also .tif). We need to know, for every pixel, how many of the subsequent yearly maps keep exactly the same land-cover class as the baseline map, so that we can create a reliability mask showing where the classification has remained unchanged over time.

We are comparing how often different climate models agree on the same temperature anomaly value for each location across Europe. Twenty annual temperature-anomaly rasters (GeoTIFF, 1 km resolution, from the CMIP6 archive) have been gathered for the year 2020, and a reference map of observed 2020 anomalies (also GeoTIFF, 1 km) is available from the E-OBS gridded dataset. Produce a new European map that records, for every pixel, the count of model rasters whose anomaly value exactly matches the observed anomaly in that same pixel.

The regional climate office has compiled a set of 30 yearly GeoTIFF surfaces showing projected summer temperature anomalies (°C above the 1961-1990 baseline) from an ensemble of downscaled CMIP6 models.  They also hold a single reference GeoTIFF of the observed 2023 summer anomaly grid.  To see how often each model reproduces the 2023 pattern cell-by-cell, they need a new grid that records, for every pixel, the count of model years in which the projected anomaly value exactly matches the corresponding 2023 observed value.
Tool: Raster boolean OR\nAlgorithm ID: n: A regional wildlife authority has compiled three binary suitability masks—each stored as separate GeoTIFFs with 10 m pixels—indicating where water proximity, dense canopy, and low human disturbance are individually satisfied (value 1) or not (value 0) across a 50 km² mountain reserve. They need a single map that flags every location where at least one of these three favourable conditions is met, adopting the spatial details of an existing reference vegetation raster already covering the reserve, so they can quickly identify candidate areas for field surveys.

A regional conservation team has prepared a set of binary GeoTIFF layers (each pixel marked 1 for “present” or 0 for “absent”) showing where five different critical habitat factors—such as water within 500 m, dense canopy cover, low road density, gentle slopes, and protected status—occur across the province. They need to identify every place that satisfies at least one of these factors so that any such location can be considered potentially suitable for the target species. The output should be a single map that keeps the same cell size and boundaries as the existing provincial elevation raster already used in the office.

As part of a rapid flood-risk screening for the lower delta, we have three binary GeoTIFF layers—one marking zones where the 1-in-100-year water level is exceeded, another showing areas where ground elevation is below 2 m above mean sea level, and a third indicating places with high soil saturation—each stored as 1 (condition met) and 0 (condition not met). We need to produce a single map that highlights every location where at least one of these three risk factors is present, adopting the grid extent, cell size, and coordinate system of the regional elevation model already on file.

As part of a rapid flood-risk screening project, we have three binary GeoTIFF layers indicating where each of (a) low-lying areas, (b) high soil saturation, and (c) proximity to drainage channels exceed critical thresholds. We need to merge these separate hazard flags into a single map that shows every place where any one of these three conditions is present, so planners can immediately see the combined area that could be prone to flooding.

The geological survey team possesses three binary GeoTIFF layers—each marking areas where at least one key indicator for copper-gold mineralisation (magnetic high, potassium radiometric low, or iron-oxide spectral signature) is present. They need a single map that shows every location where any one or more of these indicators occurs, using the extent, resolution and coordinate system of the regional aeromagnetic grid already on file.

The geological survey team has prepared a set of binary GeoTIFF layers (1 = presence, 0 = absence) that mark favourable conditions for mineralisation derived from separate evidence themes—structural proximity, geochemical anomaly, and magnetic high response. Using one of these layers as the spatial template, we need to merge the evidence so that any location flagged as favourable in at least one theme is retained in a single prospective mask that will guide follow-up field work.

A regional climate-monitoring programme holds yearly GeoTIFF masks that mark pixels contaminated by cloud, cloud shadow, or snow across a mountain catchment. To prepare a single map showing every pixel that was affected by any of these disturbances during the five-year period, the team needs to combine the five binary masks so that a pixel is flagged if it was contaminated in at least one of the years. The output should match the extent, resolution, and coordinate system of the 2023 reference mask already used in the archive.

A regional climate-monitoring project has produced a set of GeoTIFF masks, each flagging cloud, shadow, or snow pixels as 1 and clear pixels as 0 across the same Landsat tile for successive dates. The project now needs a single combined mask that marks any pixel as contaminated (1) if it was flagged in at least one of the individual masks, so that only pixels consistently clear across all dates remain unflagged (0).

The city planning office has received a set of binary change-indicator GeoTIFFs produced from consecutive annual Landsat pairs (each pixel is 1 where built-up area appeared or disappeared that year, 0 otherwise). To quickly map every location that experienced urban change at least once during the five-year span, they need to merge these five rasters into a single layer that flags every pixel where change occurred in any year, adopting the extent and cell size of the 2023 layer.

The city planning department has a set of binary land-cover rasters (1 = built-up, 0 = non-built) for 2010, 2015 and 2020, all aligned to the same 10 m grid. To monitor rapid urban growth they need a single map that flags every pixel that became built-up in any of the three years so that subsequent field teams can focus on areas that experienced change at least once.

The state’s Department of Natural Resources is updating its wetland inventory and needs a single representative location for every multi-part wetland polygon recorded in their statewide .shp file so that field crews can navigate directly to the approximate center of each site for rapid ground-truthing.

To speed up later species-richness modelling, we need a companion layer that shows the smallest upright rectangle that can fully contain each patch, together with the width, height, area and perimeter of every such rectangle.

A national park authority has received a detailed .shp file that outlines every hiking trail and scenic viewpoint polygon across its reserves. To speed up the creation of printable visitor maps, they need a simplified rectangular outline drawn around each individual feature so that map labels can be placed neatly without tracing every bend of the trail or irregular edge of the viewpoint area.

To accelerate collision checks for a nationwide set of high-voltage power-line corridors stored as a single .shp file, we need to derive the smallest rectangular outline around each individual corridor so that preliminary overlap screenings with planned construction zones can be done using these simplified shapes instead of the original complex routes.

A maintenance team has a shapefile of high-voltage power-line corridors across the state and needs to know the smallest rectangular extent that encloses each individual corridor so they can quickly dispatch field crews to any section that might be hit by construction activity or storms. Provide a new layer that shows these tight-fitting rectangles and records their width, height, area, and perimeter for rapid reference during daily briefings.
Tool: Convert GPX feature type\nAlgorith: A hiking club has recorded a series of GPS waypoints marking key viewpoints and rest stops along an intended trail and now needs these individual points turned into a single continuous route file so the leader can load it onto a handheld navigator and guide the group in the correct sequence.

A hiking club has recorded a series of planned rest stops as waypoints in a .gpx file downloaded from their handheld GPS units; they now need these points turned into a single continuous suggested walking route so the trail leader can load it back onto the devices and follow it in sequence on the upcoming expedition.

A recreational geocaching club has collected a sequence of planned stops recorded as a GPX route file from their last field outing. They now need to turn that sequence into individual point markers so each waypoint can be loaded onto members’ handheld receivers as separate cache targets.

A local hiking club has recorded a series of geocache locations as a sequence of waypoints in a .gpx file gathered during weekend walks. They would like to turn these scattered waypoint stops into a single, ordered trail so newcomers can follow the same treasure-hunt path on their GPS devices.

Our drone flight records are stored as a GPX file containing the continuous track points captured during each survey. To simplify post-processing and sharing with field teams, we need to transform these dense track points into a single, ordered route that summarizes the flown path.

For the national search-and-rescue mission archive, we have a folder of .gpx files that were originally recorded as a sequence of individual position markers left by field teams during last winter’s alpine operations. We now need each file rewritten so that those scattered markers are turned into a single continuous trail that shows the exact path the teams walked, allowing incident reviewers to replay the route on standard mapping software.

The mountain-rescue archive holds a .gpx file that records every waypoint the helicopter crew marked while scanning the valley last month; we need to turn these scattered marker points into a single continuous flight path so the incident review board can replay the exact route taken during the search.

The race committee has recorded the intended buoy positions as a set of waypoints in a .gpx file provided by the committee boat’s handheld GPS. To prepare the official race chart, these individual positions need to be joined into a single continuous route that the mark-set boat can follow during setup.

A yacht club preparing for a weekend regatta has a GPX file of planned turning marks around the bay. To load these marks into the race-management tablet as a single continuous course, they need the individual waypoints turned into a route that can be followed in sequence.

To facilitate regulatory review, a drone operator has a flight log saved as a .gpx file that holds only discrete recorded positions. The requirement is to transform those scattered points into a single, ordered flight trace so reviewers can see the exact route taken during the mission.
Tool: Shortest path (point to point)\nAl: The city fire department needs to know the quickest driving route from Central Fire Station (provided as a single-point .shp file) to a large industrial complex on the city’s eastern edge (also supplied as a single-point .shp file). A street-centerline shapefile of the entire road network is available. The goal is to obtain the fastest possible path the engine company should follow during an emergency call.

The city’s emergency dispatch centre needs to determine the quickest driving route from the main fire station (provided as a single-point shapefile) to a reported high-rise fire (a second single-point shapefile) so that the first engine can reach the scene in the least travel time. The road network is available as a line shapefile showing all drivable streets with speed limits.

A municipal utility company needs to determine the quickest route for a repair crew to travel from the main depot to a reported leak on a residential street. The city’s road centerlines are held in a shapefile, and the depot and leak locations have each been recorded as single points in a separate file. The goal is to obtain a single line showing the fastest drivable path between these two locations so the crew can be dispatched immediately.

A city logistics company has a road-centerline shapefile of the downtown area and two GPS-tagged addresses stored as separate point shapefiles—one for the distribution depot and one for a priority customer. They need to identify the quickest driving route the delivery van should follow between the depot and the customer so dispatch can provide turn-by-turn directions and an accurate arrival-time estimate.

For the regional fiber-optic backbone project, the engineering team has a .shp file showing all existing roads and needs to identify the most direct physical route for laying new cable between the central switching station (a single point feature) and the planned suburban hub (another single point feature).

A municipal water utility holds a shapefile of all city pressurized mains and valves. Upon service-loss notification from 42 Maple Street, the operations team has already identified the nearest active valve and the customer’s meter as two separate point files. They now need the precise chain of mains the crew should traverse between these two points, favoring the path that involves the least total pipe length.

The city logistics division holds a .shp file of the urban street network and two single-point .shp files marking the Central Depot and the Riverside Distribution Hub. They need to identify the quickest driving route between the precise depot location and the hub location along the street lines.
Tool: Check validity\nAlgorithm ID: qgis: Before merging the municipal parcel map received from the county surveyor’s office with our local zoning shapefile, we need to verify that the parcel polygons are free of drawing mistakes such as dangling lines or self-crossing boundaries. The parcel layer is stored as a GeoPackage file named cadastral_parcels_2023.gpkg. Please examine every lot outline and tell us which ones are geometrically sound, which contain flaws, and provide a separate point list showing the exact spots where any problems occur.

We have received a municipal parcel map (.shp) digitised from old paper plans that will be used for a city-wide spatial join to attach updated tax records. Before proceeding, we need to verify that every lot outline is free of drawing mistakes such as self-crossing lines or missing corners so that the join results are reliable. Please examine the parcel layer and tell us which lots, if any, contain outline errors, where exactly those problems occur, and how many there are, so we can clean the map in advance.

As part of preparing a city-wide street-centreline dataset for turn-by-turn navigation, we have received a single .shp file holding all road segments supplied by the local surveying office. Before building the network we must be sure every line is clean; therefore we need a report that lists any stretches whose shapes are broken or self-crossing, pinpoints the exact spots where problems occur, and separates the good lines from the doubtful ones so the survey team can focus repairs only where necessary.

A cadastral authority has received a new GeoPackage file holding parcel boundaries digitised by external contractors. Before accepting the dataset for the official land-register, staff need to know whether any outlines are drawn incorrectly so they can be returned for correction. They therefore require a review that flags every plot outline with drawing mistakes, pinpoints the exact locations of those mistakes, and separates the clean plots from the questionable ones.

A municipality has received a freshly digitised set of parcel boundaries in shapefile format from a contracted survey team. Before these lots are accepted into the land-registry system, the planning office needs to confirm that every polygon boundary is correctly drawn and free of drawing mistakes such as dangling lines, self-crossing edges, or missing corners. The office therefore requires a report that lists each problematic lot, pinpoints the exact location of any flaw, and separately provides a clean set of parcels that can safely be used for legal purposes.

To ensure the reliability of the forthcoming catchment boundary map, the hydrology office has received a single .gpkg file holding the draft river network lines digitised from aerial photos.  They need to know which stretches have drawing problems such as loops or gaps so these can be corrected before the lines are used to trace watershed divides.

The national hydrological service has received a new set of river-basin polygons digitised from recent aerial imagery and now needs to confirm that every outline is free from drawing mistakes before the file is accepted into the official catchment atlas. Using the delivered .shp file of these freshly captured basin boundaries, please examine each polygon and provide separate lists of any outlines that contain gaps, overlaps, or other sketch errors, together with a note of exactly where each problem occurs so the field teams can return to the drawing and correct them.

As part of preparing a public-facing web map of city parks, we have received a shapefile of park boundaries from the Parks Department. Before the layer is uploaded to the online atlas, we need to be certain that every park polygon is free from drawing mistakes such as overlapping lines or missing corners so that the map displays correctly and users can rely on the boundaries shown. Please examine the file and provide separate lists of any parks whose outlines are problematic, pinpointing exactly where each issue occurs.

Before publishing a new cycling-routes layer on the city’s public web map, the GIS team wants to confirm that every line in the supplied .shp file is free from drawing mistakes that could confuse cyclists or break the online display. They need a report that lists any faulty routes, pinpoints exactly where each problem occurs, and separates the clean paths from the questionable ones so only reliable data go live.

To ready a municipal street dataset for traffic modelling we imported an OpenStreetMap GeoPackage of road centrelines. Before any further processing we must confirm that every individual line is geometrically sound—free of self-crossings, reversed segments, or other drawing flaws that would obstruct later editing. Please inspect the GeoPackage and report which lines are clean, which contain formal drawing errors, and the exact coordinates of each problem so our GIS editors can correct them before building the network.
Tool: Relief\nAlgorithm ID: qgis:relief\: To aid the delineation of hydrological catchments, we have a GeoTIFF elevation model of the region and need a visually intuitive map that shows height differences across the terrain so field teams can quickly identify ridgelines and valley floors while planning survey routes.

To support the creation of realistic 3-D scene textures for a regional landscape visualization project, we have a GeoTIFF of elevation measurements supplied by the national mapping agency. The goal is to turn this single-band height map into a smoothly shaded color image that clearly shows hills, valleys, and plains so it can serve as the base color layer for the final textured terrain model.

For a new 1:25 000 topographic map of the Pine Ridge uplands, a 1-metre cell-size elevation raster (.tif) supplied by the regional survey office will be used to produce an illumination layer that shows the shape of the land in natural-looking shadows and highlights; the cartographer prefers the software to pick the colour ranges automatically so the final hill-shade can be dropped straight into the map layout.

For a forthcoming ground-truthing season we have a 1-m resolution digital elevation model (GeoTIFF) of the survey valley. We would like a picture-like layer that shows the hills and valleys in natural-looking shadows and colours so field teams can quickly recognise landforms on their tablets while walking the terrain.

A ski-resort planning group has a high-resolution GeoTIFF showing ground heights across the mountain. They need a picture-like layer that depicts sunlit and shadowed slopes so that skiers can instantly see where the terrain looks gentle or steep on a piste map.

For a feasibility study of a new ski-resort area we have a 1-metre resolution elevation grid covering the candidate mountain valley. We would like to produce an easy-to-read hill-shade picture that clearly shows every ridge, spur and gully so planners can visualise the terrain’s texture when selecting lift corridors and ski-run alignments. Please generate a relief image from this elevation grid, automatically choosing the shading colours and keeping the vertical scale as it is.

A national mapping agency is preparing a 1:50,000 topographic series for a mountainous province. They possess a 10 m resolution GeoTIFF of ground heights and require a separate shaded-relief raster that highlights every ridge and valley for subsequent cartographic finishing. The relief should be generated with a 50 % vertical exaggeration so that subtle landforms remain visible, and the colour tones for illuminated and shaded slopes should be chosen automatically to harmonise with the broader map palette.
Tool: SpatiaLite execute SQL\nAlgorithm: The Geological Survey has compiled a province-wide lithology map in a SpatiaLite database.  After field verification, geologists need to standardise the rock-type names currently stored in the ‘lith_unit’ column so that every occurrence of ‘Grano-diorite’ is changed to ‘Granodiorite’ and every ‘Basaltic Andesite’ is shortened to ‘Andesite’.  Only the database file itself is to be updated; no new map layer is required.

We have a SpatiaLite database (.sqlite) that stores geochemical sample locations together with their laboratory results. To support the QA/QC review, we need to flag every record whose copper value exceeds 500 ppm and mark it as “high Cu” in a dedicated text column so that reviewers can immediately spot anomalous samples.

Within a SpatiaLite database holding geochemical sample points, identify and flag any records whose coordinates place them outside the permitted national territory so that the QA/QC team can later review or exclude suspect entries.

A mineral exploration company maintains a SpatiaLite database holding existing tenement polygons and needs to mark every parcel that is currently under application so that field teams do not accidentally peg overlapping ground. Using the database file supplied by the tenements office, update the status column of each polygon record to ‘Application Pending’ wherever the existing value is null.

A geologist has a SpatiaLite database (.sqlite) holding collar coordinates for historic drill-holes and a separate table with the most recent digital elevation model (DEM) values stored as point heights. To check whether the collar elevations recorded in the field still match the current ground surface, they need to run an update that replaces the old collar height in the drill-hole table with the latest elevation taken from the DEM points that fall at the same x,y location.

Within a SpatiaLite database that stores both the collar coordinates of exploration drill-holes and a recent high-resolution DEM, update the collar elevation field so that each hole is assigned the ground-surface height recorded in the DEM at the same horizontal position.

A marine geophysics team has combined several years of seismic-reflection survey tracks into one SpatiaLite database and now needs to remove duplicate line segments that appear more than once in the same file so that only unique survey paths remain for mapping.

A marine geophysics team has consolidated several years of seismic-reflection survey tracks into a single SpatiaLite database (.sqlite) that now contains duplicate line entries with identical start-end coordinates and cruise IDs. They need to remove these repeated records so that each unique survey line is represented only once, ensuring the final dataset can be trusted for subsurface mapping without inflated coverage statistics.

We have a county-wide geological map stored as a SpatiaLite database (.sqlite) that was compiled during a recent survey. Each polygon currently carries provisional age descriptions such as “Cretaceous undifferentiated.” The state board now requires every polygon to instead show the formal stratigraphic formation name (e.g., “Pierre Shale,” “Niobrara Formation”). Provide a SpatiaLite-ready SQL statement that will update the formation-name field in-place for every polygon record so the map can be submitted without creating an additional layer. The statement must include the complete mapping logic (CASE block or reference table join) that translates each provisional age description into the correct formation name.

A mineral exploration team keeps a SpatiaLite database (.sqlite) that records every granted lease and cadastral boundary.  Before heading into the field they need a list of the 1-minute by 1-minute grid squares that remain unclaimed inside the boundary of a new licence application already stored in the same database.  Using only the information already held in the database, produce a table that flags each relevant grid square identifier as either occupied or still open, so crews can focus staking efforts on the open squares without leaving the SQL environment.

A web service that streams live bus positions needs to update each vehicle’s geometry in the database so that the point snaps to the nearest road segment whenever a new GPS reading arrives; the database already stores the bus table and the road centerline table and is refreshed every 30 seconds.

After this spring’s street-tree survey, the city’s urban-forest officer needs to update every tree record in the SpatiaLite database that is attached to the QGIS project: change the ‘condition’ field from ‘unknown’ to ‘good’ for every oak that was revisited and rated healthy, and set the ‘survey_year’ to 2024 for those same rows. The database already contains the point layer with all city trees and the two fields to be updated.

After completing a street-tree inventory field survey, the city’s urban forestry team has loaded the updated measurements into the same SpatiaLite database that already holds the existing tree layer. They now need to refresh the ‘last_surveyed’, ‘height_m’, and ‘condition’ values for every tree record so that the digital map reflects the latest site information without creating an additional file.

A city planning department maintains a SpatiaLite database of all road segments in the municipality. They need to update each record in the roads table so that it permanently stores the measured length of that segment, expressed in metres, to support annual maintenance budgeting and pavement-wear modelling.
Tool: Join attributes by location (summa: A regional planning office needs to know the total and average number of people living inside each municipality polygon. They have a shapefile of municipal boundaries and a separate point shapefile in which each point carries the population count of the small settlement it represents. The requirement is to add two new numbers—sum and mean population—to every municipality’s record so planners can immediately see how many residents each town contains and how densely settled it is on average.

The regional planning office has a .shp file of municipal boundaries and a second .shp file of census blocks with population counts. They need to know, for each municipality, the total, average, and maximum population found in any of the census blocks that fall inside or touch that municipality, so they can prepare a concise demographic summary for the regional development plan.

A regional water authority holds a shapefile of watershed boundaries and a separate shapefile of high-resolution slope raster cells converted to polygons, each carrying its slope value. The authority needs to know, for every watershed, the average slope of the land surface lying inside that watershed so it can prioritize erosion-control efforts.

We have a shapefile of watershed boundaries (polygons) and a shapefile of slope raster cells converted to points, each point carrying its slope value in percent. Produce a new watershed layer where every polygon lists the average slope calculated from all slope-points that fall inside it, so planners can quickly see which basins are steepest without manual inspection.

To support a regional groundwater-quality study, we have a shapefile of 120 monitoring-well points and a companion shapefile of 1,300 topsoil-sample polygons with measured heavy-metal concentrations. We need to attach summary statistics of the surrounding soil contamination (mean, maximum, and count of samples) to each well location so that the wells can be ranked by the contamination level in their immediate vicinity.

A municipal planning department is updating its land-use statistics. They have a shapefile of every land parcel in the city and a second shapefile showing the road network. Each road segment carries its length in metres. The planners need to know, for every parcel, the total length of roads that lie inside or cross the parcel boundary so that they can compute road density per parcel.

A university agronomy lab has digitised 120 experimental maize plots as polygons in a shapefile and has a separate raster-derived shapefile in which every small polygon carries the mean NDVI value extracted from Sentinel-2 imagery for the same growing season. The researchers need to append a single representative NDVI figure to each plot so they can relate yield measurements to vegetation vigour. They therefore require a new plots layer that adds, for every plot polygon, the average of all NDVI values from the NDVI polygons that fall inside or cross that plot.

A crop‐science study needs to attach average NDVI values to each experimental wheat plot.  The plots are provided as a shapefile of field boundaries, while a second shapefile holds the mean NDVI measured in 10 m grid cells across the same region.  Produce a new plot map that carries, for every plot polygon, the average NDVI of all grid cells that fall inside or cross that plot.

A state environmental agency is mapping average heavy-metal concentrations around each groundwater monitoring well to identify hotspots. They have one polygon shapefile in which every feature is a 500 m-radius circle centred on a monitoring well (150 circles in total) and a second point shapefile of over 3 000 soil-sample locations that record lead, cadmium, and zinc levels in mg/kg. The agency needs a single dataset that keeps every well-circle and appends the mean, maximum, and standard deviation of the three metals calculated from all soil-sample points that lie inside each circle, so that wells can be ranked by contamination severity.

A city planning office holds a shapefile of land-parcel boundaries and a separate shapefile of city streets. The office needs to know, for every parcel, the average and maximum posted speed limits of all streets that either run through the parcel or touch its boundary, so it can identify areas where lower speed limits might be warranted.

To assist the city police department in identifying crime hotspots, we have a shapefile of neighborhood boundaries and a second shapefile recording every theft incident as a point location. We need to know how many theft incidents fall inside each neighborhood so that patrol resources can be allocated accordingly.

We have two shapefiles: one holds parcel polygons with owner names and purchase dates, and the other holds building footprints with construction years and floor counts. We need to create a single list that shows, for every parcel, the owner name, purchase date, and the total number of floors of all buildings that fall inside that parcel.
Tool: Sum line lengths\nAlgorithm ID: na: A municipal planning department is updating its land-use statistics. They have a shapefile of every land parcel in the city and a second shapefile showing the road network. Each road segment carries its length in metres. The planners need to know, for every parcel, the total length of roads that lie inside or cross the parcel boundary so that they can compute road density per parcel.

A regional planning office is reviewing how much roadway mileage lies within each municipality to prioritize maintenance budgets. They have a .shp file showing the boundaries of every town and another .shp file holding the road centerlines for the entire region. They need to add to the town boundary file the total kilometres of roads that fall inside each town as well as the number of separate road segments so they can rank towns by overall road density.

A regional planning office has a set of municipal boundary maps in shapefile format and a national roads dataset also provided as a line shapefile. The office needs to quantify how much road infrastructure exists within each municipality so it can allocate maintenance budgets proportionally. Specifically, they want to know the combined kilometres of roads falling inside each municipal boundary and how many separate road segments are present, so that every municipality’s road inventory is recorded in the same attribute table as the boundary information.

A regional water-resources study requires a tally of the total length and number of stream reaches that lie inside each watershed polygon across the province.  The analyst possesses a provincial watershed boundary map (.shp) and a separate file of the province’s stream network (.shp).  The goal is to add, to each watershed’s record, the combined kilometres of streams and the count of stream segments that occur within that watershed.

We are updating the watershed management plan for the Red Cedar basin and need to know, for every sub-watershed polygon in our existing .shp file, how many kilometres of stream (held in the separate .shp file of river centre-lines) run through it and how many distinct stream segments that represents.

A municipal works department needs to know how much overhead electricity cable runs across each privately-owned land parcel in the city’s cadastral map. They have a shapefile showing parcel boundaries and another shapefile of the utility company’s medium-voltage line routes. They would like to add, for every parcel, the total metres of cable that pass through it and the number of separate cable sections involved.

The city’s engineering office has a shapefile showing every land parcel in the downtown district and a second shapefile recording all overhead and buried utility cables. They would like to know, for each parcel, the total length of cables that cross it and how many separate cable runs are present so they can prioritise inspections and allocate maintenance budgets efficiently.

The regional agricultural agency needs to update its annual fencing inventory for each paddock on a cattle station. It holds a paddock boundary map (polygon shapefile) and a separate map of all existing fence lines (line shapefile). The agency would like each paddock to show the combined length of fences running through it and how many separate fence sections are present, so that maintenance budgets and materials can be allocated accordingly.

A grazing cooperative manages a large cattle station. They have a shapefile that shows every paddock boundary on the property and another shapefile that records every fence line. To plan yearly maintenance budgets, they need to know, for each paddock, the total kilometres of fencing that run through it and how many separate fence sections are present.

For a regional pipeline exposure assessment we have a shapefile showing the boundaries of flood-risk zones and another shapefile recording the routes of all buried pipelines. We need to know, for each risk-zone polygon, how much pipeline mileage lies inside it and how many separate pipeline segments are present, so that emergency planners can prioritise inspections and reinforcements accordingly.

To support the pipeline exposure analysis per risk zone, we have a polygon shapefile that delineates different risk zones across the study area and a polyline shapefile containing the routes of all buried pipelines. We need to know, for each risk zone, the combined length of pipelines passing through it and how many separate pipeline segments are present, so that priority areas for inspection and maintenance can be identified.
Tool: Near black\nAlgorithm ID: gdal:nea: A municipal planning office has received a set of compressed aerial photographs in GeoTIFF format that will be used to create a seamless city-wide mosaic for the upcoming land-use map update.  Around the edges of each image, faint pale fringes—artifacts from earlier lossy compression—are visible and interfere with smooth edge-matching.  The office needs to identify these almost-white border pixels and recolor them to pure black so that, when the images are stitched together, the fringes disappear and the mosaic shows uninterrupted imagery.

A municipal planning office has received a set of 15 cm-resolution aerial photographs delivered as uncompressed GeoTIFFs.  Around every frame there is a ragged, nearly-black border left by the scanning process; these dark edges are preventing the images from blending seamlessly into a single mosaic of the city.  The office needs to turn all pixels that are close to pure black along these collars into true black so that the mosaic can treat them as transparent and show only the city area in each photo.

A regional planning agency has received a set of compressed satellite images (GeoTIFF format) that show faint, off-black collars around the scene edges. These collars interfere with seamless mosaicking for a new land-cover map. The agency needs to turn the almost-black edge pixels into true black so the collars become uniformly transparent during the mosaic assembly.

A regional land-monitoring programme has received a set of compressed satellite images (.tif format) that show pale, almost-white stripes along their edges where the scenes were mosaicked. These faint border pixels are interfering with subsequent visual interpretation and need to be standardised to a uniform black tone so the full image set can be merged cleanly for further analysis.

A heritage society is digitising a set of 1940s scanned topographic maps so they can be stitched together into a seamless historical atlas.  The original scans have pale grey borders introduced during digitisation; these borders need to be turned to solid black so the adjoining sheets will blend cleanly when the images are merged.  Each map is available as a GeoTIFF file.

A library is digitising a collection of 1940s topographic map scans that were previously georeferenced but exhibit pale grey collars around the edges after compression. To prepare the sheets for seamless mosaicking into a single historical basemap, the librarians need to turn these almost-white border pixels to pure black so they can be made transparent and the adjoining map content can blend naturally.

A provincial mapping agency has received a set of 1 m resolution compressed airphotos (GeoTIFF) that will be mosaicked to create a seamless basemap for emergency response.  The individual images contain pale, nearly-white borders introduced by lossy compression, and these borders must be identified and converted to uniform black so that they can be treated as transparent during the mosaicking process.  The agency needs a cleaned raster for each photo that is ready for seamless stitching.

A provincial mapping agency has received a set of 1 m resolution airphotos delivered as GeoTIFFs after lossy compression for online transfer.  Along every image edge the compression introduced faint off-black collars that show up as dark smudges when the tiles are mosaicked for the new topographic base map.  The agency needs to remove these nearly-black edge artefacts so the seams disappear and the mosaic presents a clean, uniform background across the entire province.

A regional planning office has received a set of compressed aerial photographs in GeoTIFF format that will be used to create a seamless basemap for a new land-use atlas.  Around the edges of each image, lossy compression has left faint pale bands that show up as unwanted borders when the photos are stitched together.  The office needs to turn these almost-white collar pixels into uniform black so the edges disappear and the mosaic appears continuous.

A regional planning office has received a set of compressed aerial photographs in GeoTIFF format that were supplied by a contractor. Along the edges of each image, faint grey and off-white compression artefacts appear where the photographs meet the surrounding collar, making the pictures unsuitable for seamless mosaicking across the study area. The planners need to clean these photographs so that any pixel around the border that is nearly black, white, or the specific light-grey tone of the artefacts is set to pure black, ensuring the collar areas can be treated as transparent when the images are stitched together for the final land-use map.
Tool: Grid (Moving average)\nAlgorithm I: We have a survey of ground elevation points collected by LiDAR for a valley that will be used for a new flood-risk study. The data are delivered as a .shp file holding the ground-return points with their measured heights. We would like to turn these scattered height measurements into a smooth elevation surface so we can see the overall shape of the terrain across the valley.

To create a smooth elevation surface for the Danube floodplain, we have a .shp file of LiDAR ground-return points collected last spring by the national mapping agency. The goal is to produce a continuous raster showing average heights across the region so that planners can identify low-lying areas potentially at risk during spring floods.

A regional soil-health study has collected nitrate measurements at 327 field-sampling points stored as a shapefile of locations with recorded ppm values. The team needs a continuous surface showing typical nitrate levels across the entire study area so that farmers can identify zones likely to need fertiliser adjustment. Produce a smooth predictive map from these point samples, averaging readings within a local neighbourhood to represent gradual soil changes rather than abrupt jumps.

We have a set of GPS-tagged soil-nitrate measurements collected across a 2 000 ha farm (provided as a point shapefile). To guide variable-rate fertiliser application, we need a continuous map that shows typical nitrate levels in every 10 m patch of the field, smoothing out local spikes while still reflecting broad patterns.

The regional climate office holds a CSV file listing 47 weather stations with their longitude, latitude and yesterday’s mean temperature. To produce a continuous temperature surface for the whole province at 1 km resolution, we need to spread the point measurements across the land so every pixel receives a value derived from nearby stations. The search should look within a 50 km radius east–west and 35 km north–south, and at least three stations must contribute to any pixel; where coverage is insufficient the pixel should be marked as unknown.

We have a CSV file listing 3 000 sonar-grab sample locations across the continental shelf, each with measured sediment thickness in centimetres. To create a smooth map that shows how sediment thickness varies across the seabed, we need to convert these point measurements into a continuous surface where every 50 m cell carries an average value derived from all samples found within a 2 km search radius around it.

We have a set of point measurements from sonar grabs recording sediment thickness across a section of the continental shelf, stored in a .shp file. The aim is to produce a continuous map of sediment thickness across the survey area by averaging nearby observations within an adjustable search window, allowing gaps to be filled only where enough nearby readings exist.

A municipal environmental office possesses a set of GPS-tagged noise measurements recorded every second by sensors mounted on refuse-collection vehicles that drove through the city last month; the file is a simple point shapefile with each record holding the measured decibel value. The office needs to create a continuous city-wide noise-level surface so residents can see typical sound exposure on any street; they want every 10 m pixel to show the average of all measurements taken within 50 m of that location, provided at least five readings are available, otherwise the pixel should be marked as having no data.

A city environmental office has collected 12 000 spot measurements of street-level noise (in dB) from smartphones carried by volunteers last month; the file is a point shapefile with coordinates and decibel values. They need a continuous noise-level surface for the entire urban area so that quiet-street corridors can be identified for future cycling-route planning. Produce a 10 m resolution raster that smoothly represents average noise across the city, using a circular 150 m neighbourhood and requiring at least 5 readings to trust a cell value.

A regional climate office maintains daily mean temperature readings from 47 weather stations across a 150 km by 120 km river basin. To prepare the continent-scale road network for fast routing, we need to split the nationwide .shp file of highways and major roads into smaller, simpler sections so that no single piece contains more than 256 points, ensuring quicker indexing and smoother spatial queries during route planning.

The goal is to obtain a new shapefile of the same zones, now stored as collections of smaller, easier-to-handle parts that still represent the full extent of each national maritime area.

To prepare the single large polygon that outlines the UAV orthomosaic for Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF tiling, split that outline into many smaller pieces so that each piece contains no more than 200 vertices, producing a new shapefile of the resulting simpler footprint parts.

The recoded surface will then be used directly in their connectivity model without further processing.

The city planning office has a satellite-derived surface-temperature raster (GeoTIFF) covering the entire metropolitan area. A national park service is monitoring vegetation recovery across a large burn scar using a time-series of 30-meter Landsat NDVI rasters (one for each growing season from 2019 to 2023). To identify areas that consistently remain in the lowest quarter of greenness each year, they need a single map that records, for every pixel, the value that is exceeded by 75 % of the yearly observations. The resulting layer will guide field crews to sites where reseeding efforts are most likely to be required.

The city’s climate office has compiled a set of twenty summer daytime land-surface-temperature rasters (GeoTIFF, 10 m resolution, same city extent) from the past five years. They need a single city-wide heat-risk surface that shows, at every location, the temperature that is cooler than three-quarters of the recorded summer values across the years. This reference surface will be used to identify neighborhoods that regularly experience unusually high temperatures and to prioritize cooling interventions.

The city planning office has compiled a set of 30 annual summer daytime land-surface-temperature (LST) raters (GeoTIFF) from satellite images spanning 1993–2022. They need a single heat-stress baseline surface that represents the temperature exceeded on only the hottest one-quarter of all observed years across the metropolitan area, to support the urban heat-island severity assessment.

A regional planning authority has compiled a set of annual landslide susceptibility maps (GeoTIFF format, 10 m resolution, 2010–2022) covering a mountainous province. To guide emergency preparedness, they need a single map that shows, for every location, the value that is exceeded in only one out of every four years across the historical series.

The regional planning office possesses a collection of yearly landslide-susceptibility index grids (GeoTIFF, 10 m) covering the past thirty years for the mountain province. To support the new building-code review, they need a single map that shows, for every location, the value that was exceeded only 10 % of the time across the historical series, effectively highlighting the most conservative (safest) estimate of potential instability. A reference elevation model is available to ensure the final map aligns with the standard provincial grid extent and cell size.
Tool: Variable width buffer (by M value): To map the zones likely to be flooded along the main river, we have a polyline shapefile supplied by the hydrology office showing the river centre-line; each vertex of this line carries a pre-calculated peak-flow width (stored as the line’s M-coordinate) recorded during the last major flood. We need to turn this line into a single polygon layer that outlines, for every reach, the land that would lie under water when the river expands to those recorded widths.

To support a regional flood-risk assessment, we have a polyline shapefile of the main river network where each vertex carries a pre-calculated peak-flow width stored as a measure (M) value. We need to turn these lines into polygons that represent the maximum water extent during flood peaks, so that the resulting layer can be overlaid on land-parcel maps to identify properties at risk.

To support a pavement-width inventory project, we have a linear-referenced road centerline shapefile whose vertices carry milepost-based measurements stored as M-values. We need to turn each road segment into a polygon whose width at every point matches the pavement width recorded in those M-values, producing a single layer that shows the exact paved surface for the entire network.

The state highway department maintains a linear-referencing route system in which each milepost vertex stores the actual pavement width measured during last year’s survey. To support resurfacing-cost estimates we need to turn the centerline shapefile into a set of roadside-to-roadside polygons whose widths match those recorded milepost values.

A regional gas company needs to map the safety corridor along its high-pressure transmission pipelines. The corridor width must vary along each pipe according to the ground-level hazard index stored in the route’s vertex measure (M) values—wider where the index is high and narrower where it is low. Starting from a .shp file that contains the pipeline centerlines with these M values already recorded, produce a polygon layer that outlines the dynamic setback zone around every line.

A gas utility company is updating its safety plan for a high-pressure transmission pipeline that runs through mixed urban and rural zones.  The company has a .shp file showing the exact centre-line of the pipeline, and each vertex of this line carries a pre-calculated setback distance (stored as the line’s M coordinate) that reflects local land-use, population density, and pressure class.  The company needs to turn this line into a single corridor polygon whose width at every point matches the corresponding setback distance, so the safety officers can see precisely how much land on each side of the pipe must remain clear of new structures.

A conservation group has surveyed a mountain hiking trail recorded as a .shp line file, and at each surveyed vertex they noted the measured width of visible erosion. They need to draw the exact strip of ground that is currently affected along the entire trail so the park service can plan restoration work.

A coastal risk assessment project requires the creation of a multi-year setback zone from a line shapefile that records cliff-top positions surveyed each year and stores the annual retreat distance as a measure (M) value at every vertex. The goal is to generate a corresponding polygon layer that shows, for every point along the cliff, the land area that should be kept clear of new development based on how far the cliff is expected to retreat in the coming year.

A backcountry recreation office has a polyline shapefile whose vertices store, as M-values, the field-measured half-width of the bare, eroded ground on either side of a hiking trail. The staff need to convert this measured centre-line into a polygon layer that depicts the exact eroded corridor along the entire trail so it can be overlaid on park maps for maintenance planning.

To begin a cost-distance analysis for identifying least-cost routes across the region, I need a starting surface that marks every cell with the same travel-friction value. The coordinates were saved as a .gpx file on a laptop. The team now needs to transfer these recorded positions back into the same Garmin device so that local rangers can navigate to each tree for monitoring without re-entering the coordinates by hand.

A wildlife-tracking team has collected a set of recorded stopover sites during a two-week expedition and stored them in a GPX file. They now need to transfer these site coordinates to their Garmin handheld so the sites appear as searchable destinations when they return to the field next month.

A mountain-rescue team has prepared a GPX file with the planned hiking route for this weekend’s search-and-rescue exercise. They need to transfer this route from the office computer to the Garmin handheld unit that each field team carries, so that every navigator can follow the pre-planned path without having to redraw it manually on the device.

A recent field survey was conducted using handheld GPS units, and the resulting tracks have been post-processed to correct for positional drift; the cleaned-up .gpx file is now ready to be sent back to the same Garmin devices so that field teams can retrace the verified paths during the upcoming validation visit.
We need to send the cleaned-up survey paths, stored in a GPX file, back to the handheld Garmin unit so the field team can see the corrected tracks on their device during the next outing.

I have the backup file in GPX format on my computer and the device is connected to COM3. Please transfer the waypoint collection from this GPX file back onto the Garmin so I can use my original points in the field again.

After a firmware reset of their Garmin handheld unit, the stored waypoints were erased. They now need to transfer the survey plot locations back onto the device so they can revisit each site for a follow-up assessment.
Tool: Fuzzify raster (small membership)\: To support the municipal flood-risk mapping initiative, a 1 m-resolution GeoTIFF showing terrain elevation across the lower valley has been supplied by the regional survey office. The planning team needs to identify locations where the land surface lies at the lowest elevations, because these spots are most likely to collect water during heavy rainfall. Please convert this elevation map into a new layer that grades every cell on a scale from 0 to 1, giving the highest values to the lowest ground heights, so planners can immediately see which areas most strongly qualify as the valley’s natural sinks.

A regional planning office has a GeoTIFF showing elevation values across a river valley. They need to convert these elevations into a soft classification that highlights how "low-lying" each pixel is, so that areas most likely to collect water during heavy rainfall can be quickly identified. The resulting layer should rate every cell on a scale from 0 (not low at all) to 1 (clearly the lowest ground).

To support a regional climate-adaptation study, we have a 10 m resolution elevation raster (GeoTIFF) covering a high-relief valley network. We need to identify locations where cold air is most likely to accumulate overnight, expressed as a gradual surface that ranks every cell from “very unlikely” to “very likely” pooling points. Preference is given to the lowest elevations, with certainty dropping off gently as height increases.

A regional climate service is modelling how likely each valley pixel is to host cold-air pools on clear, calm nights. They have a 30-m DEM (GeoTIFF) giving ground elevation for every cell. To feed the next step of their fuzzy logic model they need a new grid that expresses, on a 0-to-1 scale, how “small” (i.e. low) each elevation value is across the area, so that the lowest hollows receive values close to 1 while higher ridges approach 0.

A regional health agency is mapping potential exposure to low-level airborne pollutants emitted by a chemical plant.  They have a GeoTIFF showing ground-level concentration values (µg m⁻³) recorded by a dispersion model.  To highlight neighbourhoods where concentrations are considered ‘uncomfortably low’—i.e., where lower readings still warrant attention—the agency needs the same grid converted into a 0-to-1 scale in which cells with the smallest concentrations receive the highest score and larger values taper off toward zero.

A regional environmental agency is evaluating how strongly different areas belong to the category “very close” to a known soil-contamination source.  They have a single-band GeoTIFF showing measured lead concentrations across the site.  They need to convert these concentration values into a scale from 0 to 1, where 1 means “definitely very close” (i.e., low concentration) and 0 means “not close at all,” so that the resulting map can be used directly in a suitability model for prioritizing clean-up zones.

We have a GeoTIFF raster from the national weather service showing yesterday’s soil-moisture index across the province, where lower numbers indicate drier conditions. To support a drought-early-warning study, we need to translate these index values into a graded map that highlights places most likely to experience moisture shortage, with the greatest emphasis on the smallest index readings.

A regional water-management study has produced a GeoTIFF of daily soil-moisture-deficit values for the past summer. To identify zones where the deficit is characteristically low—indicative of areas least prone to drought stress—I need the original raster converted into a new layer in which every cell carries a suitability score from 0 (not low) to 1 (very low), so that planners can immediately see where moisture conditions remain most favourable for crops and natural vegetation.

To support a night-time light pollution screening study, we have a GeoTIFF showing artificial sky-brightness values across the region. We need to identify the places where the brightness is considered low, so we would like each pixel to be given a score from 0 to 1 that indicates how strongly it belongs to the ‘low brightness’ category, with higher scores meaning the pixel is more likely to be in darker areas. The resulting scored layer will be used on its own to map zones that are still relatively free of light pollution.

To support the night-time light pollution screening project, I have a GeoTIFF raster showing city-wide artificial sky brightness values measured in nano-lamberts. I need to create a new map layer that rates each pixel by how strongly it belongs to the category “very dark sky”, so that planners can quickly see which areas already suffer the least from artificial light. The rating should range from 0 (not a dark-sky spot) to 1 (a perfect dark-sky spot), treating the lowest brightness readings as the best candidates.
Tool: Union\nAlgorithm ID: qgis:union\nD: We are integrating two independently mapped land-cover datasets for the same region—one from a 2023 Sentinel-2 classification stored as a polygon shapefile and another from a 2022 municipal survey delivered as a separate polygon shapefile—so that every patch of land is represented once and any places where the two sources disagree are kept as distinct pieces.  Produce a single layer that preserves all outlines from both datasets and records, for every resulting piece of land, which source (or both) claimed it and what class each source assigned.

To support a nationwide land-cover harmonization project, we possess two separate polygon datasets—one from the forestry ministry’s 2022 stand map and one from the agriculture department’s 2023 crop inventory—each delivered as shapefiles. We need a single layer that splits the landscape into distinct parcels wherever the two maps agree or disagree on land use so that every sliver of forest, field, or overlap carries the attributes of both sources.

The provincial boundary commission has received a single shapefile that merges the current administrative municipalities layer with the newly proposed electoral districts layer.  They need a single, clean map that shows every possible piece of land so that each fragment can be clearly labelled as belonging to one municipality and one electoral district, or to show where any boundary lines cross and create overlaps.  The goal is to produce one consolidated file that contains all these distinct land pieces, each carrying the names of both the municipality and the electoral district it falls within, ready for public review and legal drafting.

The Independent Electoral Commission has received a shapefile of the current municipal wards and a second shapefile of the newly proposed suburb boundaries. Both files cover the same city. The Commission needs a single map layer that shows every possible piece of land so that each fragment can be reviewed to see whether it falls inside an old ward, a new suburb, or both, together with the names and codes carried over from the original files.

The regional land-registry has provided a single .shp file holding every property parcel in the lower valley. Because several parcels overlap—for example, where a condominium complex sits atop an underground garage that is recorded separately—we need one clean layer that shows every distinct piece of land, whether it stands alone or lies beneath another parcel, and keeps the original ownership attributes attached to each resulting piece.

The regional planning office holds two shapefiles: one outlining the 100-year flood-plain as surveyed by the environmental agency, and another recording every privately owned parcel within the county. They need a single map that splits every parcel and every flood-plain segment wherever they cross or overlap, so that each resulting piece carries both the parcel ID and the flood hazard class, allowing clerks to tag individual land fragments with their exact risk level for insurance coding.

A state geological survey has provided a shapefile of active mining tenements and a separate shapefile of national parks and nature reserves.  The department needs a single map layer that shows every distinct piece of land, indicating where a tenement sits inside, outside, or partly overlaps a protected area so that compliance officers can immediately see every possible conflict without manually comparing the two maps.

To support a regional geochemical-sampling campaign, we have two polygon shapefiles: one mapping the different soil types and another outlining distinct geological units across the survey area. We need a single layer that shows every possible combination of soil type and geological unit so that sampling points can be assigned to unique soil–geology pairs and no overlap is missed.

I have two polygon shapefiles: one shows the different soil-type zones across the county, and the other shows the mapped geological units. I need a single map layer that splits every place where a soil zone crosses a geological boundary so that each combination of soil type and rock unit appears as its own separate piece. This will let me see every unique soil–geology pairing for planning geochemical sampling sites.

As part of reviewing potential overlaps between granted mining tenements and national parks, I already have two separate shapefiles: one holding the tenement boundaries and another holding the park zones. I need to split both sets so that every place where a tenement and a park share the same ground becomes its own separate piece, carrying the original labels from both files. The result should be one new layer that shows every distinct section—shared or not—so I can clearly see and tally the conflicting areas.

The provincial planning office has received two shapefiles from different departments: one showing the boundaries of proposed administrative districts and another containing mapped ecological protection zones. They need a single map layer that combines both sets of boundaries so that every possible overlap between an administrative district and an ecological zone becomes its own distinct piece, carrying the names and codes from both original files. This will let them see exactly where districts coincide with protected land and prepare a consolidated zoning report for the governor.

The regional land-use committee has received two shapefiles—one delineating municipal administrative wards and another mapping designated ecological protection zones. They need a single map layer that shows every possible combination of ward and protection-zone coverage, so that each fragment of land can be labelled with the names of both the ward and any overlapping protection status. This consolidated layer will be used to prepare a colour-coded atlas for public consultation.

The regional planning office holds a single shapefile that contains both the flood-hazard zones and the property parcels for the county. Because the polygons overlap in an uncontrolled way—some parcels sit entirely inside a hazard zone, some straddle several zones, and some hazard zones cover parts of multiple parcels—the office needs the file re-worked so that every separate piece of land (whether overlapped or not) becomes its own distinct polygon carrying the original flood-hazard and parcel identifiers. This will let staff know exactly which fragment of every property lies in which risk category before sending notices to landowners.

The Department of Mines is preparing a reconciliation report that must show every distinct piece of land within a mineral-exploration licence area so that each portion can be matched against any overlapping native-title claim. We have one shapefile holding the current licence boundaries and a second shapefile holding all registered native-title polygons. We need a single layer that splits the licence area wherever claims cross it, producing separate patches for every unique combination of licence and claim so that officers can assign the correct legal status to each patch.

The Department of Mines has received two shapefiles from the Geological Survey: one outlining current mining tenements and another recording registered native title claims across the same region. To prepare a single map for negotiation meetings, the Department needs a consolidated layer that shows every distinct parcel of land, indicating where tenements sit entirely outside claims, where claims overlap tenements, and where multiple claims or tenements coincide, while preserving the original identifiers and attributes from both files so that legal officers can quickly see which tenement numbers and claim names apply to each parcel.

The regional planning office has separate shapefiles for 100-year flood-hazard zones and cadastral parcels. To prepare compensation tables, staff need every distinct polygon that represents floodplain alone, land alone, or land that is also flood-prone, each carrying the attributes of its original theme. They will first combine the two files into a single layer that holds all boundaries, then run the same procedure again on that result so that any overlaps within the merged set are also split into their own pieces, yielding a final map where no polygons overlap and every unique area is individually listed.

Tool: Merge lines\nAlgorithm ID: native:: A city planning office has a .shp file of street center-lines delivered by a contractor; the file stores each block segment as a separate piece even when several pieces form one continuous street. The office needs a single, seamless line for every whole street so the map is cleaner and easier to read for public consultation.

To support a city-wide traffic-flow study, we have a street-centerline shapefile downloaded from the municipal open-data portal; each street that was digitised in segments now appears as many short pieces. We need to reunite every set of adjacent pieces that belong to the same street so the network can be displayed and analysed as continuous road lines.

The regional water board is digitising a new hydrographic map from 1:25 000 survey sheets. They have a shapefile of river reaches that were captured as separate segments for every tributary junction; these segments need to be combined into continuous river courses so the dataset can be published as a single, simplified drainage network.

After last month’s storm, the city’s public-works department has a .shp file of the damaged water-supply network where each pipe segment is stored as a separate piece even when they lie end-to-end along the same street. We need a single, continuous line for every stretch of pipe that is actually connected so that the reconstruction crew can see the full length of each run without the clutter of dozens of tiny fragments.
