They have a NetCDF file that gives the river’s temperature on an unstructured grid each hour, and a shapefile with the exact locations of the intake screens.  A table is required that lists, for every intake screen point, the hourly temperature values recorded by the mesh throughout the summer period.

To monitor how sediment accumulates in the harbour’s berth pockets, we have a continuously recorded mesh model of suspended-sediment concentration covering the entire mooring area and a separate .shp file marking the exact centre points of each pocket. We need to pull out the changing concentration values at those pocket centres for every saved time step so that the port authority can track when and where deposition is most likely to occur.

To support siltation monitoring at the harbour’s berth pockets, we have a continuously updated netCDF mesh that records predicted suspended-sediment concentration every hour across the entire mooring area. We also hold a shapefile with the exact positions of the six berth-pocket soundings that are surveyed weekly. We need to pull the hourly concentration predictions recorded at each of those sounding locations for the past fortnight so the port authority can compare them with the measured mud levels and judge when maintenance dredging is required.

The city’s environmental department maintains an hourly 3-D model of airborne particulate concentrations produced by Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service. They also have a shapefile with the locations of all primary schools. To issue timely health alerts, they need a spreadsheet showing how PM2.5 levels evolved over the past week at each school gate, so nurses can decide when to cancel outdoor activities.

The city’s environmental office has a daily air-quality forecast that comes as a gridded netCDF file showing hourly nitrogen-dioxide concentrations across the metropolitan area.  They also maintain a shapefile with the locations of all public elementary schools.  To prepare health advisories for the coming week, they need a table that lists, for every school, the predicted NO₂ value at the school’s location for each hour of the next seven days.

A regional agronomy office needs to monitor how the modelled groundwater elevation beneath 47 soil-monitoring wells changes every three hours across the irrigation season. They possess a NetCDF mesh of modelled groundwater elevations covering the district and a shapefile marking the exact locations of the wells. The office would like a single table listing the evolving groundwater elevation recorded at each well from 1 April to 30 September, rounded to two decimal places for coordinates and values, saved as a CSV file for direct comparison with their land-surface elevation data to later derive water-table depths.
Tool: Fix geometries\nAlgorithm ID: nati: A municipal GIS team is updating its open-data portal for property parcels.  They have a PostGIS table of lot polygons downloaded from the county auditor that still contains sliver polygons and self-intersections left over from earlier edits.  They need to run an in-place cleaning routine that removes these geometric errors so the layer can be republished without creating any new output files.

Ahead of merging municipal parcel maps from several towns into a single regional layer, the planning office has noticed that some of the submitted shapefiles contain lots with missing sections, twisted outlines, or overlapping corners that prevent the files from fitting together cleanly. Provide a cleaned version of the parcel shapefile in which every lot boundary is whole and properly closed, ready for seamless combination with the neighbouring datasets.

As part of preparing parcel boundaries for a regional land-use overlay study, we have received a .shp file of municipal cadastral polygons that contains several self-crossing and sliver parcels reported by local surveyors. We need to obtain a clean set of closed lot outlines that can be reliably used in subsequent analyses without losing any original corner points.

A municipal heritage office has received a .shp file of 19th-century building footprints digitised by volunteers. Several polygons appear distorted or split, preventing accurate area calculations for conservation grants. The office needs the outlines cleaned so every historic block is represented as a single, properly closed shape without losing any of the originally traced corners.

A municipal heritage office has received a .shp file of historic building footprints digitised by volunteers during a weekend mapping event. Several outlines appear broken or incomplete on screen, preventing the layer from being used in the official heritage register. The office needs the outlines restored so that every building is represented by a properly closed shape, ready for adoption into the register without redrawing from scratch.

While assembling a 3D city model from municipal records, planners received a shapefile of building footprints that contains apparent drawing errors—some outlines cross themselves and others have tiny gaps—so they need the layer cleaned so every footprint forms a proper closed outline ready for extrusion into 3D.

The city planning office has received a digital map of building footprints in .shp format from the cadastral survey team, but the accompanying note warns that several polygons appear distorted or incomplete, which could introduce errors in the forthcoming 3D city model. Before the data are passed to the modelling contractor, the planners need a cleaned version in which every outline is properly closed and no self-intersections remain, so the subsequent extrusion to 3-D volumes will proceed without artefacts.

A regional planning office is preparing statistical zones for an upcoming population census and needs accurate area figures for each zone. The office has received a .shp file of proposed zone boundaries drawn by local staff, but several polygons appear distorted or incomplete when displayed. To ensure reliable area calculations, the office requires a cleaned version of the boundary file in which every zone outline is properly closed and free of drawing errors, ready for subsequent tabulation.

The national statistics office is preparing new population-density tables and has received a municipal boundary map (.shp) from the cadastral agency. Several district outlines fail to form closed rings, preventing reliable area measurements. Provide a cleaned version of the same map in which every district boundary is a complete, properly formed polygon so that accurate surface areas can be calculated for each statistical zone.

A metropolitan planning unit has received a crowd-sourced .shp file of cycle paths intended for public bicycle routing. Some paths contain drawing errors—lines that cross themselves or have tiny breaks—making the dataset unreliable for any spatial measurement or display. Please clean the path drawings so that each line is mathematically sound and free of such errors, ensuring the layer can safely underpin further cartographic or analytical work.
Tool: Transect\nAlgorithm ID: native:tra: For a hydrological study of the River Lea, we have a .shp file showing the centre-line of a 12 km reach. We need to generate short cross-lines perpendicular to the river at every surveyed vertex so that field crews can record bank-to-bank elevation profiles; each cross-line should extend 25 m on both sides of the centre-line.

For a flood-risk study along the Mekong River we have a .shp file showing the river’s centre-line surveyed in 2022. We need to generate short cross-river sampling lines at every surveyed point so that field teams can record water-edge and bank-top elevations. Each cross line should extend 75 m to both sides of the river, run straight across the flow, and carry the original survey point ID so the elevation measurements can be linked back to the correct location.

A regional transport-planning team is assessing how road noise propagates laterally from a newly surveyed centre-line shapefile of the A-42 highway. To support an environmental-health study, they need to generate straight measurement spokes extending exactly 250 m to each side of every vertex along the road so field crews can place sound-level meters at consistent offsets. The team has the road alignment as a polyline layer in a local geopackage and wants the resulting set of spokes delivered as a separate line layer that retains the original road ID for easy cross-reference.

The regional transport agency wants to understand how airborne pollutants disperse laterally from the A14 motorway embankment. From OpenStreetMap they have a .shp file showing the centre-line of the 12 km stretch that passes through the river valley. They need a set of straight measuring spokes, 300 m long, drawn outward from the road at every vertex so that portable air-quality sensors can be placed at regular intervals across the fields on both sides of the carriageway.

As part of a coastal-erosion monitoring programme we have a recent .shp file showing the baseline shoreline traced from aerial photos. We need to draw short, straight survey spokes sticking out from every point along this shoreline so that field teams can walk exactly those lines next month and record how far the cliff edge has retreated. Each spoke should extend 25 m landward and 25 m seaward of the baseline, giving a 50 m cross-shore profile centred on the original line.

For a coastal erosion monitoring programme, we have a recent polyline shapefile that traces the high-water mark along a 12 km stretch of shoreline. We need to generate short, perpendicular marker lines at every vertex of this shoreline trace so that field teams can position ranging poles exactly 25 m landward and 25 m seaward of the line. These marker lines will serve as the fixed baseline from which annual beach-profile measurements are taken.

A regional power utility needs to verify that every guy-wire attached to its 11 kV overhead line remains within the permitted easement corridor. The company has a recent .shp file that records the centre-line of the line. For each pole position (vertex) along this line, they would like to draw short measuring spokes that extend 15 m to each side of the line so that field crews can quickly see whether any guy-wire crosses the corridor boundary.

A conservation team has mapped the proposed wildlife-corridor routes as a polyline shapefile. To check how wide the natural openings are at regular points along each route, they need short crossing lines drawn outward from every vertex of the corridor paths, reaching 25 m on both sides so field crews can later measure vegetation density along these short spans.

A municipal utility company has a shapefile of planned medium-voltage power-line routes whose vertices mark exact pole positions. To preview how far guy-wire anchors could reach, it needs short crossing lines drawn only at these pole points, each carrying the route identifier already stored in the file and a unique sequence number. The company accepts that any extra vertices between poles will also receive crossing lines and is prepared to remove those afterward; the essential deliverable is a new line layer holding the perpendicular strokes with the original route names preserved.

To evaluate how wide the intended wildlife corridor feels to animals at the points where the guiding centre-line already bends, we have a single .shp file that traces the planned corridor path. Produce a set of straight measuring sticks that run left-and-right across the corridor, each 300 m long and perpendicular to the path at every bend, so field teams can later walk these lines and record vegetation density and human disturbance.
Tool: Nearest neighbour analysis\nAlgori: The city police department has compiled a .shp file of every reported street robbery in the past year, each recorded as a single point location. To decide whether extra patrols should be concentrated in specific districts or spread evenly across the city, they need to know if these crimes tend to bunch together, scatter randomly, or stay evenly spaced across the urban area.

The city police department has compiled a .shp file of every reported street robbery in the past year. They would like to know whether these incidents are scattered randomly across the city or tend to group together in certain areas, to decide if focused patrol strategies are justified.

A national supermarket chain is assessing whether new outlets opened last year are positioned too close together and risk stealing customers from one another. The planning team holds a .shp file with the locations of every store opened in the past twelve months. They need a statistical summary that shows whether these stores are clustered, spread out, or randomly situated across the country, so they can decide if further spacing adjustments are required.

In a retail store cannibalisation study, we have a shapefile of existing store locations across the city and need to know whether these outlets are clustered, spread out evenly, or positioned at random so we can judge if new openings would compete too closely with current ones.

As part of a wildfire ignition pattern study, researchers have a shapefile of lightning-strike locations recorded over the past decade across a national forest. They need to know whether these ignition points tend to cluster together, scatter randomly, or spread evenly across the landscape so they can better target prevention resources.

To support wildfire ignition pattern analysis, we have a .shp file recording the exact locations of every lightning-caused ignition recorded in the Sierra Nevada over the past decade. We need to know whether these ignition sites tend to cluster together, scatter randomly, or spread evenly across the landscape so that fire-management teams can better decide where to pre-position resources.

Within a regional soil-fertility study, we have a .shp file of 247 field-sampling sites collected last season. We need to know whether these sampling locations are spread out evenly across the landscape, clustered in certain areas, or positioned without any particular pattern, so we can judge if the current spacing fairly represents the whole region or if future campaigns should adjust the site arrangement.

To evaluate whether the planned soil sampling locations across the study area are arranged in a spatially random, clustered, or evenly dispersed pattern, I have a point shapefile recording the proposed sample site coordinates. I would like a statistical report that shows how closely the sites lie to one another compared with a purely random layout, so I can judge if the sampling design provides unbiased coverage of the region.

A regional archaeological survey has catalogued 1 847 artefact scatters across the lower Rhine valley, stored as a shapefile of find-spot coordinates. To judge whether ancient settlement favoured certain landscape zones or spread evenly, the project needs a concise statistical statement on how tightly or loosely these discovery locations cluster across the valley floor.

A regional heritage office has compiled a .shp file recording the exact locations of every known prehistoric settlement in the lower river valley. They need to know whether these sites are scattered randomly across the landscape, clustered together, or evenly spaced, so they can decide if environmental preferences or social networks influenced ancient occupation patterns.
Tool: Generate points (pixel centroids): A national park needs to create a set of sampling locations along its main hiking trail to monitor elevation changes and terrain characteristics. The park has a GeoTIFF elevation model covering the entire area and a shapefile of the trail path. They want to identify the exact center points of the elevation grid cells that the trail passes through, so rangers can later visit these specific spots to record field measurements.

To verify vegetation vigour along a newly surveyed gas-pipeline corridor, we have a high-resolution NDVI satellite image (GeoTIFF) and the exact centreline of the route delivered as a shapefile of the pipeline. We need to extract the precise locations where the image pixels intersect the pipeline so that field teams can visit those exact spots for ground-truthing NDVI values.

A regional transport-planning study needs to know the exact spots along the national highway network where VIIRS night-time light imagery shows a pixel centre; the imagery is held as a GeoTIFF and the roads as a .shp file of centre-lines, and the aim is to create a set of point locations marking each pixel that the roads cross so these can later be joined to the light values.

A regional planning office has a 30 m resolution night-time light intensity raster and a shapefile of national highways. They need to create a set of observation points that fall exactly on the road centreline so they can later extract the brightness value at each location for an audit of roadside lighting efficiency.

During a soil-carbon auditing project, a satellite-derived reflectance grid (GeoTIFF) and a set of straight survey transects (Esri Shapefile of lines) have been delivered. We need to identify the exact centre of every grid cell that each transect passes through so that ground-truthing samples can be placed precisely on those spots.

To support a soil-carbon auditing project, we have a satellite-derived geotiff showing surface organic-matter content and a shapefile of straight transect lines walked during field surveys. We need to extract the exact centre points of every image pixel that lies underneath these survey lines so that each measured carbon value can later be paired with its precise image pixel for calibration.

A regional climate study requires temperature readings at regular intervals along the main river channel to correlate water-surface temperature with surrounding land-surface temperature.  The team has a high-resolution thermal infrared image (GeoTIFF) captured at the same time-of-day as a detailed river centerline shapefile surveyed by GPS.  They need a set of point locations that fall exactly on the river line and represent the center of every pixel the river passes through, so that the temperature value of each corresponding pixel can be extracted for subsequent statistical analysis.

To support a thermal pollution study along the Lower Green River, we have a 10 m resolution Landsat-derived surface-temperature raster (GeoTIFF) and a shapefile of the 2023 river centerline surveyed by the USGS. We need to extract the exact locations where each pixel of the temperature image touches the river line so that field crews can revisit those spots for in-situ temperature checks.

A national-park trail-management study requires an inventory of all 1 m elevation postings that lie directly beneath the official hiking trail so that maintenance crews can verify the exact DEM values used in slope stability models.  We have a 1 m resolution digital elevation model (GeoTIFF) and a shapefile representing the trail as a single line.  The goal is to extract every DEM cell centre that the trail touches, producing a set of precise spot heights tied to the underlying elevation grid for quality assurance of the park’s hazard maps.

To map the precise locations where a newly surveyed pipeline crosses individual pixels of a satellite-derived NDVI image, I have a GeoTIFF of NDVI data and a shapefile of the pipeline centerline. I need a series of points placed exactly at the center of every pixel that the pipeline traverses, so that I can later attach the corresponding NDVI values for field-team validation of vegetation conditions along the route.
Tool: Clip raster by mask layer\nAlgorit: A regional water-resources study needs the portion of a 10 m digital elevation model (GeoTIFF) that falls inside the officially mapped boundary of the Pine River watershed (provided as a shapefile of the basin outline) so that hydrological modelling can be restricted to the exact upland area contributing surface flow.

A regional water authority needs elevation information for the Blue River watershed to model flood risk. They have a GeoTIFF of national elevation data and a shapefile outlining the watershed boundary. The task is to isolate only the elevation pixels that fall inside the watershed so the hydrologic model can focus on the relevant terrain.

A regional agricultural office has a recent 10 m Sentinel-2 GeoTIFF covering the entire county and a farm-boundary shapefile that outlines one grower’s field. They need to isolate only the pixels that fall inside that single field boundary so the grower can monitor crop health without the surrounding landscape.

The regional agronomy office has a 10 m Sentinel-2 GeoTIFF covering the entire county and a farm-boundary shapefile provided by the farmer. They need to isolate only the pixels that fall inside the single field boundary so the extension service can focus on computing vegetation indices for that specific parcel without the distraction of surrounding land.

The regional planning office possesses a GeoTIFF file showing 10 m land-cover classes for the entire county and a shapefile that outlines the adopted urban-growth boundary. To restrict the land-cover map to only the area inside this boundary for forthcoming urban-expansion studies, please produce a new raster that covers exactly the boundary extent and retains the original pixel values.

The regional planning office possesses a GeoTIFF land-cover map covering the entire county and a shapefile outlining the adopted urban growth boundary. Staff need to generate a new land-cover image that shows only the area inside the boundary so it can be used in a forthcoming report on permitted development zones.

Inside a national park, we need to keep only the portion of a GeoTIFF showing annual mean temperature that actually lies within the park boundary; the boundary is supplied as a shapefile of the protected area.

A regional climate service has published a nationwide 1-km temperature grid as a GeoTIFF. We possess an official shapefile delimiting the boundaries of a national park and need to obtain the portion of the temperature grid that falls within the park so that rangers can produce a focused climate summary for internal planning.

To prepare the topographic map for an exploration lease, extract the elevation grid that falls exactly inside the lease boundary provided as a shapefile, so the final map shows only the terrain within the licensed area.

To prepare a topographic map for the new mining lease, we need to isolate the elevation data that falls exactly within the lease boundary. We have a GeoTIFF file covering the entire region’s elevations and a .shp file outlining the approved lease perimeter. Please provide a new elevation raster that shows only the heights inside the lease area, trimmed precisely to the lease boundary.
Tool: Create attribute index\nAlgorithm: In a province-wide cadastral maintenance project, staff query a 2.3 million-row parcel shapefile by owner name several times each day. Because each search currently takes over a minute, we need a way to make the owner-name look-ups respond almost instantly without altering the file’s content or structure.

A national land-registry office holds a nationwide shapefile of cadastral parcels whose attribute table contains a unique parcel identifier column. Staff must repeatedly look up parcels by this ID during daily title-verification calls, but searches are currently slow. They need a way to make searches on the parcel-ID column respond almost instantly without altering the file’s visible content.

A city traffic management center maintains a live GeoPackage of road incidents updated every minute. To keep the dashboard that filters and tallies incidents by severity-level responsive, the center needs the incident-type column inside the GeoPackage to be internally organised so queries run faster.

To accelerate repeated look-ups of soil-carbon sample IDs during the national campaign, we need to prepare the field plots shapefile (plots.shp) so that searches on the ‘plot_code’ column respond instantly.

During the national soil-carbon sampling campaign, we have a country-wide point shapefile containing over 200 000 field plots with a ‘sample_id’ column used for linking laboratory results. Repeatedly selecting subsets of plots by this identifier for follow-up analyses is becoming slow; we therefore need the file adjusted so that searches on the sample_id run faster without altering the data itself.

To accelerate the identification of feeder segments during utility-network tracing, we need to prepare a municipal water-pipe map (delivered as a shapefile) so that searches on the pipe-diameter column respond instantly.

To accelerate downstream tracing queries on the city’s water-supply pipe layer (a GeoPackage of mains and laterals), the utility team needs the ID column that stores each pipe’s unique identifier to be internally organised so searches by that number respond instantly during network isolation exercises.

A national retail chain is evaluating thousands of potential store locations stored in a GeoPackage file that lists each candidate site with its unique site-code. Because the analysts will repeatedly filter and sort the list by site-code while running suitability checks, they need the file prepared so these look-ups respond instantly.

A retail-chain analyst has a nationwide GeoPackage of shopping-centre locations with a ‘footfall_score’ column that records daily visitor counts. To speed up repeated filtering of high-traffic centres during the site-suitability study, the analyst needs to prepare the dataset so that selections on the visitor-count values respond instantly.

A live-updating GeoPackage of traffic incidents for the metro area is refreshed every 30 seconds. Dashboards and public feeds must filter instantly by incident type, severity, and road name, yet queries on any one of these fields are lagging. To ensure rapid retrieval, we need to prepare the layer so that searches on incident type, on severity, and on road name each respond without delay.
Tool: Highest position in raster stack\n: I have a set of monthly NDVI (greenness) satellite images covering the same region for a full year, each stored as a separate GeoTIFF. I need to determine, for every pixel, which month shows the peak greenness value so I can map the timing of maximum vegetation activity across the area.

We have a time series of monthly NDVI GeoTIFF layers covering the same region for the past three years. To identify which month each pixel reaches its peak greenness, we need a single map that records, for every cell, the number of the month (1–36) in which its NDVI value was highest across the entire series.

A regional water authority needs to decide which of five historical flood-extent maps (each stored as a separate GeoTIFF showing maximum water depth reached in a different return-period event: 5-, 10-, 20-, 50-, and 100-year) best represents the worst-case scenario for every 10 m cell across the lower valley.  They have the five aligned depth rasters and a reference DEM covering the same area and wish to produce a single map that indicates, for each cell, which of the five events produced the greatest water depth, so that planners can immediately see where the 100-year (or any other) event dominates and focus mitigation resources accordingly.

To support the selection of design flood recurrence intervals for a proposed levee upgrade, we have a set of 50-year, 100-year, and 500-year flood-depth GeoTIFF grids covering the Lower Mississippi reach. Produce a single grid that records, for every cell, which of these three scenarios shows the greatest water depth, so engineers can immediately see which recurrence interval governs at each location.

A regional planning office holds a time-series of annual land-cover probability grids (GeoTIFF, 30 m) spanning 2000–2020 and needs to know, for every pixel, in which single year the probability of ‘urban’ first became the highest among all years.  The answer should be delivered as a new grid that simply records the year number (1 = 2000, 2 = 2001, …) when urban likelihood peaked, using the 2020 layer as the spatial template for extent and cell size.

We have a set of 12 yearly GeoTIFF surfaces from an ensemble of climate models, each showing the predicted number of days above 35 °C for every 1 km grid cell in the region. To see which single model most often projects the highest heat-stress levels across the landscape, we need a new map that records, for every cell, the rank (1–12) of the model that consistently produces the greatest number of extreme-hot days. The output should match the extent, resolution, and coordinate system of the supplied reference layer.

The regional climate consortium has produced a set of twenty downscaled annual-maximum-temperature forecasts for 2050, each stored as a separate GeoTIFF covering the entire river basin. Using the basin’s 30 m land-mask grid as the guiding layer, determine for every cell which of the twenty forecasts records the hottest projected temperature and return a single map that simply labels each cell with the number (1–20) of the forecast that shows the highest value there.

A mining company has compiled a set of GeoTIFF grids showing copper-concentration values measured during nine separate airborne geophysical surveys flown over the same prospect area in successive years. They need a single map that indicates, for every 25 m cell, which survey recorded the highest copper reading, so that follow-up drilling can prioritise the most anomalous survey blocks. One of the grids will serve as the spatial template for the final result.

A junior geologist assisting a mineral-exploration team has prepared a set of ten GeoTIFF grids, each showing the predicted favourability for copper across the same survey area, but generated by different modelling methods. The team needs to know, for every location, which single modelling run returned the strongest prediction so that follow-up field checks can be prioritised accordingly. The grids share the same extent and cell size, and one of them can be used as the spatial reference for the final map.

A regional climate-impact study has compiled a stack of 21 yearly GeoTIFF rasters (30 m) that record, for each pixel, the probability of human settlement expansion during 2000–2020. Investigators need a new raster in which every cell simply states the order (first, second, …, twenty-first) of the layer that first shows the highest probability value across the series, so they can later translate this order into the corresponding calendar year and pinpoint the earliest timing of urban-growth hotspots.
Tool: Reproject\nAlgorithm ID: pdal:repr: A cross-state LiDAR elevation survey was flown with adjoining blocks delivered in separate .las point clouds. The contractor used the local state-plane coordinate system for each block, but the final merged dataset must adopt the new national reference frame (NAD83 2011) so it aligns with neighboring federal datasets. Convert each block’s reference frame accordingly.

For a coastal-change study using UAV photogrammetry, we have a .las point cloud of the shoreline captured in a local drone grid. The dataset needs to be provided in the same coordinate framework as existing regional topographic maps so it can be merged seamlessly for erosion-accretion comparisons.

To align a UAV-derived point cloud of the eroding shoreline—currently stored as a .las file—with the national topographic map series, the dataset needs to be placed in the same position-reference system (EPSG:27700) so it can be combined seamlessly with existing Ordnance Survey layers for seasonal change comparison.

A multinational mining consortium has acquired overlapping lidar point-cloud surveys along a frontier ridge that straddles two national datums. The raw .las files were flown in the local CRS of each country; to merge them into a single seamless model for cross-border ore-body modelling they must all be expressed in the same international framework (EPSG:4978). Please prepare the unified dataset.

A mining company has acquired a LiDAR point cloud of a prospective ore body that straddles the national border; the survey was flown in the neighbouring country’s official grid, but the company’s GIS works in the national system. Provide a copy of the point cloud expressed in the company’s standard coordinate framework so it aligns seamlessly with domestic lease maps and topography.

A city planning office is updating its flood-risk models for low-lying districts. They possess a .las point cloud captured by aerial lidar after last spring’s flood, but the data were delivered in a global coordinate framework while the city’s engineering drawings use the regional grid. To align the elevation measurements with existing street and drainage plans, the office needs the point cloud expressed in the local survey system so that water-surface levels can be compared directly with curb and inlet elevations.

The regional flood-mitigation team has collected an airborne LiDAR survey covering the lower downtown area as a .las point-cloud file. All coordinates are referenced to the local engineering grid used since the 1990s, but the new city-wide elevation model the survey must feed into is referenced to a modern national coordinate framework. To integrate this dataset seamlessly, the survey needs to be re-expressed in the same national framework while preserving its original accuracy.

A research team studying glacier volume change has collected aerial LiDAR scans of an alpine ice field stored as a .las point cloud referenced to a local grid used by the mountaineering survey. To integrate these measurements with regional satellite elevation data that follow the standard European Terrestrial Reference System, they need the point cloud expressed in that common framework.

We are studying how three valley glaciers in the southern Andes have thinned since 2015. Field teams have provided a .las point cloud collected by airborne lidar in 2022, but it was delivered in the data collector’s local grid. To compare these recent measurements with earlier elevation models referenced to WGS-84 / UTM zone 19S, the point cloud must be placed in the same geographic framework.

A state mapping agency has received two adjacent county LiDAR point-cloud files (.las) that were originally captured in differing local grid systems. Before combining them into a single statewide dataset, each file must be translated into the common statewide coordinate framework so that every elevation and horizontal measurement is expressed in the same referencing system.
Tool: Sieve\nAlgorithm ID: gdal:sieve\nD: The National Land-Cover Mapping Programme has produced a 10 m resolution raster map of the country that distinguishes forest, cropland, wetland, urban and water surfaces.  Field checks revealed that the initial classification contains many tiny, isolated pixel clusters—often fewer than a dozen cells—misclassified as wetland or water within broad agricultural areas.  These speckles hinder the readability of the final 1:250 000 printed atlas and must be eliminated while preserving the larger, genuine wetlands and ponds.  A single GeoTIFF file of the national land-cover grid is available.  The programme now needs a cleaned version of this grid in which any group of contiguous cells smaller than about 1 000 m² (equivalent to roughly ten 10 m pixels) is reassigned to the most common surrounding class, yielding a smoother, cartographically acceptable product.

The National Land-Cover Mapping Program has produced a 10 m resolution GeoTIFF showing forest, water, built-up and agricultural areas across the province. Field checks revealed that many isolated clumps of misclassified pixels—each covering fewer than 500 m²—create a speckled appearance and inflate the apparent number of small forest patches and farm plots. We need to tidy the map so that any such tiny, isolated groups of pixels are removed and their space is filled with the class of the largest neighbouring area, delivering a cleaner, more cartographically plausible land-cover layer for 1 : 50 000 scale printing.

We have a national wetland inventory derived from 10 m Sentinel-2 imagery that is stored as a GeoTIFF where each pixel marks open water, marsh, bog or dry land.  After the initial classification many tiny, isolated pixel groups—mostly single mis-classified pixels—appear within large wetland units, creating a noisy map that hampers area summaries and visual interpretation.  We need a cleaned version of this inventory in which any cluster of fewer than 20 pixels is eliminated and the vacated cells are reassigned to the most common neighbouring wetland type, producing a smoother, more reliable wetland mask for subsequent habitat modelling.

We have a classified land-cover raster (GeoTIFF) produced from satellite imagery that delineates water bodies across a river basin; many tiny, isolated ‘water’ pixels appear as noise amid larger, coherent water surfaces. To prepare a clean hydrological mask for watershed modelling, we need to eliminate all water patches covering fewer than 20 pixels and have them filled with the value of the surrounding dominant land-cover type.

A 1-m resolution land-cover raster derived from 2023 Sentinel-2 imagery shows thousands of very small clumps of pixels that were mis-classified as individual forest stands. To prepare a cleaner map for the provincial forest inventory, we need to erase any group of forest pixels that covers fewer than 50 square metres (i.e., 50 pixels) and have those spots automatically take on the class of the surrounding larger patch. The cleaned raster will be delivered as a GeoTIFF for further stand-delineation work.

The provincial forestry service has produced a 1 m resolution land-cover raster from this summer’s multispectral drone survey. Many tiny clumps—often single pixels—of mis-classified ‘clearing’ appear inside mature stands, complicating the planned compartment map. We need to clean the raster so any such clumps smaller than roughly 10 m² are merged back into their surrounding stand type, yielding a more realistic forest-stand layer for operational planning.

A regional land-survey office has produced a classified soil-type map from satellite imagery; the resulting GeoTIFF contains many tiny, isolated patches of a single soil class that are too small to represent real field units. To prepare a cleaner map for publication at 1:100 000 scale, we need to eliminate every cluster of pixels whose total area is below roughly one hectare (about 10 pixels at 30 m resolution) and have those spots take on the soil type of the surrounding larger zone.

To prepare a simplified county soil-type map for classroom use, we have a classified GeoTIFF (30 m resolution) showing 12 soil categories, but the map is cluttered with many tiny patches of only a few pixels. We need to clean the map so that any isolated soil patch smaller than about 0.8 ha (roughly 9 pixels) is merged into the surrounding larger soil area, producing a cleaner raster still showing the same 12 categories.

The regional planning office has a GeoTIFF produced from night-time light intensity values that is intended to serve as a built-up mask for the province. The file contains many scattered bright specks—tiny clusters of just a few lit pixels—that are noise from isolated farmsteads, passing vehicles, or sensor error rather than true settlements. To prepare a cleaner mask that retains only substantial urban areas, we need to eliminate every group of lit pixels smaller than a chosen size and have those gaps filled automatically with the value of the largest neighbouring lit patch, producing a revised GeoTIFF ready for land-use statistics.

A national mapping agency has produced a 30 m resolution GeoTIFF of built-up areas derived from night-time lights imagery. The agency wishes to obtain a cleaner version of the map in which any such tiny, disconnected patches of lit pixels are eliminated and their cells are reassigned to the value of the largest adjoining patch, so that only coherent built-up zones remain visible.
Tool: Simplify\nAlgorithm ID: native:sim: For a 1:250 000 scale road-atlas project we have received a detailed .shp file of the national highway network where every straight-line segment is stored as a sequence of closely spaced vertices. We need to derive a cleaner, curved representation of the routes so that the printed maps show smooth, visually pleasing lines rather than jagged sequences of short straight segments, while keeping the new lines within one millimetre (at map scale) of their original position.

A municipal web-mapping project needs to display simplified road geometries from a city-wide line shapefile. The original file contains curved arterial roads that appear jagged when zoomed out; we must redraw these curves so that no point on the new straight-line version drifts more than 2 m from the original curve while leaving already-straight sections untouched.

To prepare a nationwide road network dataset for fast web-map rendering, we have a shapefile of highways and major streets that still contains smooth curves originally captured at high precision. We need to redraw those curved stretches so that every bend is approximated by short, straight segments that deviate from the original line by no more than 5 metres, ensuring the simplified geometry remains visually faithful while reducing file size and speeding up display.

To support the Coastal Zone Buffer Generation project, we have a shoreline map (a .shp file) that contains curved bays and capes. We need to redraw every curved stretch of the shoreline so that no point on the new straight-line version is more than 25 metres away from the original curve, ensuring the simplified outline can be used for later coastal planning without losing important detail.

A research team has collected a set of drone flight trajectories saved as a line shapefile, but the GPS readings contain small positional jitter that makes the paths appear jagged. They would like all vertex positions to be shifted to the nearest points on a regular 1 m × 1 m grid so the tracks look cleaner and consistent with their 1 m resolution elevation model.

To meet cartographic clarity standards for the smaller scale, the intricate water outlines need to be rendered with fewer bends and detail while preserving their essential shapes.  Produce a streamlined version of these line and polygon features that keeps the overall coastal and drainage appearance yet removes excessive vertices, ready for inclusion in the generalized map product.

To support the creation of a 1:50 000 topographic map, the national mapping agency needs to reduce the detail of its master 1:10 000 coastline and river datasets (provided as polygon and line shapefiles) so that the features appear cleaner at the smaller scale while keeping their recognizable shapes; produce a simplified version that retains the essential bends and inlets but removes unnecessary bends smaller than 25 m.

For a national park web-map that will be viewed on phones, we have a detailed shoreline polygon (.shp) of Lake Emerald that contains too many bends and points, causing the mobile tiles to load slowly. We need a cleaner version of the same shoreline that keeps the overall shape but removes the tiny wiggles, so the tiles render faster while still looking natural to visitors.

For a national park web-map project, we have a detailed .shp file of hiking trails with very high-resolution curves that slow tile loading. We need a lighter version of the same trail file that keeps the overall shape recognizable but uses fewer points, so the tiles render faster on mobile devices.

To support a study on reducing GPS-track noise, we have a .shp file of hiking trails recorded by handheld devices that contain many closely spaced points, causing jagged lines. We need a cleaner version of these trails with fewer points while keeping the overall shape, so the paths look smooth on maps and are easier to share online.

A research team has collected a high-resolution coastline shapefile from an open-data portal to model storm-surge inundation for a low-lying delta. The original file contains an excessive number of detail points that slow subsequent simulations; they need a version with fewer points while keeping the overall coastal outline recognisable so that the hydrodynamic model can run efficiently.

To speed up the hydrological model runs, the watershed boundary map delivered as a detailed polygon shapefile must be turned into a lighter version that keeps the overall outline but removes unnecessary detail along the edges; the simplified layer should still be saved as a shapefile for the next modelling step.

To speed up a forthcoming hydrological simulation, we need to lighten a polygon shapefile that outlines the river catchment boundaries across the study region while keeping the overall outline recognisable; the file is in .shp format supplied by the regional water authority. Please produce a cleaner version with fewer detail points so the model can read it faster.

To harmonize the municipal land-use map for web display, we need to reduce the complexity of a polygon shapefile that stores detailed parcel boundaries for the entire county; the file is too large for smooth online rendering, so we require a version that keeps the same lots but with smoother outlines and fewer turning points, delivered as a new shapefile.

A regional planning office holds a province-wide land-use polygon shapefile whose boundaries are recorded at 1:5 000 scale and contain extremely detailed vertices that severely slow every subsequent map export and online visualization. The office needs a version of the same layer that keeps the general shapes of fields, forests, and urban blocks while using far fewer boundary points, so it can be published quickly in public atlases and shared with neighbouring municipalities without the current heavy file size.

A field survey team has delivered a .gpkg file holding GPS-tracked river centre-lines, but the recorded paths contain repeated points that add unnecessary detail and risk confusing downstream analysis. We need to clean these lines so that each stretch is represented by a single, continuous set of points without redundant recordings, while preserving the true shape of the river.
Tool: Points displacement\nAlgorithm ID:: A city tourism department needs to publish an interactive online map of cafés, museums, and hotels in the historic quarter. The current spreadsheet of addresses (.csv with latitude/longitude) was converted to a point file (.shp), but dozens of markers sit almost on top of one another along the main pedestrian street, making the map unreadable. To give visitors a clear view while preserving every location, they want any markers that are within roughly 10 m of each other to be gently spread out in a small ring so that every site remains visible and clickable.

The city tourism board is preparing a visitor map that highlights restaurants, museums and bus stops stored in a single .shp file of point locations. Because many attractions cluster within a few metres of each other, symbols currently overlap and labels are unreadable. We need a cleaned layer in which any points lying within roughly 5 m of one another are gently spread out around their common centre while keeping the original geographic reference, so the final map remains clear at 1:5 000 scale.

A public-health team has geocoded the home addresses of participants in a city-wide nutrition survey; the resulting spreadsheet (exported as a shapefile of household locations) shows dense stacks of markers in several downtown neighborhoods. To prepare an atlas for community briefings, we need to create a map where every surveyed household is still visible as a separate dot, even in the most crowded blocks, so that stakeholders can clearly count participation per block without symbols hiding one another.

A set of 2 600 legacy drill-hole collar coordinates delivered as a .shp file by the exploration contractor shows numerous collars plotted on top of one another at the 1:5 000 map scale used for the tenement report, making individual holes impossible to label and risking misinterpretation of the drilling density. To prepare a clear collar location plan for the upcoming investor briefing, we need to automatically separate any collars that lie within 25 m of each other by arranging them evenly around their common centre while retaining the original geographic coordinates in the attribute table, then export the adjusted locations as a new point file for direct use in the map layout.

A mineral-exploration company has compiled a .shp file of drill-hole collar coordinates across a prospective lease where many holes were twinned or spaced within a few metres of each other, causing symbols to overlap on the map. To improve visibility of multiple 112 calls reported from almost the same street address, we have a dataset of caller locations saved as a point shapefile from the city’s computer-aided dispatch system. The fire brigade needs a version of this map in which any calls that fall within roughly 25 m of one another are gently spread out around their common centre while keeping the original geographic reference, so incident icons no longer overlap on the screen and each can be selected individually during the response.

During last night’s multi-agency response to a gas-leak alarm in the city centre, control-room staff logged every 999 call as a dot on a live map. Because several callers reported the same incident from neighbouring buildings, the dots now sit almost on top of one another, making it impossible for the duty officer to see how many distinct calls were received. Using the exported .shp file of caller locations, separate any dots that are within 25 m of each other and spread them evenly around their common midpoint so that each emergency call is visible on the incident map.

Wildlife researchers have accumulated several years of GPS-collar fixes for a herd of deer saved as a point shapefile.  Because animals often linger in favoured meadows, many locations stack on top of one another on the map, hiding the true number of observations and cluttering the display.  The team needs a version of the same file in which any fixes that fall within 15 m of each other are gently spread out around their common centre so that every single location remains visible and can be counted.

A wildlife research team has collected a year-long GPS-collar location time-series for a herd of elk, stored as a point shapefile. Because the animals often rest in tight groups, many recorded positions overlap on the map, making it impossible to see how many individuals were present at any site or to label them clearly for public outreach maps. The team needs to separate these stacked points so that every collar location remains visible and identifiable on the final map, while keeping each point as close as possible to its true coordinates.

A health department has geocoded a city-wide survey on access to green space and now needs to prepare the map for a public consultation meeting. Because many residents living in high-rise blocks gave identical or near-identical addresses, the resulting dots pile on top of one another and hide the true density of responses. Starting from the provided point layer derived from an Excel-exported .csv of respondent coordinates, generate a new set of locations that spreads out any answers falling within 25 m of each other so that every reply remains visible while still showing the general neighbourhood where the cluster arose.
Tool: Export cross section dataset value: We have a hydrological study of the lower reach of the Red River that needs to chart how water depth changes along several planned navigation channels. The requirement is to obtain a table showing the simulated water-surface elevation every 10 m along each channel line for the peak-flow time step so the design team can plot depth profiles and check clearance under bridges.

The regional water authority is updating its flood-risk maps for the lower reach of the River Dane. We have a 2-D hydrodynamic model saved as a UGRID NetCDF mesh that stores bed-elevation values for every cell, and a separate shapefile with proposed cross-section survey lines drawn perpendicular to the channel. We need to pull the bed-level heights along each of those lines at 5-metre intervals so the engineers can plot accurate elevation profiles without returning to the field.

To verify turbine-siting guidelines, the project team has a NetCDF-based wind-farm terrain model giving slope values for every 5 m of the site and a shapefile of the proposed turbine access roads drawn as centre-lines. The offshore wind-farm developer has supplied a UGRID netCDF file holding hourly modelled wind speeds over the lease area for the month of March 2023. A separate .shp file marks the exact alignments of the planned turbine rows. A groundwater modelling study has produced a 3-D numerical mesh showing arsenic concentrations across the site. We need to pull the arsenic values from the mesh onto these survey lines at regular 5-metre intervals so that the sampled points can later be plotted as a concentration profile.

We have a 2-D hydraulic model that produced a time-series mesh of dissolved benzene concentrations across an alluvial aquifer.  A consulting firm has supplied a .shp file with several straight survey transects that run from up-gradient to down-gradient across the plume.  The environmental agency needs the benzene values recorded every 5 m along each transect for the snapshot that corresponds to 15 June 2022, delivered as a table so they can plot concentration profiles.

A university research group is monitoring coastal cliff retreat along a 15 km stretch of shoreline in southern England. They possess a time-series of gridded elevation models stored as NetCDF meshes, each representing the cliff face at six-month intervals over the past five years. To monitor seasonal cliff retreat along a 5 km stretch of coastline, we have a series of UGRID netCDF files from a coastal hydrodynamic model that give hourly water-level and wave-energy values for the past two years, and a shapefile of straight transect lines drawn perpendicular to the cliff edge every 50 m. We need to pull the modelled water-level and wave-energy values along each transect at a 1 m spacing so that we can relate them to the corresponding measured cliff-top positions.

A geological survey team has a 3-D mesh model of subsurface rock properties and a polyline shapefile marking the planned tunnel centre-line. They need to obtain the property values (e.g., density, strength) sampled at regular 5-metre intervals along the entire alignment so that the overburden thickness and rock quality can be checked before construction begins.

A geotechnical team needs to verify the overburden thickness above a planned tunnel alignment. A regional forest authority holds a shapefile of distinct management compartments and a point layer of GPS-located tree-infection sightings. Tool: Sample raster values\nAlgorithm ID: During field verification of a satellite-derived land-cover classification, we have a set of GPS waypoints stored as a shapefile and the corresponding classified raster map in GeoTIFF format. A field survey team has collected GPS coordinates of 200 verification sites and needs to compare the on-site observations with the land-cover categories shown on a classified satellite image. Tool: Create random raster layer (expone: To support a synthetic flood-inundation probability study, we need a raster layer spanning the Lower Mississippi Valley (supplied as a bounding box in WGS 84) with 30 m cells whose values represent the likelihood of water presence; each cell should hold an independent random floating-point number drawn from an exponential distribution with mean 1.
