Tool: Download vector tiles\nAlgorithm I: A forestry survey team needs to take a detailed road-and-trail basemap into a mountain region where mobile coverage is unreliable. They have identified an online vector tile service that shows roads, trails, rivers, and contour lines. They would like to capture all tiles covering their 25 km² survey block (maximum scale 1:5 000) and store them in a single offline file so the map can be viewed in the field without any internet connection.

A forestry service needs to equip field teams with a detailed, zoomable map of the concession area for an upcoming two-week inventory in a region without reliable internet. They have access to an online vector-tile basemap that shows roads, streams, and stand boundaries. To ensure the crews can pan and zoom without connectivity, the service wants to save the tiles covering the entire concession to a single file that can be copied onto tablets before departure.

After last night’s flash-flood emergency, the county EOC needs an up-to-date street-and-building map covering the 5 km evacuation zone around the Rock River levee breach. We have the state’s online vector tile service for roads, structures, and parcel lines. Please pull a local copy of that map for the area inside the coordinates 41.48°–41.53° N, 90.22°–90.15° W, zoomed in enough to show individual buildings and down to no more than 100 tiles so the file can be shared offline with field crews.

The National Park Service is upgrading its trail-kiosk information displays and needs the most current trail and facility data for the entire Blue Ridge Parkway unit. We have access to a live online map service that shows roads, trails, campgrounds, and ranger stations as vector tiles. The goal is to capture all visible features that fall within the Parkway’s corridor from milepost 0 near Rockfish Gap, VA, to milepost 469 near Cherokee, NC, and store them in a single local file that can be used offline at the kiosks.

For a new series of interactive trail kiosks being planned across Yellowstone National Park, the park service needs to obtain an offline set of detailed park roads, trails, rivers, and contour lines that will be displayed on the kiosks’ built-in maps. The data must cover the entire park boundary and be saved as a compact file that the kiosk software can read quickly without an internet connection. The source is the park’s existing online vector tile service, and the download should capture all detail levels visible when zoomed in as close as a hiker would view a trail junction.

To establish a baseline for historical change-detection of riverbanks in the Lower Mekong Delta, we need to obtain the 2010 vector tile layer served by the national mapping agency at https://maps.mekong.gov/2010-rivers. Please capture all tiles covering the deltaic reach from Kratie to the South China Sea, up to the most detailed zoom level, and save the resulting tiles locally for subsequent comparison with recent imagery.

For a historical change-detection study covering the 1950–1970 period, we have located an online vector-tile layer that displays scanned 1960-era topographic linework. We need to save a local copy of this layer that covers the entire lower downtown district of Riverton, so that the 1960 street network and building footprints can later be compared with present-day maps. Please extract and store the tiles for that district, zooming in enough to capture individual building outlines while staying within a reasonable download size.

The Urban Planning Office is compiling a reference set of OpenStreetMap vector tiles covering the entire metropolitan area to support offline thematic mapping at town-hall briefings. They have identified an online vector tile service that hosts up-to-date city layers and need to obtain a local copy for the rectangular area enclosing Metroville’s administrative boundary (the north, south, east, and west limits are already known and will be supplied as decimal degree coordinates) up to the most detailed zoom level practical, while keeping the download within a reasonable tile count. The resulting file should be stored on the office server so planners can overlay it with future zoning and infrastructure datasets without requiring an internet connection.

A municipal planning office has already added the city’s online street-level basemap service to its project and now needs to take a portable copy of the central district to the field where connectivity is unreliable. The service, rendered as a vector tile layer in the current map, is to be harvested for every tile that intersects the district boundary at a scale fine enough to depict individual buildings, poles, and kerbs. The office expects a compact local file that survey tablets can open offline for orientation and on-site feature checks.

The Provincial Emergency Operations Centre has located an online map service that streams road networks and building footprints as vector tiles for the cyclone-affected district. To equip field teams with a detailed, offline reference, they need to extract the portion of this service that falls within the district’s boundaries and save it as a local file, ensuring the finest practical detail is captured for street-level navigation and structure identification.
Tool: Download file\nAlgorithm ID: qgis:: To support a watershed delineation study for the upper Green River basin, retrieve the 1-arc-second digital elevation model hosted at https://prd-tnm.s3.amazonaws.com/StagedProducts/Elevation/1/TIFF/n47w122/USGS_1_n47w122.tif so it can be used locally.

The regional council is updating its hydrological models for the upper Riverdale catchment and needs the latest 1-arc-second elevation dataset published by the national mapping agency. The dataset is hosted at https://data.gov/riverdale_dem.tif and must be retrieved so it can be used to delineate watershed boundaries and derive flow-direction grids.

Before heading into the field next week, the survey team needs the most recent OpenStreetMap extract for the district. A direct link to the latest "district-latest.osm.pbf" file hosted at https://download.geofabrik.de/asia/district-latest.osm.pbf should be retrieved so the handheld devices can load the current basemap.

To support a habitat-suitability study for a rare alpine plant, a research team needs the latest 30-year climate raster time-series (available as a public GeoTIFF at https://data.climate.gov/alpine/temperature_1991-2020.tif). Please retrieve this file so it can be used in downstream analyses.

The regional climate office has published a new 30-year monthly precipitation raster series at https://climate.region.gov/monthly-precip-30yr.tif; please retrieve this file so it can be used to assess long-term habitat moisture conditions for the upcoming species distribution study.

Our regional agricultural office needs to start this season’s crop-health monitoring. We have located a recent Sentinel-2 scene at https://scihub.copernicus.eu/dhus/odata/v1/Products('a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890')/$value that covers our county. Please retrieve this file so we can inspect the latest multispectral imagery before distributing it to local agronomists.

As part of a province-wide crop-health monitoring initiative, the agricultural office needs the most recent Sentinel-2 satellite scene (provided as a direct download link from the national geoportal) saved to the local shared drive so analysts can begin assessing this season’s vegetation vigor.

The national mapping agency has published a new reference boundary set for administrative units at https://example.gov/data/admin_boundaries_2024.zip. We need to fetch this file so it can be unpacked and compared against our existing geodatabase holdings during the quarterly QA/QC review.

To support the geodatabase quality-assurance review, we need to obtain the official municipal boundary shapefile that is published at https://data.city.gov/boundaries/city_limit.zip and save it locally so it can be compared against our in-house version.
Tool: Z values\nAlgorithm ID: native:dro: A national mapping agency updating its 1:50 000 topographic series needs to simplify the coastline layer stored as a .gpkg file that was originally captured with elevation heights attached to every vertex. To meet the 2-D-only specification of the new generalized product, the dataset must be delivered with all height information stripped from the geometry coordinates while preserving the shoreline shape itself.

A national mapping agency is modernising its 1:50 000 topographic series for web delivery and needs to simplify the coastline layer supplied as a GeoPackage containing three-dimensional coordinate strings (x, y, z). The vertical heights embedded in every vertex are surplus for the final 2-D map and must be stripped away before further generalisation, ensuring the resulting layer contains only plain latitude-longitude pairs.

For a city-wide pedestrian-network project, we have received a three-dimensional street-centerline dataset (.gpkg) that includes height information for every vertex; the modelling software we must feed accepts only simple, flat lines. Please provide the same lines with the height details stripped away.

A city transport department is preparing a road-centreline dataset downloaded as a .gpkg file from the provincial mapping portal. The file contains three-dimensional coordinates plus linear referencing measures that are not recognised by the department’s older traffic-modelling software. They need a version of the same road layer that keeps the geometry but discards the elevation and measure attributes so it can be imported without errors.

A municipal planning office has received a three-dimensional shapefile of building footprints that includes height information stored as extra elevation numbers attached to each corner. Their legacy mapping software cannot read these extra numbers and crashes when the file is loaded. They need a version of the same file with the height numbers removed so the footprints display correctly on their flat map.

A municipal engineering office has received a three-dimensional shapefile of the city’s street centerlines exported from a CAD-based survey system. The file carries unwanted elevation numbers attached to every vertex, causing the office’s standard mapping software to mis-interpret the geometry and display lines at incorrect heights. The office needs a clean copy of the same street network with the elevation information stripped away so it can be used in routine cartographic products and route-planning tasks.

The regional planning office is preparing a simplified parcel dataset for sharing with a neighbouring province whose GIS platform cannot handle height or linear-measure attributes.  We have a .gpkg file holding the county’s land-parcel geometries, each recorded with rooftop elevation figures and chainage values along boundaries.  Produce a version of this file that keeps the same shapes but strips away all height and distance-along-line numbers so the dataset can be imported without error.

A regional planning office needs to share its 3-D building footprint dataset (.shp) with a municipal partner whose software cannot read height information. Produce a version of the file that contains only the flat ground-level outlines so it can be imported without errors.

A municipal planning office has received a detailed 3-D building footprint dataset (.shp) from the national mapping agency. Because the downstream statistical software used for housing-density studies cannot process height information stored with each shape, the planners need a copy of the layer with the height values removed while keeping every other attribute intact.

A municipal planning office has received a detailed 3-D building footprint layer (.shp) from the cadastral survey that includes floor-by-floor height information stored as extra numbers on every outline; they need a plain, flat copy of the footprints without these height numbers so the simplified geometry can be imported into their legacy SQL database that only recognises two-dimensional shapes.
Tool: List unique values\nAlgorithm ID:: To support a province-wide land-cover inventory, we have received a shapefile of 2023 land-use polygons from the Ministry of Natural Resources. We need to know every distinct land-cover category recorded in the dataset and how many different types exist, so that the inventory report can list the complete set of classes before further area calculations are carried out.

As part of a province-wide land-cover inventory we have received a shapefile of 2023 land-use polygons from the Ministry of Environment. We need to know every distinct land-cover class that appears in the dataset and how many different classes there are so we can check that our legend is complete before printing the atlas.

A regional soil survey team has compiled a polygon shapefile of field-delineated map units across the county; each polygon carries a ‘SoilType’ label. To prepare a concise legend for the forthcoming soil-type reconnaissance report, they need to see every distinct soil type name that occurs in the dataset and know how many different names there are in total.

During a soil-type reconnaissance project, a field team has digitised each sampled plot into a shapefile that records the dominant texture class observed (e.g., clay, sand, loam). To prepare a summary for the pedology report, we need to know how many distinct texture classes occur across the surveyed plots and how many plots fall into each class. The shapefile ‘soil_plots.shp’ contains a column named ‘texture’ with these descriptions.

The regional statistics office is reviewing the administrative unit boundaries layer (a .shp file supplied by the mapping agency) to ensure coding consistency. They need to see every distinct category name recorded in the ‘ADMIN_LEVEL’ column together with how many times each appears, so they can quickly spot any misspelled or duplicate entries before the dataset is approved for publication.

The regional audit office has received a shapefile of all administrative units in the province. They need a concise roster showing every distinct category currently recorded in the "unit_type" column, together with how many units fall under each category, so they can verify that the classification scheme is complete and up-to-date.

A national park service is compiling a species distribution checklist for a newly surveyed wetland reserve. They possess a single .shp file listing every plant and animal observation recorded during the field campaign, with each entry containing a column labelled "Species_Name". To complete the checklist they need to see every distinct species name that appears in the file, together with how many separate observations were logged for each one.

A wildlife research team has compiled a point shapefile of verified bat sightings across the state, with each record noting the species name in a column labelled 'species'. They need a concise report listing every distinct bat species that has been documented, along with how many records exist for each, so they can quickly verify whether a newly observed species should be added to the state’s official species distribution checklist.

To verify the completeness of elevation band coverage in the regional topographic survey, the planning office has received a shapefile of 1 km grid cells covering the entire mountain province. Each cell record includes an ‘ElevBand’ attribute (values such as 0–200 m, 200–400 m, 400–600 m, etc.). The planners need a concise list of every distinct elevation band present in the dataset and a count of how many grid cells fall within each band so they can confirm whether all expected elevation ranges are represented.

A national park authority has received a shapefile of hiking trails within the park and needs to confirm that every recorded trail is tagged with one of the three approved difficulty ratings—Easy, Moderate, or Hard—before publishing the next visitor map. The authority would like a concise list showing which of these ratings actually appear in the file and how many trails carry each rating, so they can spot any missing or incorrect labels.
Tool: Statistics by categories\nAlgorith: The regional statistics office is reviewing the administrative unit boundaries layer (a .shp file supplied by the mapping agency) to ensure coding consistency. They need to see every distinct category name recorded in the ‘ADMIN_LEVEL’ column together with how many times each appears, so they can quickly spot any misspelled or duplicate entries before the dataset is approved for publication.

The regional audit office has received a shapefile of all administrative units in the province. They need a concise roster showing every distinct category currently recorded in the "unit_type" column, together with how many units fall under each category, so they can verify that the classification scheme is complete and up-to-date.

A regional planning office holds a shapefile of land parcels that records each parcel’s municipality name, its land-use category (residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, etc.), and its area in square metres. The office needs a concise table showing, for every municipality, the total area covered by each distinct land-use type so that elected officials can quickly review how land is distributed across the region.

A city planning office has received a geopackage with every building footprint in the metropolitan area, each record listing the neighborhood name, the decade it was built, and its exact height in metres. The planners need a summary table that shows, for every combination of neighborhood and construction decade, how many buildings exist and what their average height is, so they can quickly compare development intensities and typical vertical scale across different parts of the city and across different historical periods.

A city planning office holds a shapefile of all buildings that includes each building’s height, neighborhood name, and construction-era label. It needs a summary table that shows, for every combination of neighborhood and era, the average building height and the total number of buildings.

A regional agricultural office has a shapefile of soil-sample points that record, for each location, the measured nitrogen content in mg/kg, the mapped soil type (e.g., loam, clay, sandy), and the slope class (flat, moderate, steep). The office needs a concise summary table that shows the average, minimum, and maximum nitrogen content for every combination of soil type and slope class across the study area.

A regional soil survey team has compiled a .shp file of soil sample points across the province, each point carrying numeric nutrient levels, a soil-type label, and a slope-class label. They need a summary table showing the average, minimum, and maximum nutrient levels for every combination of soil type and slope class so that agronomists can quickly compare fertility conditions across land units.

A regional road-safety study has compiled a point shapefile of all traffic crashes recorded over the past five years, with each point carrying attributes for crash severity, road class, and weather condition at the time of the incident. The research team needs to know, for every combination of road class and weather condition, the average severity score and the total number of crashes, so they can identify which roadway and weather pairings produce the most serious outcomes.

A state highway safety office has compiled five years of traffic-crash records in a point shapefile that records, for each incident, how many people were injured and whether the crash happened on an interstate, US highway, state road, or local street.  The file also notes the weather at the time (clear, rain, snow, fog, etc.).  The office needs a summary table that shows, for every combination of road type and weather, the total number of crashes, the total people injured, and the average number of injuries per crash so it can identify which road-weather combinations are most harmful.

The regional planning office holds a single shapefile in which every land-use polygon across the province already carries a pre-calculated numeric field expressing its area in hectares; each record is further tagged with its municipality name and land-use class (residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, recreational). We need a concise table that adds up the hectare values for every combination of municipality and land-use class so the totals can be inserted into the forthcoming annual report.

A national park authority holds a single point layer in which every 30 m cell inside the park is represented by a point carrying the mean summer NDVI value, the land-cover label (forest, grassland, wetland, etc.), and the name of the protection zone it falls within. To support habitat-health reporting, the authority needs a summary table that lists, for each combination of protection zone and land-cover type, the average NDVI across all points sharing that combination.

A conservation agency has a single polygon shapefile in which every polygon already stores both its protected-area zone name and its land-cover label, along with a field of precalculated NDVI values. They need to obtain the average NDVI for each distinct pairing of protection zone and land-cover type to compare vegetation health across management categories.
Tool: Set M value\nAlgorithm ID: native:: The state highway department has imported a statewide road centerline file (Esri shapefile) into a new linear-referencing project. Each route currently carries only x,y coordinates; to enable mile-post-based event mapping, every vertex along every line must now carry the same initial distance measure of 0.0 so the department can begin calibrating routes with known mile-point values in a later step.

For the initial planning of a new natural-gas pipeline corridor, the engineering team has received a .shp file that traces the proposed centerline through the county. Before sending this line to the survey crew for mile-by-mile annotations, every vertex along the route must be tagged with the starting chainage of zero so that later field measurements can simply accumulate distance from this uniform baseline. Please update the geometry so that each point on the proposed route carries this initial reference value.

A geodetic survey office has received a freshly collected set of GPS tracks stored as a .gpkg file representing a new hiking trail network. To prepare the data for a linear referencing system that will later support mile-post signage, every vertex along each trail needs to carry the same initial distance measure of zero. Provide the file so that all geometries are updated in place with this uniform starting measure.

The Department of Transport is preparing a statewide road centerline file for a future linear-referencing upgrade. As an initial step, each line must first be tagged with a uniform reference value of 0.0 so that later, specialized routines can replace this placeholder with true mile-point measures. A single shapefile holding the current road centerlines is on hand, and the task is to embed this starting value into every geometry.

To prepare the preliminary centerline of a new gas-pipeline corridor, we have received a polyline shapefile from the survey contractor that traces the proposed route across the county. Before this line is handed to the risk-analysis team, every vertex along the route must be marked with a constant reference value of 100 for compatibility with the downstream linear-referencing system. Please update the file so that each geometry is assigned this uniform value, ensuring the layer is upgraded to support the required linear-referencing attribute.

A national park’s trail-maintenance team has a .gpkg file that records the exact path of the park’s main hiking route. The team wishes to tag every line in the file with a uniform mile-marker reference value of 0.0, thereby preparing the dataset for a later stage in which more detailed, point-by-point distance measures will be added by another process. They therefore require the route file to be updated so that each line geometry carries the same initial reference number across all its vertices.

To mark river-reach centerlines with a simple distance flag before more detailed coding, we need to attach a single reference value (10 km) to every line in the polyline shapefile that stores the river network; this uniform tag will later tell any downstream step that these reaches have been pre-processed and are ready for further distance-based identification.

A municipal engineer has received a .gpkg file containing the centreline of a newly constructed cycling path. The geometry is currently plain X,Y only, yet the asset-management database expects every vertex to carry the same linear-measure placeholder so the layer can later accept vertex-specific distances computed elsewhere. Please assign a uniform value of 0 to every vertex so the path geometry is upgraded to include measure support and is ready for subsequent distance tagging.
Tool: Raster surface volume\nAlgorithm I: We are updating the water-resource plan for a mountain catchment and need to know how much water the natural basin above the proposed dam wall can hold. A 1 m resolution DEM of the valley floor and surrounding slopes is available. Please determine the total air-space volume between the land surface and the proposed normal water level of 1 250 m above sea level, so we can estimate the live storage that would be created if the basin were filled to that elevation.

A regional water authority needs to know how much water can be stored above the planned spillway crest at a candidate dam site.  They have a 1-metre resolution GeoTIFF showing ground heights across the valley and wish to determine the total space that lies higher than the proposed crest elevation of 315 m above sea level.

A mining company has acquired a 1 m resolution digital elevation model (GeoTIFF) of an open-pit mine surveyed before any excavation began. To plan overburden removal, they need to know how much rock and soil lie above the 650 m elevation plane across the entire pit area. Provide the total volume of material that sits higher than this reference level so that the engineers can estimate haulage requirements and associated costs.

An open-pit mine operator holds a GeoTIFF elevation model of the current pit floor and needs to know how much rock and soil sit above the 1 200 m elevation plane so that overburden removal costs can be estimated; the mine survey department can supply the elevation model and wishes to receive a concise report listing the total material volume, the corresponding surface area, and the number of cells used in the calculation.

A research team studying regional glacier retreat needs to quantify how much ice has vanished from a 2005 digital elevation model stored as a GeoTIFF. They would like to know the total amount of material that once stood above the local equilibrium-line altitude of 2,800 m so that the result can be compared with repeat LiDAR surveys planned for next season.

A research team studying glacier retreat has a GeoTIFF elevation model of a mountain range surveyed in 2020. They need to know how much ice remains above the equilibrium-line altitude of 3,200 m so they can compare it with future surveys and estimate water-storage loss.

A regional emergency-management office has received a 1-m resolution GeoTIFF elevation model of the lower valley. They need to know how much water could be stored above the valley floor if the river overtops its banks and spreads evenly up to the 5-m contour, so they can size temporary retention basins accordingly.

A regional emergency-management office has received a 1-m resolution GeoTIFF elevation grid covering the lower reach of the Red River. They need to know how much water would be stored above the valley floor if the river were to overtop its banks and fill all land below the 235 m elevation contour, in order to size a planned detention basin.

To support ongoing landfill operations, we have a recent GeoTIFF elevation model of the active disposal area. We need to know how much airspace remains above the current waste surface up to the permitted final elevation of 1,525 ft (MSL) so the site manager can schedule incoming loads and plan cell development.

The regional waste authority needs to know how much empty space is left in the existing landfill so it can schedule the next cell expansion.  They have a recent 1-metre resolution elevation model of the site supplied as a GeoTIFF that shows the current top surface of the waste mound.  Using the approved final ground level of 315 m above sea level as the reference, they want the exact cubic metres of airspace still available above that height across the entire facility.
Tool: Rename field\nAlgorithm ID: qgis:r: The National Statistics Office is preparing county-level population tables from the 2020 census for release to the public. One GeoPackage file holds the county boundaries together with an attribute column currently labeled “POP_2020_EST”; for consistency with other datasets, this heading must appear simply as “Population_2020” in the final product. Provide a new version of the layer that keeps all existing information intact while displaying the updated column title.

A national statistics office is updating its 2021 census dissemination platform to align with the new international metadata standard. Among the delivered files is a county-level shapefile whose attribute table still labels total population as “POP_TOT_21”, whereas the standard requires the plain heading “TotalPop2021”. The office needs a fresh copy of the layer in which that single column heading is changed to the prescribed form so it can be published without further editing.

A county soil survey office has received a shapefile of agricultural parcels where the field recording crop type is labelled ‘CROP_TYP’. To match the naming convention used in the annual land-use report, the office needs the same file returned with that column heading changed to ‘CropType’ while keeping all other information intact.

The regional soil survey provided a shapefile where the field storing soil pH values is labelled “pH_2019”, while the national database we need to merge it with expects the same information under the heading “Soil_pH”. We therefore need to take the delivered shapefile and produce a new copy in which that column is simply given the correct name so the two tables will match during the later joining step.

Our company has adopted a new enterprise-wide GIS naming standard, and the parcel shapefile supplied by the county assessor still uses the old column heading “PARCEL_NUM”. To comply with the standard, we need the same dataset returned with that column relabelled as “ParcelID” while keeping every other attribute intact.

The city’s planning department maintains a shapefile of zoning polygons whose attribute table includes a column still labelled with the legacy internal code ‘ZONE_CD’. To bring this dataset into line with the corporate naming standard, they need to replace that heading with the official public name ‘ZoningClass’ while keeping all existing records intact.

The city’s open-data portal is preparing a downloadable GeoPackage of public parks that currently contains a field labelled "MNG_UNIT". To make the dataset more intuitive for non-technical users, the portal needs the same file returned with that column relabelled as "ManagingAuthority" while keeping all other information intact.

A municipal open-data portal is preparing to release a shapefile of city-maintained street trees. The dataset’s attribute table currently labels the species column with the internal code “spp_code”, a name that is unclear to the public. Before publication, the portal needs the column to appear as “TreeSpecies” so residents can easily understand and use the information.

A regional planning office is merging two municipal parcel datasets, both delivered as shapefiles. One file calls the ownership column “PROP_OWNER” while the other uses “OwnerName”; to avoid confusion in the combined map, the office needs the first file’s column to carry the same heading “OwnerName” before the datasets are brought together.

A regional planning office is preparing to merge two municipal parcel datasets, both delivered as shapefiles. Each file contains a column labeled “ZONE” that stores land-use codes, but the offices that produced the datasets use slightly different naming conventions for the codes. Before the datasets can be combined, the office needs to change the heading of the zone column in one of the shapefiles to “ZONE_CAT” so that the two tables can be distinguished after they are joined.
Tool: based)\nAlgorithm ID: native:dtmsl: A city planning office wants to separate bare-earth elevations from buildings and trees in a 1 m resolution LiDAR-derived elevation grid (GeoTIFF) covering the downtown core so that only ground heights remain for storm-runoff modelling in a flat-to-rolling urban landscape.

The city engineering office has a 1 m-resolution elevation grid from last year’s airborne survey covering the downtown core. To refine the storm-runoff model, they need a bare-earth surface that excludes buildings, trees, and cars so that only true ground heights remain.

A LiDAR-derived elevation raster covering the proposed forest road corridor is available, but it includes tree canopies and understory vegetation that obscure the underlying ground shape. To design a road alignment that follows natural terrain, we need to isolate the bare-earth surface by removing all above-ground features from the elevation model while preserving the true ground elevations.

During a forest road network planning study in a hilly catchment, we have a GeoTIFF elevation grid from airborne lidar that still shows tree crowns, buildings and power-lines. We need to separate the bare-earth surface from everything that sits above it so that later hydraulic modelling can be fed only ground heights. Please process the elevation grid to give back two fresh grids: one that keeps just the ground heights and another that isolates all off-ground objects.

A provincial geological survey team needs to separate bare-earth elevations from vegetation and buildings in a 1 m-resolution airborne LiDAR elevation grid covering steep, forested mountain slopes so that the cleaned ground surface can be used to map landslide-prone areas; the team has the original elevation grid in GeoTIFF format and wants two new grids back—one showing only the ground heights and the other showing everything that was removed.

We have a 1 m-resolution elevation raster covering a steep mountain catchment where past landslides left scattered building-sized boulders on the slopes. A separate field campaign provided the raw elevation surface but it still contains these boulders, cars, and small retaining walls that are not part of the natural ground. To prepare a clean ground-only elevation layer for the subsequent landslide-susceptibility zoning, we need to remove all above-ground objects from the dataset while preserving the underlying terrain.

A regional archaeological project in the semi-arid interior has acquired a 1 m-resolution elevation model (delivered as a GeoTIFF) from an airborne lidar survey flown to reveal subtle prehistoric burial mounds that rise only 0.3–1 m above the surrounding plain. To isolate the mounds from modern disturbances such as low walls, dirt roads and animal burrows, we need to separate the genuine ground surface from all elevated objects. Please process the elevation grid so that we receive two new grids: one showing only the bare earth and another highlighting everything that sits above it.

As part of a coastal-erosion monitoring programme, we have a 1 m-resolution elevation grid covering a rapidly retreating cliff top that was surveyed by airborne lidar last month. We need to separate the natural ground surface from vegetation, buildings and other objects so that we can track true terrain changes between surveys. Please process the elevation grid to produce two new grids: one showing only the bare-earth heights and another highlighting everything that sits above the ground.

To support annual coastal-erosion mapping, the regional planning office possesses a 1 m lidar-derived elevation grid (GeoTIFF) that still contains dunes, boardwalks, and beach furniture. They need a clean surface that shows only the bare beach and fore-dune ground levels so that successive yearly surveys can be compared to quantify volume change.
Tool: Project points (Cartesian)\nAlgori: A maritime safety study needs to create a set of emergency rendezvous positions for vessels transiting a busy strait. Starting from an existing .shp file of recorded AIS ship positions, each original location must be shifted 2 nautical miles ahead along the reported heading so planners can visualise where assistance tugs should station themselves. The result should be delivered as a new point layer showing these forward-shifted rendezvous spots.

To plan a straight-line transect for geological sampling, we have a single GPS point marking the starting location of a proposed traverse across an outcrop belt. From this spot we need to generate the exact position that lies 1 200 metres away on a bearing of 065° (measured clockwise from north), so that field crews can navigate directly to the end-point and lay out sampling stations evenly between the two locations. The supplied data are the initial waypoint stored in a shapefile of point features.

To plan a geological sampling transect, we have a .shp file of existing sample-site coordinates collected during last year’s reconnaissance. For each of these points we need to mark the location exactly 200 m farther along the planned compass bearing of 45° (north-east) so field teams can place the next sampling station in a straight line.

A licensed surveyor has recovered the original iron pin at the north-east corner of a rural 5-hectare lot and needs to re-establish the other three boundary corners from the 1898 field notes. The notes state that, starting from the found pin, the southern corner lies 210.5 m at a bearing of 178°, the western corner is 150.2 m at 268°, and the north-west corner is 210.5 m at 358°. The survey office has supplied a shapefile showing only the recovered pin’s location. The task is to plot the exact positions of the three missing corners so that new pegs can be set in the ground prior to the forthcoming subdivision survey.

A licensed surveyor has a .shp file of original cadastral corner pegs from 1952 and needs to re-establish two missing boundary corners. For each missing corner, the historical field notes give a compass bearing and a ground distance from an existing peg. The task is to plot the exact ground location where each new corner should be set out, expressed as a new set of points.

A regional energy consultancy has received a shapefile of household locations reported as sensitive to shadow-flicker from a proposed wind farm. They need to shift each residence marker 500 m due south to represent the position where the same occupants would first experience turbine-blade glint in the late afternoon, enabling them to update the receptor map for the environmental statement.

To support an environmental-impact study on shadow-flicker annoyance, we have a .shp file that records the exact coordinates of each wind-turbine mast. For every turbine we need to generate the location where a receptor would first experience flicker at sunrise, assuming the sun rises exactly due east and the first shadow extends 500 m from the tower. Provide a new set of points marking these 500 m sunrise-shadow receptor positions.

A coastal shipping company holds a .shp file of existing lighthouse beacons along a busy channel, stored in a projected coordinate system with units in metres. To plan nightly routes, they need to generate a second set of positions 3 704 m ahead of each beacon along the heading the ships normally steer when passing it (given in degrees from north). The new points will serve as advance waypoints so masters know when to start their next course change.
Tool: Overlap analysis\nAlgorithm ID: na: The regional land-registry office holds a shapefile of land parcels covering the coastal county; each parcel record already stores its area in square metres. After a separate step has produced a new column giving the area of each parcel that lies within the state-declared protected shoreline zone, the office now wishes to add a further column that expresses this overlapping area as a simple percentage of the parcel’s total area, enabling taxation incentives to be assigned without further manual arithmetic.

A regional conservation office holds a shapefile of all Ramsar-listed wetlands and a second shapefile of nationally designated protected areas. They need to identify only those wetlands that lie inside any protected area so they can report on the proportion of wetland habitat already under protection.
Tool: Extend lines\nAlgorithm ID: native: The city’s public-works department has a shapefile showing the centre-lines of planned residential streets. Before finalising the junction design, they need each street to be lengthened by 20 m at the beginning and 15 m at the end so that the new ends will meet and form proper intersections. A fresh shapefile is required that contains the lengthened street lines.

The coastal planning office has a polyline shapefile of river centrelines that stop 30 m short of the shoreline shown in a separate aerial image. We need the lines to be prolonged so they visibly reach the coast, lengthening the upstream end by 20 m and the downstream end by 10 m to close the gap.

A municipal utilities department has a shapefile of water-pipe centerlines that were captured during a GPS survey. Some pipes appear to stop just short of the curb stop valves shown on as-built drawings, leaving apparent gaps of roughly 1–2 m at each end. The engineers need the pipe traces to reach the valves so that the network graph will connect properly for pressure-loss modeling. They therefore require the line layer to be prolonged by a uniform 1.5 m at every starting point and by 1.0 m at every ending point, producing a new line set that can be fed directly into the connectivity model.

The water company has a .shp file of its pressurised mains, but many pipes appear to end just short of the next fitting. To close the apparent gaps and create a topologically connected network for flow modelling, the utility needs to lengthen every main in the file by 5 m at the upstream end and 3 m at the downstream end, following the existing alignment.

A cadastral survey team has a .shp file of incomplete parcel boundary sketches digitised from field notes; the lines stop short of meeting neighbouring parcels by roughly 3 m at each end. Produce a revised line layer in which every boundary sketch is prolonged by 3 m at both its start and finish so the segments can later be connected into closed parcel polygons.

The engineering team has a .shp file showing the surveyed centre-lines of a proposed fibre-optic cable route. Before preparing the final splicing diagrams they need each line to be visually prolonged by 15 m at the beginning and 25 m at the end so that the ducts appear to run neatly into the planned joint chambers and termination boxes. Provide a new layer with these slightly longer route traces.

In preparation for generating splicing diagrams for a new fibre-optic cable route, we have a .shp file holding the surveyed centre lines of the ducts that will house the fibres. To ensure the drawn cables visibly reach the splice chambers at each end and overlap slightly for clear annotation, we need to lengthen every line so it continues a short, fixed distance beyond its current start and finish points.

The city’s public works department is digitising its road centre-lines from a recent survey delivered as a GeoPackage file. Several cul-de-sacs and minor residential streets were captured just short of the kerb intersections; each line must be prolonged by 10 m at both ends so that, once the layer is updated, the geometry reaches the adjoining roads and the network can be used for connectivity modelling without gaps.

A municipal cadastral office holds a .shp file of parcel boundary line work surveyed from field notes. Owing to minor measurement imprecision, every line terminates a uniform 0.25 m short of its intended junction, so neighbouring ends fail to touch and no closed parcel polygons can be formed. The office wishes to add exactly this fixed length to the start and end of every line so that all ends meet their counterparts, enabling straightforward compilation of complete parcel outlines without re-surveying.
Tool: Grid (Nearest neighbor)\nAlgorithm: A civil engineering firm has collected 12 000 individual height readings across a future construction site using a high-precision GPS rover. The points are stored in a shapefile with x-, y-coordinates and an ‘elev_m’ field. The company now needs a continuous elevation surface so that any planned location on the site can be assigned the exact height measured at the closest survey point. Provide a GeoTIFF raster that covers the surveyed area and carries these closest-measured elevations in each cell.

A regional geology office has conducted a GPS-based height survey; the resulting .shp file lists thousands of single-point elevation readings scattered across a mountainous county. To prepare a printable base map for planners, they need to turn these discrete spot heights into a continuous surface so that every 10 m cell carries the elevation recorded at the closest survey point.

A regional agricultural agency has surveyed 3,000 field observation points recording the current crop type at each location and saved them as a point shapefile. To create a quick-reference wall map for county extension officers, the agency needs to turn these scattered observations into a continuous grid that assigns every 10 m cell the crop type measured at the closest survey point, leaving cells blank where no point is found within 200 m.

We have a point shapefile containing field measurements of soil type at sample locations across a 10 km² watershed.  We need to turn these spot records into a continuous categorical raster map (10 m cell size) that assigns each pixel the exact soil class recorded at the nearest sampling point, leaving any cell whose nearest point lies beyond 200 m unclassified.

The marine survey team has collected a set of single-beam depth soundings saved as a .shp file with point geometry and a depth attribute. To provide an immediate overview for the cruise report, we need to turn these scattered measurements into a simple gridded image where every cell shows the exact depth recorded at the closest sounding, leaving cells blank where no measurement exists within a 25 m radius.

A marine survey has delivered a dense set of single-beam depth soundings stored as a .shp point file. To let the project team inspect the coverage and general shape of the seafloor before final processing, produce a quick-look raster that gives every grid cell the exact depth recorded at the closest sounding within a 25 m search distance, marking any gaps as “no data”.

A mining survey team has collected several thousand point measurements of gold concentration in grams per tonne across an open-pit bench. The coordinates and assay values are stored in a CSV file that can be opened as a point layer. To guide daily ore-waste decisions, the geologists need a continuous picture of grade across the entire bench so they can instantly read the expected value at any spot. They therefore require a regular grid where each cell simply carries the assay value measured at the closest sample point, leaving cells blank only where no sample exists within a 25 m search distance.

To support a regional climate-monitoring bulletin, we have a point layer of yesterday’s noon temperature readings recorded at 150 weather stations across the state. We need to turn these point measurements into a continuous surface so that every 1 km grid cell carries the exact temperature value reported by the closest station, producing a quick-reference temperature snapshot map for emergency managers and the public.

The regional climate office has compiled a point layer of yesterday’s noon temperature readings from 200 weather stations scattered across the province, with each point carrying the measured temperature. To quickly visualize the spatial pattern of these readings, we need to create a continuous temperature surface raster that simply adopts the value recorded at the closest station for every cell, treating any gaps beyond the station network as unknown.

A mine survey has provided a point layer of thousands of assay sample locations with their recorded gold grades in grams per tonne. The geology team needs a regular grid surface showing the exact grade measured at the closest sample point for each 5 m by 5 m cell across the entire ore body, so that daily grade-control decisions can be based on a clear map of the sampled values without any smoothing or averaging.
Tool: Snap points to grid\nAlgorithm ID:: To prepare GPS-surveyed tree positions from a .shp file for a city-wide canopy-change study, we need to round every recorded location to a uniform 5-metre neighbourhood grid so that later comparisons with older raster maps will line up consistently.

To prepare a set of GPS-collected tree positions (provided as a .shp file) for a change-detection study, we need every recorded point to be shifted to the nearest intersection of a 5 m × 5 m reference grid so that subsequent raster comparisons can be made on perfectly aligned cell centres.

To support a study on generalising noisy drone GPS trajectories, we have a .gpkg file holding the raw flight paths recorded at one-second intervals. We need every point of these paths to be shifted to the nearest intersection of a 2-metre-square mesh so that the tracks align cleanly with the planned survey grid and subsequent elevation comparisons are not biased by sub-metre wobble.

A research team has collected a set of drone flight trajectories saved as a line shapefile, but the GPS readings contain small positional jitter that makes the paths appear jagged. They would like all vertex positions to be shifted to the nearest points on a regular 1 m × 1 m grid so the tracks look cleaner and consistent with their 1 m resolution elevation model.

To prepare the collar coordinates of 3,000 exploration boreholes (stored as a .shp file) for a regular 3-D block model, adjust each collar location so it aligns with the nearest node of a 25 m × 25 m horizontal grid, leaving the elevation unchanged. The result should be a new layer of collar points whose coordinates are rounded to this grid.

We have a CSV file of collar coordinates from recent exploratory drilling across the licence block. The points were recorded to centimetre precision, but for consistency with the existing 3-D block model grid (which uses 10 m nodes) we need to shift every collar location to the nearest model grid intersection before building the triangulation and assigning grades.

To support a hex-bin visualization of geotagged social-media posts, we need to align every post location from the provided GeoPackage file to a perfectly regular grid so that all points fall on consistent, evenly spaced positions; the grid should have 500-metre intervals in both east-west and north-south directions, producing a uniform mesh ready for downstream aggregation into hexagonal bins.

To prepare a set of geotagged social-media posts stored as a point shapefile for hex-bin mapping, we need to align every post location to an invisible regular grid so that posts falling within the same tiny square are given identical coordinates, ensuring they will later occupy the same hexagonal cell.

The national cadastral authority is preparing to stitch together neighbouring 1:5 000 map sheets covering the border region between two provinces. Before the sheets can be merged, the parcel corner coordinates in the southern sheet (held as a Shapefile of point features) must be rounded to the national standard 0.5-metre coordinate resolution so that identical boundary points on adjacent sheets coincide exactly.

During the preparation of cadastral parcel data for seamless joining of neighbouring map sheets, surveyors noticed that the corner coordinates of parcels along the sheet edges are recorded to millimetre precision, causing tiny misalignments when the sheets are brought together. To create a clean, unified fabric, all parcel vertices in the GeoPackage file ‘parcels_edge.gpkg’ need to be adjusted so they fall on a regular 1-centimetre grid, ensuring that matching boundaries snap together perfectly without gaps or overlaps.
Tool: Points along lines\nAlgorithm ID:: To support a pavement-condition survey, we have a recent .shp file of road centerlines for the county. We need to mark exact inspection spots along each road at the halfway point so field crews can stop, photograph, and rate the surface. Produce a new point file showing one location per road positioned at the middle of its length.

The regional water authority needs to mark exact sampling positions along each stretch of the river network stored as a polyline shapefile so that field crews can stop at the midpoint of every reach to collect water-quality data.

The provincial water authority has a polyline shapefile showing the centre-lines of the 120 km main river stem and its major tributaries. To design a cost-effective monitoring network they need to mark the exact location on each river reach that is halfway along that reach, ensuring every branch is represented. These midpoint spots will later be visited to install in-situ water-quality sensors, so the deliverable must be a new point file with one site per line.

Our rural electrification project has received a freshly surveyed .shp file showing the planned routes for new medium-voltage power lines. We need to identify where to plant each utility pole so that every pole sits at the midpoint of its corresponding line segment. The goal is to obtain a new set of locations marking these midpoints, which will serve as the official pole-placement map for construction crews.

A national park service is preparing an updated hiking-map series and has received a set of .shp files that trace every trail within the park. To mark where hikers can expect to reach key halfway landmarks, the cartographers need a new set of points placed exactly halfway along each trail line so these locations can be labelled and symbolised on the final maps.

The national park service is preparing a new hiking map for the 42 km Ridge-to-River trail. They have a .shp file showing the exact centre-line of the trail and need to mark the halfway resting point for hikers. Please create a single point exactly halfway along the trail line so it can be printed on the final map as the official rest-stop location.

For a municipal cadastral update, a shapefile of every parcel’s boundary line is available. The need is to mark the exact midpoint of each boundary line so that a field crew can place a physical monument there; the resulting set of mid-position markers must be delivered as a new point file.

A municipal land-registry office has a .shp file holding the surveyed boundary lines of every parcel in the city. To prepare a new cadastral reference map, they need to mark the exact midpoint of each boundary line so that surveyors can place physical center stakes in the field.

A highway maintenance department has a .shp file of road centerlines for the state network and needs a single inspection stop placed exactly halfway along each road segment so field crews can photograph pavement condition; the resulting list of precise mid-segment stop locations should be delivered as a new point file.

A rural electric cooperative has just finished stringing new primary distribution conductors along freshly surveyed center-lines supplied as a .shp file. To anchor the line at mid-span it needs the precise halfway point of every segment, thereby ensuring sag measurements can be taken from a representative low-point rather than from an end.
Tool: Interpolate point on line\nAlgorit: The national park service is preparing a new hiking map for the 42 km Ridge-to-River trail. They have a .shp file showing the exact centre-line of the trail and need to mark the halfway resting point for hikers. Please create a single point exactly halfway along the trail line so it can be printed on the final map as the official rest-stop location.

The highway authority needs to mark the exact location 250 m from the start of each road segment in a Shapefile of city centre thoroughfares, so maintenance crews can install advance warning signs at that fixed distance.

A rural electric cooperative is designing a new 12-km overhead distribution line represented by a single polyline shapefile. To plan where the first wooden pole should be planted, they need to mark the exact spot that lies 250 m from the start of the line, measured along the route the cable will follow.

The rural electrification programme has surveyed a new 12 km overhead distribution line as a .shp file following the planned route. To prepare the materials list, we need to know the exact location where a pole should stand exactly 4 500 m from the start of the line so that the procurement team can schedule delivery of that particular pole and its fittings.

The state park authority has a .shp file of the planned 12 km hiking trail and needs to mark the exact spot 5 km from the trailhead where a way-finding kiosk will be installed. Provide the precise location as a single point feature.

To help hikers orient themselves along the newly mapped 15 km ridgeline trail, the park planning team has a .shp file that traces the trail centre-line. We need to mark the precise spot exactly 6 kilometres from the southern trailhead so a way-finding kiosk can be installed at that location.

We are updating the railway milepost inventory for the regional network. From the infrastructure department we have received a .shp file that shows every main and branch track centre-line. We need to identify the exact location that lies exactly one mile (1,609.34 m) from the start of each track segment so that field crews can verify the physical milepost markers; please provide a point layer giving that one-mile position along every line.

The provincial highways department is preparing a tender for reflective kilometre-marker posts on the main inter-urban route. They possess a shapefile whose features trace the road centre-line, already trimmed so each segment begins exactly at the city boundary. From this prepared line they need the precise coordinates 5 000 m onward from that boundary so the survey crew can navigate straight to the spot and commence staking out the markers.

A maintenance team has digitised a single railway corridor as a centre-line inside a .shp file and wants to confirm the position of a recently installed kilometre marker. Provide an exact point 6.2 km from the corridor’s starting location so inspectors can compare it against the physical post.
Tool: Tapered buffers\nAlgorithm ID: nat: To support a riverine flood-inundation mapping project, we have a .shp file showing the surveyed centre-lines of the main river channels. We need to create a zone around each channel that begins at the ordinary low-flow water’s edge and widens downstream to the expected maximum flood extent, so that the resulting outline can serve as the basis for detailed inundation modelling.

To support mapping burn-severity patterns, we have a set of wild-fire progression polylines digitised from successive infrared flights (provided as a .shp file). Each line shows the fire front at a given moment and is orientated from the ignition point toward the advancing tip. We need to create zones that visually emphasise the width of the initial fire footprint at the start of each line while gradually expanding to the final breadth at the advancing end, so that the resulting polygons can serve as a base for assigning severity classes.

A national park needs to outline the widening corridor that a wildfire burned as it advanced from its ignition point toward the residential edge. From a shapefile showing the daily progression lines of the fire front, the park wants to create a zone that starts 30 m wide at the ignition end and fans out to 200 m wide at the final perimeter, so rangers can quickly see how far the scorching extended on each side of the fire’s travel path.

A coastal management office has a .shp file showing the centre-lines of active sea-cliff edges mapped from recent aerial imagery. They need to depict a hazard band that starts at the current cliff top with a 5 m wide safety margin and widens steadily to 25 m at the seaward end, producing a single polygon layer that visually highlights the increasing erosion risk zone.

To create a map that shows the widening strip of cliff at risk of collapse as one moves from the northern headland toward the southern tip, we need to take the polyline that traces the top edge of the cliff (.shp file supplied by the regional coastal survey) and generate a hazard band that begins 5 m wide at the northern end and steadily broadens to 20 m wide by the southern end; the resulting polygon will be used on its own to visualise the erosion danger zone for emergency planning.

The city’s transport authority is preparing a widening plan for a main arterial road. We have a shapefile of the current road centre-line and need to know the exact footprint that will be affected if the road is gradually widened from 10 m at the western end to 25 m at the eastern end, so planners can see which adjoining properties fall inside this expanding corridor.

A city engineer has a .shp file of planned road-widening alignments and needs to show, for public consultation, the exact footprint that will be affected along each alignment, starting 5 m from the beginning of every stretch and widening to 15 m by the end, so residents can see which properties and green areas fall inside this steadily expanding corridor.

To visualise how the valley floor widens downstream, we have a shapefile holding the centre-line of a glacial trough and need a single polygon that starts narrow at the headwall and steadily fans out toward the mouth, showing the expanding cross-sectional footprint along the entire valley length.

To examine how the width of a U-shaped glacial valley changes along its length, I have a polyline shapefile tracing the valley axis from the cirque headwall down to the valley mouth. I need to create a zone that starts 200 m wide at the upper end and gradually widens to 800 m at the lower end, so that I can later extract elevation profiles across this zone to study the valley’s cross-sectional evolution.

To support flood-inundation mapping along the Lower Red River, we have a shapefile of the surveyed centre-line of the river reach. We need to generate a single widening zone that starts 5 m wide at the upstream limit and expands to 50 m at the downstream limit; this outline will later be divided along the centre-line to delineate separate left- and right-bank areas for the subsequent high-resolution inundation modelling.
Tool: Viewshed\nAlgorithm ID: gdal:views: A national telecom provider is selecting the first 5G mast location for a rural valley that currently lacks coverage.  They have a GeoTIFF elevation model of the valley (1 m resolution, supplied by the national mapping agency) and have shortlisted a single candidate mast position on a ridge at 1 400 m above sea level.  The planners need to know every place on the surrounding terrain that will be able to see the new mast at a standard handset height of 1.5 m, within a 15 km radius of the proposed site, so they can confirm the extent of reliable signal before submitting the planning application.

As part of the environmental impact assessment for a proposed offshore wind-farm, planners have a GeoTIFF elevation model of the coastal landscape. They need to determine exactly which parts of the shoreline and inland hills would be visible from the top of the tallest turbine (150 m above sea level) once the farm is built. The goal is to map the zone of potential visual influence so that stakeholders can evaluate where the turbines might alter the existing seascape view.

A regional planning office is reviewing a proposal to install a cluster of wind turbines on a ridge within a protected landscape. To inform the environmental-impact chapter of the draft report, the office has received a 10 m resolution elevation model (GeoTIFF) covering the entire ridge and surrounding valleys. They need to map every place on the ground that would have a direct line of sight to the proposed turbine site, assuming a turbine hub height of 120 m above ground, so that visual-impact zones can be presented to stakeholders.

To support the placement of a new wildfire lookout tower in the Sequoia National Forest, we have a 1-meter resolution elevation grid (GeoTIFF) from the USGS 3DEP program. We need to determine precisely which parts of the surrounding landscape would be visible from a candidate tower site located at 36.523°N, 118.269°W, assuming the observer’s eye level is 12 m above the ground and we are interested in terrain visibility out to 25 km.

The forest service is evaluating a 1-m resolution LiDAR DEM covering the Klamath National Forest to decide where a new wildfire lookout tower should be placed. From the proposed tower site coordinates (41.3128° N, 122.8765° W, 2 m above ground), we need to know exactly which ridges, valleys, and distant slopes can be seen without obstruction so we can confirm the tower will provide full visibility across the high-risk western slopes. The analysis should limit the search to 30 km to match standard watch range and treat both the observer and potential fire sources as being roughly 2 m above the ground.

To support the selection of the most scenic stretches for a new mountain highway, planners need to know exactly which ridgelines, valleys, and landmark peaks can be seen from a series of proposed observation turnouts. A 1-metre resolution digital elevation model supplied by the national mapping agency is available. The task is to produce, for each candidate turnout coordinate, a visibility map that marks every cell the eye can reach within a 15 km radius, assuming an observer height of 1.6 m above ground and targeting features at least 2 m tall. The resulting raster layers will be compared to identify the turnout locations offering the broadest and most varied vistas.

A military unit has received a 30 m resolution elevation grid covering the frontier ridge and needs to know exactly which ground can be watched from a planned observation tower placed at 45.732° N, 7.342° E, 12 m above the local surface. The study must limit the check to a 25 km radius and treat both the observer and any potential intruder as being 2 m tall, producing a visibility map that shows every location reachable by line-of-sight from the tower.

A military reconnaissance team has a 10-m resolution elevation grid covering the border ridge. They need to know every patch of ground that can be seen from a planned observation post at 34.745° N, 76.221° E, assuming an observer standing 1.8 m above the surface and any potential intruder 1.5 m tall. Visibility must be assessed out to 25 km to guarantee early warning coverage.

A regional telecom provider is selecting the first site for a 30 m mast in a hilly province. They have a GeoTIFF elevation model supplied by the national mapping agency and have pre-selected one summit coordinate. Before committing to the location, they wish to obtain a map layer that marks every cell in the landscape that can be seen from the top of the proposed antenna, so their engineers can later compare this visibility surface against printed atlases of villages, roads and valleys when drafting the final coverage report.

A regional tourism board is evaluating a single, highest-priority scenic overlook along a proposed mountain highway. We have a 1-m resolution digital elevation model (GeoTIFF) covering the ridgeline corridor and one candidate coordinate at a hair-pin bend. The board needs to know which stretches of the surrounding landscape would be visible to visitors standing 1.6 m above the ground, limited to a 15 km radius, so they can confirm the site offers an expansive vista before construction begins.
Tool: Export contours\nAlgorithm ID: nat: A coastal engineering team has produced a hydrodynamic mesh model that simulates the water-surface elevation during a storm-surge event. To prepare a flood-inundation map for emergency managers, they need to extract smooth lines that join all points sharing the same water level at the peak of the surge, and to obtain enclosed areas that show where the water reaches each specific elevation. The model is available as a mesh layer with scalar water-level results for the selected time step.

A regional flood-forecasting team has produced a time-varying hydrodynamic simulation stored as a mesh that records predicted water depths across the valley floor. They need to draw the boundary lines that separate each one-metre interval of water depth at the forecast’s peak time so these can be overlaid on emergency-response maps showing which neighbourhoods will lie beneath 1 m, 2 m, 3 m, and deeper water.

A regional planning office has received a high-resolution numerical terrain model saved as a mesh file that includes slope values for every cell. They need to draw smooth slope lines across the landscape at 5-degree intervals so the map reader can quickly see where inclines are gentle, moderate, or steep. The office would like these slope lines delivered as a standalone line layer that can be styled and shared with local councils.

A regional planning office has been provided with a high-resolution DEM stored as a mesh layer that records ground elevation across a mountainous watershed. They need to obtain smooth, labeled lines and filled areas that join points of equal height so these can be overlaid on base maps for slope-based land-suitability discussions. The required deliverables are a set of elevation lines and a companion set of elevation bands, both covering the full spatial and temporal extent of the supplied mesh.

To support the delineation of air-quality plume boundaries, a regional environmental agency has received a NetCDF-formatted numerical weather prediction model output that contains hourly ground-level ozone concentration across the study area for the forecast day. The agency needs to extract smooth outline shapes that connect all locations sharing the same concentration value so that distinct plume zones (e.g., 70, 90, 110 µg/m³) can be mapped and compared with monitoring-station observations.

A coastal engineering team has been given a finite-element mesh dataset produced by a recent tide-surge model that reports hourly water-surface elevations referenced to the model’s own mean-sea-level datum. The mesh already incorporates a 0.5 m rise above present-day geodetic datum (MSL-1988) so the 0.5 m value in the dataset is the projected 2050 water level ready for direct comparison. From this adjusted mesh the team needs to trace the corresponding shoreline for the chosen future time step and save it as a line layer that can be overlaid on current aerial photographs.

For a coastal vulnerability study, I have a numerical-model output in UGRID format that gives projected water-surface heights across the estuary under a 2050 sea-level rise scenario. I need to extract all height isolines from the mesh so that, after picking the line that matches mean sea level, planners can map the expected new land–water boundary; the outcome should be a shapefile of lines containing every height contour, from which the shoreline will be selected separately.

A regional water authority has a 3-D groundwater flow model saved as a NetCDF mesh that contains simulated hydraulic head values across a coastal aquifer system. To support their upcoming stakeholder meeting, they need to draw the lines that join all points having the same water-level elevation for the predicted conditions on 1 January 2030, and also to map the areas enclosed by those elevation zones. The outputs are to be delivered as shapefiles the authority can overlay on existing administrative and infrastructure maps.

To support the regional aquifer management plan, we have on hand a mesh layer already loaded into the project that holds the state water survey’s time series of simulated groundwater head across the modeled area for the last dry season. We now need to draw the lines that connect points of equal water level for the week when heads were lowest, so planners can visualise the potentiometric surface and pinpoint areas of steep gradient that may require additional monitoring.

For a hydrological survey of the lower reach of the River Dane, we have a three-dimensional finite-element model saved as a .nc file that contains daily simulated water-level and velocity arrays for the past year. We need to turn the grid lines of the water-level surface for last week’s peak-flow date into a simple polyline map so the field team can plot them against surveyed cross-sections in AutoCAD.
Tool: Eliminate selected polygons\nAlgor: A national mapping agency is updating its provincial boundary dataset after receiving a new set of municipal polygons from the statistics office. The merged files contain numerous narrow gaps and slivers along former borders that need to be removed so that each province is again represented by a single, clean outline. The agency has a shapefile of the current provincial layer in which the unwanted slivers have already been highlighted. They now need to merge these thin fragments into their neighbouring provinces, preferably joining each fragment to the province it touches most along the edge, so the final dataset can be published as the authoritative provincial boundaries for the year.

After dissolving municipal zoning polygons we obtained a new layer that still contains many narrow slivers where boundaries almost, but not perfectly, aligned. We have this layer as a polygon shapefile in which the unwanted slivers have already been highlighted. The requirement is to merge each highlighted sliver with the neighbouring zone that shares the longest edge with it, producing a clean, single-part zoning map.

Following the recent dissolution of municipal zoning polygons into broader districts, a GeoPackage layer contains numerous needle-thin fragments—each smaller than 200 m²—left along former parcel seams. To ready the map for the city planning board, these fragments have already been singled out within the layer; the next step is to fold each one into the neighboring district that shares its longest border, yielding a seamless set of districts without the distracting slivers.

A tiled, hydro-flattened elevation model has been turned into a polygon layer showing open water surfaces. The conversion produced numerous tiny, thread-like fragments along the tile seams that are not true water bodies. These fragments have already been identified and marked within the Esri File Geodatabase polygon layer. The requirement is to dissolve each marked fragment into the neighboring water surface that touches it along the longest shared edge, yielding a single, seamless outline for every actual water body in the final hydro-flattened product.

While preparing a hydro-flattened DEM for county-wide flood modelling, the water-body polygons from the National Hydrography Dataset were trimmed to the county limits, producing numerous thin shoreline fragments. After selecting these fragments by their small size, please merge each one into the neighboring water polygon with which it shares the longest common edge, delivering a single-part lake-and-river surface ready for DEM flattening.

We have a monthly global sea-surface temperature climatology raster (GeoTIFF) covering 1981-2010 and need to verify that the numerical range of the first temperature band is physically plausible before the dataset is published.

A regional water-resources study has compiled annual total-precipitation grids (one GeoTIFF per year for the past 30 years) covering the entire watershed. A water-management district has collected monthly depth-to-groundwater raters from 24 monitoring wells covering the past two years. A university research group has compiled a set of 30 m Landsat NDVI images (one GeoTIFF per year from 2000-2023) covering a semi-arid rangeland. For a flood-risk study in the Lower Mekong Basin we have a set of twelve 30-metre GeoTIFF surfaces, each produced by a different international mapping agency, representing ground elevation for the same region.
