Planners require a single map that indicates, for every cell, which of the five sources supplied the most conservative (lowest) height estimate, so they can trace which model consistently suggests the deepest potential flood areas and prioritize it for further validation.
Tool: Export mesh edges\nAlgorithm ID: n: For a regional coastal flood-hazard study we have a numerical-model output (.nc) that stores predicted water-level and current-velocity information across the estuary at the time of the design storm. We need to convert the outline of every computational cell into a set of lines so that the predicted values can be attached to the corresponding edges and later viewed in any standard mapping software.

The regional emergency office is preparing a coastal flood-hazard map for the upcoming storm season. We have a NetCDF file that contains the latest high-resolution wave model results, including wave height and direction data for every hour over the next five days. To update our GIS-based hazard atlas, we need to turn the model’s grid edges into simple lines that carry the forecast wave values as attributes, so planners can immediately see which sections of shoreline are expected to face the highest waves.

A hydraulic study of the lower Rhine needs the outline of every computational cell in the existing 2-D flow model so that water-level and velocity values along the edges can be passed to the river-authority’s engineering team. The model is stored as a netCDF file that includes the unstructured mesh and hourly results for the past flood season. Please provide the cell boundaries as a line shapefile, carrying the water-level and velocity recorded at each edge for the peak-flow time step.

For a hydrological survey of the lower reach of the River Dane, we have a three-dimensional finite-element model saved as a .nc file that contains daily simulated water-level and velocity arrays for the past year. We need to turn the grid lines of the water-level surface for last week’s peak-flow date into a simple polyline map so the field team can plot them against surveyed cross-sections in AutoCAD.

To support the generation of wind-field streamlines, we need to extract the grid lines from the current numerical weather prediction mesh together with the wind velocity components stored on those edges, so that the resulting line set can be used as the skeleton for plotting flow arrows and tracing streamlines.

In a groundwater barrier delineation study, we possess a 3-D finite-element mesh (.nc format) that stores hydraulic-head outputs from a transient groundwater model. To map the exact traces of subsurface barriers, we need to obtain the outline of every mesh element edge as a separate line, carrying the modelled head values along each edge, so that the resulting line map can be imported into drafting software for barrier-line interpretation.

For a regional tsunami early-warning study we have a NetCDF file that stores the computed arrival-time field on a triangular ocean mesh. We need to extract the mesh edges as a line shapefile so that each line carries the arrival-time value of the edge it represents; the time snapshot to use is the one currently shown on the map canvas.

A meteorological research group has already loaded into their mapping software a seven-day hourly wind-field forecast mesh layer produced by the WRF model. They now need to extract the grid lines together with the wind-speed and wind-direction values attached to each line for 12:00 UTC tomorrow, delivered in both x/y and magnitude/angle forms, so the results can be drawn as streamline arrows in a separate mapping package.

A regional groundwater authority wants a complete set of all the line segments that make up the computational grid of a UGRID-based groundwater model, including both the outer rim and the interior partitions, for the final hydraulic-head time step. The lines are to be delivered as a shapefile so engineers can inspect the mesh structure before deciding which segments represent the barrier alignment in their CAD design.

The regional emergency-response team has a NetCDF file from the ocean modeller that stores the predicted tsunami travel time across the offshore mesh. They need the entire set of mesh edges, each carrying its arrival-time value as a simple line, so cartographers can later identify and highlight the sections that reach the coast first when preparing public warning maps.
Tool: Service area (from layer)\nAlgorit: A regional fire department needs to know which stretches of road can be reached within a ten-minute drive from every existing fire station, so that incident-commanders can see at a glance where crews can arrive quickly and where additional coverage may be required.  We have a shapefile of the county road network and another shapefile marking the location of each station; the goal is to map every segment of road that a fire engine can access in ten minutes or less when leaving from any station.

A regional emergency management office needs to know which stretches of road can be reached within a 10-minute drive from every fire station in the county. They have a shapefile of the road network and another shapefile with the exact locations of all fire stations. The goal is to obtain a map showing every segment of road that an emergency vehicle could reach within that 10-minute limit, starting from any station.

A municipal economic-development office wants to understand how far shoppers can realistically travel from each of its existing supermarkets along the city’s street network. It has a shapefile of the road centre-lines and another shapefile with the store locations. The office needs a map layer showing every street segment—and the junctions at its ends—that a customer could reach on those roads within a 2 km walk from any store, so it can visualise the combined walking catchment for all outlets.

To support a municipal initiative promoting safe walking routes to school, we have a street-centerline shapefile covering the entire district and a point shapefile marking each school gate. We need to identify every street segment—and the junctions at its far ends—that a pupil can reach on foot within exactly one kilometre from any school gate, assuming the child follows the shortest possible route along the street network.

The city’s Safe Routes to School program needs to know which streets a child can walk along within a 1 km stroll from every primary-school gate.  We have a shapefile of the road network surrounding the schools and a separate point file marking each school entrance.  The goal is to produce a map layer showing every street segment that lies within this easy walking distance so planners can prioritise sidewalk repairs and crossing improvements.

A city transit authority needs to know which segments of its bus-route network can be reached within a 10-minute ride from every existing bus stop, so it can identify underserved corridors and plan new services; the authority has a shapefile of the road network used by buses and another shapefile with the locations of all current stops.

A city transit authority has a road layer showing all drivable streets and a point layer of planned new bus stops. They need to know exactly which stretches of road can be reached within a 10-minute drive from every one of these stops, so they can decide where to add feeder routes and signage.

A regional electricity provider has a shapefile of the road network and another shapefile marking the exact locations of its substations. After a severe storm, the company needs to know which stretches of road can still be reached from each substation within a 30-minute drive so that repair crews can plan safe and efficient access routes. The road layer is stored as a line shapefile in the local UTM projection, and the substation points are provided as a point shapefile in the same coordinate system.

Following a severe storm, the city’s utility provider needs to know which sections of the electricity-line network can still be reached within a 30-minute drive from each operational depot so that repair crews can be dispatched efficiently. The provider has a shapefile of the road network and another shapefile marking the depot locations.

A regional grocery chain is preparing to open a new store in the suburbs and needs to know which streets residents can reach within a five-minute drive of the proposed location. We have a shapefile showing the local road network and another shapefile with a single point representing the candidate store site. The chain wants a map that highlights every segment of road that a shopper could travel along without exceeding five minutes behind the wheel, so they can judge how well the store would serve nearby neighbourhoods.
Tool: Define Shapefile projection\nAlgor: A team surveyed turtle nesting sites along a barrier-island beach with a handheld GPS unit and exported the points to a .shp file. When the file is opened it appears far out in the Atlantic instead of on the coastline, suggesting the coordinate system was not recorded. Please set the file’s reference framework to the standard local survey grid used by the state’s coastal zone so the sightings plot in the correct location.

A forestry survey team has returned with a set of tree-plot locations saved as a shapefile, but the file lacks any coordinate reference information. Because the GPS units were configured to the local UTM zone before fieldwork, the plots are known to align with that system. The task is to ensure the shapefile is correctly registered so that it lines up properly with other regional maps and can be used for further planning.

During the current phase of our regional geological-survey consolidation project we have received a set of historical bedrock-polygon files (.shp) that were digitised in the 1990s but were delivered without any accompanying coordinate information. Field notes indicate the data were captured in the national Gauss–Krüger Zone 3 grid, yet the files cannot be aligned with recent mapping because no projection is recorded. We need to attach the correct spatial reference to these legacy polygons so that they register properly with the rest of the merged survey layers.

The Geological Survey of Greenvale has received a set of mineral-outcrop polygons digitised last year by a contractor, delivered as a .shp file. The accompanying projection information file was lost in transit, so the layer currently opens in the wrong location relative to other regional datasets. We need to tell the computer the correct coordinate system so that the outcrops align properly with the rest of the merged survey.

We have received a .shp file of city road centre-lines that was exported from an older CAD system; the accompanying projection file is missing, so the layer currently appears in the wrong place on our Web Mercator base-map. We know the data were originally captured in the WGS-84 coordinate system. Please set the correct spatial reference for this layer so it will align properly when we later convert it to Web Mercator for tiled web delivery.

A local planning office has received a shapefile of building footprints that lacks its coordinate reference information; to integrate the layer into a web mapping service that uses Web Mercator tiles, the office needs to specify that the file is already in WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator so the tiles display correctly.

A county land-records office has received a 1990s-era .shp file of parcel boundaries that was exported from an old CAD system; the file opens in the wrong location and scale because it lacks coordinate information. The office knows the parcels were originally drawn in the local State Plane zone and needs the dataset to align correctly with modern aerial imagery and other reference layers.

A local survey office has a parcel map that was exported from an old CAD system and saved as a Shapefile. When the file is opened in modern mapping software, the parcels appear in the wrong place on the globe because the coordinate reference information is missing. The office possesses a written record stating that the original drawing was produced in the NAD 1983 State Plane coordinate system for North Carolina. They need to attach the correct location information to the file so that the parcels align properly with other regional datasets.

While preparing a heritage trail along the River Lea, volunteers recovered a 1930s set of water-wheel locations that were digitised into a .shp file. The accompanying notes confirm the original surveyor worked in the War Office Cassini Grid, but the layer now appears without any coordinate tag. Please record that these stored coordinates are expressed in that specific grid so the software can interpret them correctly before any later alignment work is carried out.

A digital archive holds a 1938 municipal survey stored as a .shp file; the accompanying projection description is missing. The coordinates in the file are already expressed in the city’s local grid, but without the coordinate system recorded the layer appears in the wrong place on modern base maps. Archivists need the dataset to carry the correct local coordinate reference so it can be recognised and later combined with other spatial layers for historical comparison.

During the post-excavation phase of a Roman villa site survey, the field team discovered that one of the daily pottery sherd distribution maps stored as a .shp file no longer opens in the project GIS. The file appears intact but the software reports a missing support file, preventing the layer from being displayed for the final report. We need to restore access to this pottery distribution so it can be compared with the trench layout and photographed artefacts before the archive is submitted to the county heritage record.

A regional planning office has received a shapefile of municipal boundaries digitised by a partner agency. When the file is opened in the department’s mapping software, the layer appears far outside the expected study area, suggesting the coordinates were recorded in a local grid but the file was mistakenly declared to be in WGS-84. The planners need to correct the declared coordinate system so the municipal boundaries align properly with other regional datasets without altering the original geometry.

A regional planning office has received a .shp file of municipal boundaries digitized by an external consultant, but the coordinates are clearly plotted in the wrong place on the map. The dataset is believed to have been created in the national grid system used by the survey department (EPSG:27700), yet the file declares a different reference system. We need to correct the declared coordinate system so the boundaries appear in their proper locations without altering the stored geometry.

A local heritage society has received a 1998 map of listed buildings in the county as an Esri Shapefile. The map opens in their desktop viewer, but the features appear far out at sea instead of on land, indicating the layer is tagged with the wrong coordinate reference. They need to set the layer to the correct British National Grid reference so the buildings display in their proper locations for an upcoming conservation report.

A municipal archive holds a 1995 street-centerline .shp file whose coordinates appear in decimal degrees, yet the dataset is mistakenly catalogued as if it were measured in a national grid. The mis-registration causes the roads to plot hundreds of kilometres off the coast when viewed alongside modern orthophotos. The archive needs the file to be re-tagged so that its coordinates are correctly interpreted as WGS84, allowing it to align properly with contemporary base maps without altering any of the original geometry or attribute information.

A university research group has compiled a set of drone-mapped field boundary polygons saved as a shapefile, but the file opens in the wrong location on the base map. They need the layer to be tagged with the correct national grid so it aligns properly with other spatial datasets without altering the actual coordinates.

A regional planning office is packaging a set of ready-to-deliver shapefiles for local councils. One file, holding the administrative boundaries received from an external contractor, opens in the wrong place on the map. The coordinates appear to be correct but the file seems to have been given an inappropriate coordinate system tag. We need to give this boundary file the proper coordinate system label so it aligns perfectly with all other regional datasets before the package is shipped.

A national mapping agency has prepared a set of administrative boundary polygons in a Shapefile that were mistakenly catalogued with the wrong coordinate reference. Before the dataset is packaged for distribution to regional governments, the agency needs to mark the file with the correct national grid so that downstream users will see the features in their proper geographic positions without altering any of the existing geometry or attribute content.

A city planning office has received a set of utility-line drawings exported from a CAD system as a shapefile; the file’s coordinates appear to be shifted several hundred kilometres east of their true positions. After comparing the plotted lines with known reference points on the authority’s web-mapping portal, the GIS team has identified that the layer was mistakenly tagged as WGS84 and should instead be labelled with the local projected coordinate system ‘EPSG:27700 - OSGB 1936 / British National Grid’. To ensure the drawings align properly with base maps without altering any of the geometry, the layer now simply needs to be re-tagged with this correct system.

Tool: Line Density\nAlgorithm ID: native: To support a regional transport-planning study, we have been given a shapefile of all public roads in the province. The planners need a continuous map that shows how concentrated the road network is across the landscape so they can identify areas of high and low accessibility. Produce a grid-based surface where every cell records the total length of roads found within a 1 km circle centred on that cell, expressed as kilometres of road per square kilometre.

To support a regional accessibility study, we have a shapefile of all public roads in the province. We need to know how concentrated these roads are across the landscape so that planners can identify areas where travel options are abundant versus those that appear underserved. Produce a continuous surface showing, for every 50 m-wide patch of land, the total length of roadway lying within 1 km of that patch, expressed as kilometres of road per square kilometre.

To support selection of the best corridor for a new high-voltage power line, we have a shapefile of existing transmission routes compiled by the national grid operator. We need to know how crowded each candidate corridor is with existing lines so that we can favour areas with fewer competing utilities. Please produce a continuous surface that shows, for every 50-metre cell, the total length of power-line routes within a 1-kilometre circle centred on that cell, expressed as kilometres of line per square kilometre.

To support routing decisions for a new high-voltage power line, we have a shapefile of existing transmission corridors collected by the provincial energy agency. We need to know how intensively these corridors already occupy the landscape so that planners can identify stretches where additional infrastructure would least disturb the existing network. Specifically, we would like a continuous surface showing, for every 50 m spot, the total length of existing corridors falling within a 2 km circle centred on that spot, expressed as kilometres of line per square kilometre.

To evaluate how concentrated the hiking trails are across the national park, we have a .shp file showing all trail centrelines downloaded from the park authority. Produce a continuous surface map where every 20 m cell records how much trail length lies within 500 m of its centre, so planners can visually identify the most heavily trodden sectors before deciding where new board-walk or restoration work is needed.

As part of the Urban Heat-Island & Street Canyon Study we have a city-wide .shp file of street centre-lines downloaded from OpenStreetMap. We need to know how tightly the road network is packed across the entire area so that we can relate street density to measured air-temperature profiles. Please produce a continuous surface map where every 10 m grid cell shows the total length of streets lying within a 200 m radius circle centred on that cell, expressed as kilometres of road per square kilometre.

As part of an Urban Heat-Island & Street Canyon Study, we have a city-wide shapefile of street centerlines downloaded from the local open-data portal. We need to know, for every 50 m across the entire urban area, how much street length lies within a 200 m walking circle so we can map where the densest street canyons occur and relate those patterns to temperature measurements collected by the weather network.

To support evacuation planning, we have a shapefile of all drivable roads in the low-lying district and need a continuous surface showing how much road length lies within 500 m of every location, so that areas with the sparsest road access can be identified for priority reinforcement.

To support evacuation planning for low-lying districts, we have a shapefile of all drivable roads and need to know how intensively the road network is distributed across the landscape, expressed as kilometres of road per square kilometre, so we can identify where traffic flow could become most concentrated during a flood event.
Tool: Proximity (raster distance)\nAlgor: To support the wildfire risk assessment, we have a classified land-cover raster (GeoTIFF) where pixels coded 3 represent areas of dense, fire-prone vegetation. We need to know, for every location across the region, how far away the nearest patch of this high-risk vegetation lies, expressed in real-world metres, so that planners can visualise zones that are either buffered by or exposed to the threat.

A regional forestry service has a 10 m-resolution land-cover raster that marks every pixel where a past wildfire scar is present. They need to know, for every location across the landscape, how far away the nearest historic burn scar lies so they can incorporate this distance into a wildfire-risk model.

During the current flood emergency, the regional operations center has a GeoTIFF showing which cells of the regional elevation model are already under water (value 1) and which are still dry (value 0). They need to know, for every remaining dry cell, how far it is to the nearest already-flooded cell so that evacuation crews can prioritize areas closest to the advancing water. The result should be expressed in real-world meters rather than pixel counts.

During the current flood emergency, the regional command has a single-band GeoTIFF showing every cell that is already under water (value 1) versus dry land (value 0). They need a continuous surface that tells them, for every remaining dry pixel, exactly how many metres away the nearest flooded cell lies, so that responders can prioritise evacuations and barrier placement starting with the areas closest to the advancing water.

The regional water authority needs to know how far every field pixel in its Landsat-derived crop-mask raster (GeoTIFF, 30 m resolution) lies from the nearest irrigation canal pixel (value 1 in the same raster) so it can prioritise canal-extension works; provide a map where each cell records that distance in metres.

As part of an irrigation-planning study for the lower valley, we have a classified land-cover raster (GeoTIFF) that marks every canal intake pixel with the value 15. We need to know, for every field in the region, how far it lies from the nearest canal intake so that water-demand zones can be prioritised. Please produce a new raster in which each cell records its ground-distance in metres to the closest intake pixel.

A city planning team has a GeoTIFF showing all public parks (pixels coded 1) and needs to know, for every location across the urban area, how far it is to the nearest park in metres so they can map where residents live more than a 10-minute walk from greenspace.

A city planning department has a 1 m resolution GeoTIFF that marks every public park pixel with the value 1 and all other land with 0. They need to know, for every location in the metropolitan area, how far away the nearest park is, measured in metres, so they can identify neighbourhoods where residents must walk long distances to reach green space.

A geoenvironmental consulting firm has received a GeoTIFF map in which each cell storing the value 1 marks the footprint of a historic mine-tailings storage pond. To screen potential off-site migration of contaminants, the team needs to know, for every location across the landscape, how far away the nearest pond lies. The requested deliverable is a new continuous-distance map that can be loaded into their standard raster viewer.

To support an environmental impact assessment of a disused copper-mine tailings pond, we have a 1 m resolution GeoTIFF produced from drone imagery in which every pixel coded 255 marks the exact footprint of the tailings deposit. During a regional archaeological survey, researchers have gathered a set of 3-D line features (stored as a Shapefile) that trace ancient terrace walls across a rugged landscape. The city planning department is assessing rooftop solar potential across residential zones. The city planning office is mapping roof-top solar potential and has received a 3-D shapefile of building outlines that include height information. They need to record the rooftop elevation of each building as a separate number in the attribute table so that slope and sun-exposure calculations can follow.

In a coastal-cliff erosion-monitoring programme we have a three-dimensional shoreline surveyed last month, stored as a .gpkg file that records each cliff-top and toe line with height information embedded in every vertex. We need to bring those height figures into the attribute table so that, for every surveyed section, we have the minimum, maximum and mean elevation readily available for comparison with next season’s flight.

The coastal authority possesses a three-dimensional polyline shapefile capturing the cliff-top edge surveyed by drone-LiDAR last month. Tool: Join by lines (hub lines)\nAlgorit: The national aviation authority is compiling a visual atlas that shows every scheduled passenger flight in the country as a straight line linking the departure airport to its designated hub.  They have two spreadsheets that have already been converted to point shapefiles: one lists all domestic airports with their official IATA codes, and the other lists the same airports again but this time tagged with the single hub airport (also identified by IATA code) to which each airport’s flights are routed.  The authority needs a single line layer that draws a direct connection from every spoke airport to its matched hub airport so the atlas can display the complete hub-and-spoke network at a glance.

A regional emergency-management office needs to visualise which ambulance stations should respond to each incident reported during last night’s storm. They have two spreadsheets-turned-layers: one holding the storm-related incident locations (with a station-ID column indicating the nearest assigned station) and another listing the 24-hour ambulance stations (each with the same ID). The office wants a map that draws straight lines from every incident to its designated station so dispatchers can instantly see coverage links and check for any mis-assignments.

The city’s emergency-management office has a pair of shapefiles: one holding the locations of all fire stations and another with every 911 call received last month. Both files contain a shared incident-ID column that links each call to the station that was dispatched. The office needs a map that draws straight-line links from every fire station to the corresponding 911 call it answered, so planners can quickly see which stations are handling which incidents across the metropolitan area.

A retail chain needs to visualise which customers are served by each of its 120 stores.  It possesses a shapefile of store locations (each tagged with a unique store code) and a separate shapefile of registered customer addresses (each record carrying the same store code to indicate its assigned store).  The company would like a map that draws a straight line from every customer point to its designated store so management can see at a glance how customers are distributed around each outlet.

A regional electricity distributor needs to visualise which low-voltage service poles are supplied by each medium-voltage feeder pillar across the county.  They have a shapefile of feeder-pillar locations with a unique “feeder_code”, and a separate shapefile of service poles that carries the same “feeder_code” attribute.  The goal is to draw straight-line links from every pole to the feeder pillar that shares its code, producing a single line layer that clearly shows the supply relationship across the entire network.

Wildlife researchers have two point-shapefiles from a recent satellite-tagging campaign: one lists the main migratory stopover sites (each record has a unique stopover code), and the other lists the individual animals’ positions recorded during the same season (each record carries the same stopover code to show where it is heading). To visualise the flight corridors linking every animal to its intended stopover, the team needs a single line layer that draws straight connections from each animal location to the matching stopover site identified by the shared code.

A wildlife research group has two point datasets from a recent satellite-tagging campaign: one file holding the locations of seasonal nesting sites (tagged with colony IDs) and another file holding the positions of individual birds recorded during migration (each bird record carries the ID of its home colony). The team needs to visualise, for every bird position, the straight-line linkage back to its own nesting site so that flight corridors can be drawn on the map for the forthcoming report.

To support a study on global airline connectivity, we possess a point layer of 300 major airports (stored as a geopackage) and a second point layer that again lists the same airports, each tagged with the IATA code of its designated hub airport. The requirement is to produce a line layer that visually links every airport to its assigned hub so the resulting diagram can be overlaid on a world base-map for analysis of route concentration.

A national retail chain has prepared two point layers derived from its operational data: one layer holds the locations of 200 flagship stores (each record carries store name and store_id), and the other contains 1,500 loyalty-card customers who have declared one of these stores as their “home branch” (each record carries customer_id and home_store_id). Management wishes to produce a map that draws a straight line from every customer point to the store point identified by the matching store_id, providing an immediate visual summary of which customers are linked to which flagship outlet.

The regional electricity distributor needs to visualise which low-voltage service poles are supplied by each medium-voltage feeder pillar. We have two point layers: one holding the locations of feeder pillars and another holding the locations of service poles; both layers carry the same feeder-pillar identifier. Produce a line drawing that links every pole to the pillar whose identifier matches so planners can immediately see the supply relationship across the network.

During a hydrological survey, kayakers recorded the centre-line of a 45 km stretch of the River Finn with a high-precision GPS unit. The resulting .gpx track contains many repeated location fixes taken when the boats paused or drifted, leading to stacked points along several short reaches. These redundant positions need to be eliminated so that the final line portrays a single, clean path for each segment of the river without affecting its overall shape or length.

The mapping agency has delivered a city-wide cadastral parcel layer (ESRI Shapefile) that will feed the new topology-checking workflow. Reviewers noticed that many parcel polygons carry repeated corner points lying almost on top of one another, remnants of earlier digitising. While digitising the new cadastral parcel polygons we noticed that several boundary lines contain repeated coordinate points that were accidentally captured during the survey. We need to separate the already-tagged tall-vegetation returns from the rest of the point cloud so that engineers can focus solely on those points when judging where tree tops encroach on the required safety space beneath the conductors.

As part of a transmission-line corridor clearance analysis we have a .las point cloud captured from an airborne survey. A county archaeologist possesses a drone-acquired .las point cloud covering recently ploughed farmland and wishes to remove all returns labelled as tall vegetation so that the remaining dataset exposes only low, ground-level echoes in which subtle elevation anomalies—possible burial mounds—can be examined without interference from crop stubble or weeds.
Tool: Rotate\nAlgorithm ID: native:rotat: To simulate the clockwise turning of wind-turbine blades for a viewshed study, I have a shapefile showing the exact footprint of each turbine as a polygon. I need each polygon turned 30 degrees clockwise around its own centre so the new orientation can be used to model wake directions.

For a coastal wind-farm viewshed study we have a .shp file of 50 proposed turbine footprints (simple polygons). Meteorological records indicate that the dominant wind direction during the hazy season is 35° clockwise from north. To visualise how wakes would fan out across the seascape, each turbine footprint needs to be re-oriented by that same 35° while keeping every turbine in its original location, so the revised layout can be passed to the visibility model.

The National Archives has provided a .shp file of 1930s underground mine tunnel outlines surveyed with a magnetic compass; the tunnels were drawn 12° east of true north. I need to turn every tunnel line so it aligns with true north, while keeping each tunnel centred on its original position.

I have a scanned set of 1930s underground-mine working plans saved as a shapefile; the tunnels and shafts were drawn relative to the magnetic north of the day, but for modern safety assessments they must be referenced to today’s true north. Please turn the whole plan 7.5 degrees clockwise so that all tunnels, shafts and stopes line up correctly with true north.

A cartographic team is compiling a printed atlas of regional land-cover symbols and has a .shp file of rectangular legend swatches. The cartography unit has a shapefile of simple rectangular legend patches representing different land-cover types; to match the 35° italic typeface used throughout the atlas, each patch needs to be tilted by the same angle before they are placed in the final layout.

A telecommunications company has a set of antenna-coverage polygons in a shapefile, each currently oriented to magnetic north. Field engineers have reported that the actual main-lobe bearings differ from the map by a fixed 23° clockwise offset. To update the planning maps, the polygons need to be turned exactly 23° clockwise around their own centres so the coloured footprints line up with the true transmission directions.

The city planning office needs to prepare a .shp file of downtown building footprints for a forthcoming public consultation. Historical maps indicate that every outline was initially recorded 12 degrees off the true cardinal grid used in the new design guidelines. A uniform adjustment is required: each polygon must be spun clockwise by exactly that amount around its own centre so the entire dataset aligns with the consultation backdrop map.

A municipal planning office has digitised revised building footprints from new aerial imagery and, by comparing them to the existing .shp file, has calculated the angular difference for each polygon. To incorporate these corrections, the office now needs to apply the recorded rotation values to the original geometries so every footprint turns around its center and aligns with the freshly surveyed positions.

A wireless-network planning team has a single polygon shapefile that outlines the intended coverage footprint of a newly designed directional antenna; the footprint was drawn facing due north, but the antenna will be mounted on a rooftop that imposes a 35-degree clockwise offset. Provide a new layer in which the footprint is turned exactly 35 degrees clockwise around its centre so it reflects the real-world orientation.
Tool: Clip\nAlgorithm ID: pdal:clip\nDes: A municipal arborist has a city-wide lidar point cloud captured from last spring’s aerial survey and a shapefile outlining the boundaries of all public parks. The goal is to isolate only those laser returns that fall inside park parcels so the subsequent tree-identification workflow focuses exclusively on vegetation within recreational areas and excludes street trees and private yards.

The parks department has a city-wide lidar point cloud (.las) representing all above-ground features and a separate shapefile outlining the boundaries of every public park. They need to isolate only the points that fall inside these park areas so the resulting cloud can be used to identify and measure individual trees within city parks.

At a coastal-erosion monitoring site, we have a high-density LiDAR point cloud captured along the shoreline (.las) and a recent shoreline-buffer polygon derived from orthophotos (.shp) that marks the stable landward limit of interest. We need to keep only those elevation points that fall inside this buffer zone so the geomorphology team can focus their erosion analysis on the active coastal strip.

A coastal engineering team is monitoring erosion along a shoreline. They have a high-resolution LAS point cloud captured by drone lidar that covers both land and water, but they only need the points that fall inside the officially mapped shoreline buffer zone provided by the state as a shapefile. The goal is to isolate the portion of the point cloud that lies within this buffer so they can focus subsequent analysis on the narrow strip most vulnerable to erosion.

A quarry manager has a .las point cloud captured by drone photogrammetry, covering the entire active extraction area.  There is also a .shp file that marks the boundary of only the permitted stockpile zone.  The manager needs to isolate the drone points that fall inside this permitted zone so that subsequent volume calculations are restricted to the stockpile area and exclude the surrounding quarry faces.

We are surveying a limestone quarry to estimate the remaining volume of a stockpile located on the northern bench. A drone flight captured the entire site as a LAS point cloud, while the survey office provided a shapefile that marks the exact boundary of the stockpile. We need to isolate only the elevation points that fall inside this marked area so we can proceed with volume calculations.

A regional authority is compiling a high-resolution LiDAR point cloud covering the entire floodplain to support hydraulic modelling. To focus the dataset on the active channel and immediate banks, they need to discard all laser returns that fall outside the official flood-risk zone polygon supplied by the environment agency. The point cloud is stored as a .las file, and the zone boundary is available as a .shp file.

To prepare the hydraulic model, we have an airborne LiDAR point cloud (.las) covering the entire river corridor and a shapefile outlining the 100-year floodplain polygon. The goal is to keep only the elevation points that fall inside the floodplain so the hydraulic model can focus on the area most relevant to flood-risk analysis.

A LiDAR point cloud covering the survey area and a shapefile outlining the known mound boundaries have been provided. We need to keep only the elevation points that fall inside the mapped mounds so that subsequent micro-topographic analysis focuses exclusively on the archaeological features.

During a survey of an ancient settlement in the upper valley, researchers have collected a high-density LiDAR point cloud (.las) of the entire floodplain and also traced the visible edges of each burial mound as a separate polygon shapefile. To focus only on the ground returns that lie atop the mounds for subsequent micro-topographic modelling, the team needs to isolate the points that fall inside these mound outlines and save them as a new point cloud file.
Tool: Assign projection\nAlgorithm ID: g: While assembling a continent-wide mosaic from Landsat 8 scenes downloaded in GeoTIFF format, we noticed that one tile covering the Zambezi catchment lacks any coordinate reference details. Before adding it to the final composite, we need to tag it with the same WGS 84 / UTM zone 35S system used by the neighbouring tiles so that all images line up correctly.

After stitching together several Sentinel-2 scenes into a single GeoTIFF for a vegetation-change study, the merged image is missing location information. I need to attach the correct WGS 84 / UTM zone 33N coordinate reference to the file so that it aligns precisely with existing field plots and can be used for further analysis.

The county survey office has received a GeoTIFF orthomosaic produced from last week’s drone flight over the river valley. The file currently lacks any coordinate reference information, so it cannot be aligned with other local maps or used for distance measurements. We need to attach the official state-plane coordinate system (NAD83 / California Zone III) to the image so that it can be viewed in its correct geographic location and shared with partner agencies.

Our drone survey just delivered a high-resolution orthophoto covering the new industrial park. As part of a national climate-impact study, we have received a set of GeoTIFF files showing projected monthly rainfall totals from a regional climate model. The files were exported without location reference details, so the rainfall grids are not aligned with any standard map. We need to attach the correct European Terrestrial Reference System 1997 (ETRS89 / LAEA) location information to each raster so that the rainfall layers can be displayed and compared consistently with other geographic datasets across the continent.

A set of downscaled climate-model temperature rasters archived by the national meteorological service lacks proper location reference information; provide the correct world-wide grid definition so the layers align with other spatial datasets in the ongoing Climate-Model Raster Post-processing project.

To share a high-resolution elevation model (.tif) with external contractors, the dataset must first be given the correct map reference so it aligns properly with other maps they will use. Please attach the official UTM Zone 33N coordinate details to the raster before forwarding it.

A local government has received a GeoTIFF file of the city’s elevation model from a survey contractor. Before forwarding the dataset to engineering firms for infrastructure planning, the office needs to embed the official city coordinate reference into the raster’s metadata so that every downstream user can display and measure the elevation surface in perfect register with the other municipal layers.
Tool: Round raster\nAlgorithm ID: native: A 1 m resolution elevation model supplied as a GeoTIFF is too detailed for a 1:100,000 scale relief-shaded base map; the heights need to be simplified to the nearest 50 m so the terrain appears smoother and file size is reduced.

To prepare a 1 m resolution digital elevation model (GeoTIFF) from airborne LiDAR for regional relief shading, the elevation values need to be simplified to the nearest 5 m interval so that the resulting hill-shade appears smoother and more readable at 1:100 000 scale.

We are preparing a regional land-cover probability map for a climate-impact study. To keep the subsequent regional model computationally tractable, we need to simplify these continuous probability values into coarser, easily interpreted classes. Specifically, we would like every cell value to be rounded to the nearest multiple of 5 % so that the resulting layer groups similar probabilities without altering the original data type.

A regional climate-impact study needs a simplified version of a 30 m land-cover probability raster (GeoTIFF) that expresses each cell’s chance of being forest, shrub, or grass to the nearest 5 % so that the subsequent modelling workflow runs faster while keeping the thematic detail intelligible.

To prepare the temperature-anomaly GeoTIFF for the national climate atlas, we need to simplify the pixel values so they fall on clean 0.5 °C steps (e.g., –2.0, –1.5, –1.0 …) while keeping the file format and spatial resolution unchanged.

The national meteorological service is compiling a climate atlas and has a GeoTIFF of monthly temperature anomalies (°C, 64-bit float) that contains values such as 1.37, –0.84, 2.03, etc. To make the colour scale in the atlas clearer and easier to read, they need the anomaly grid simplified so every cell is expressed to the nearest half-degree (multiples of 0.5 °C) while keeping the original file format and extent.

A regional geological survey team has produced a floating-point GeoTIFF showing continuous landslide-susceptibility scores for every 10 m cell across a mountainous province. A regional geological survey team has produced a high-resolution GeoTIFF showing landslide susceptibility across a mountain district, with each cell containing a continuous probability score between 0 and 1. To prepare the layer for municipal planning documents that require simple low/medium/high susceptibility labels, the team needs to convert every cell value into the nearest ten-percent step (0.1, 0.2, … 1.0) so the map can be coloured and interpreted quickly without decimal clutter.

A national park service is preparing a high-resolution elevation GeoTIFF (1 m cell size, floating-point) for offline use on rangers’ tablets. A provincial forestry service wants to generalise a 1 m elevation GeoTIFF so that field crews can read heights quickly on their tablets without being distracted by centimetre-level detail. The layer will still be used for on-screen reference only, so keeping it as a floating-point file is acceptable. Tool: Split with lines\nAlgorithm ID: qg: A national highway authority possesses a single .shp file showing the entire inter-urban road network and another .shp file holding the boundaries of all provinces.
